# "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." Apple's verdict, by contrast, went Epic's way only in part.


---


# The store–billing relation: how Epic v. Google's two findings form one loop

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.


---


# Google's rebuttal to Epic: open Android and you hurt its users and its competitiveness

Opposing the remedy Epic Games sought at the trial that began November 6th, 2023 — breaking up Google's control of Android app distribution and in-app payment processing so developers stop paying the "Google tax" — Google argued, as reported by The Verge on November 5, 2023, that a win for Epic would rebound against Android itself. In Google's telling, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps. It would also damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone, because it (arguably) can't run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. The safety and competitiveness predictions are Google's own claims about a hypothetical outcome, not established findings, and The Verge flags them as such with "according to Google, anyhow."


---


# Google's counter-argument: iPhone substitution, not Android app stores, defines the market

Google rebutted Epic's market definition in Epic v. Google — which went to trial on Nov. 6, 2023, some 1,180 days after Epic first sued — by arguing the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. On that view, Google's app store competes with Apple's across platforms, so it is "pretty tough to argue Google has a monopoly on app stores in general." Epic's contrary position: Android app distribution and Android in-app payment processing are each their own market.


---


# Epic v. Google's outcome hinges on which market the court defines

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, the trial's outcome turns on the market definition the court adopts — the line of argument The Verge names "market definition." If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google's on the road to victory, since Google argues the real competition is Apple and buyers can choose an iPhone instead. If it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape; Epic claims illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." The hypothesis is falsified by whichever definition the judge records, including a different one entirely, as the judge in the Apple case ended up picking.


---


# Google argues its Play commission pays for more than billing

In Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023, Google contests the framing that the 15% to 30% commission it charges app developers on the sales it processes through Google Play's required first-party billing system is payment-processing markup. Its argument is that the commission instead funds other features and controls that keep Android users safe and guide them toward discovering new applications, plus the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google claims credit for reach beyond the mobile phone too: Android support across platforms, ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. It narrows the burden by noting that 99% of its developers qualify for a commission of 15% or less, based on their revenues.


---


# Market Definition in Epic v. Google: Narrow Android Market vs. All Smartphones

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, "market definition" is the name The Verge gives to the question that decides the case: a monopoly on what? Epic claims Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing", so anyone who buys or develops for Android phones is stuck paying the "Google tax". Google answers that the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. The same conduct is lawful or unlawful depending on the boundary drawn: if the court holds the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, Google is "on the road to victory"; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic is in better shape. The court could also pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in Epic's Apple case did.


---


# Index: The Verge's "Epic v. Google, explained" (Sean Hollister, 2023-11-05)

Navigation for "Epic v. Google, explained," Sean Hollister's reader-facing explainer at The Verge, published 2023-11-05 ahead of the trial that opened November 6th — "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued"; Hollister appended a December 15th, 2023 update marking it superseded. Notes grouped by the question each answers:

- **Background — the August 13th, 2020 trigger**: Epic's hotfix letting Fortnite V-Bucks be bought at a discount outside app store fees, Apple and Google pulling Fortnite, Epic's two lawsuits and the "Llamacorn" attack ad.
- **Competing legal claims**: Epic's monopoly and Play-payments-tying allegations versus Google's sideloaded-app-safety and free-app-store defenses.
- **Market definition**: "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing" versus phones and app stores generally.
- **Apple-case precedent**: the September 2021 ruling mostly in Apple's favor, with the Supreme Court possibly weighing in.


---


# Google's Competition Defense: App Stores Rivaling Google Play

Google plans to push back against Epic's claim that it faces no competition in the app store business. It will argue that Google Play competes with Apple's App Store — a rivalry that the Ninth Circuit ruling in the Apple case agreed upon, too. Beyond that, Google will point out that Android also supports competitive app stores, specifically Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore. This counters Epic's assertion that Google restrains competition in the market for distributing apps to Android users. Epic's anticipated response is that Google makes it hard for those alternative app stores to succeed and reach consumers.

Related to: How Google Play Billing and User Choice Billing work; The Epic Games v. Google antitrust trial of 2023


---


# Epic's Android App Distribution Monopoly Claim Against Google

In Epic Games' antitrust suit against Google, whose trial began on November 6th, 2023, Epic's core argument concerns Android app distribution. Epic argues that Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that Google has created an illegal monopoly. The claimed harms are twofold: the monopoly unjustly enriches Google, and it artificially drives up app prices, because other app stores can't compete. Epic calls the standard in-app payment fees the "Google tax". The remedy Epic seeks is to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods, so that developers aren't stuck paying that tax or passing the fee along to players.

Source: The Verge, "Epic v. Google, explained" (2023-11-05).

This TechCrunch roundup of November 13, 2023 indexes five sections. Under an agreement Google reached with the Canadian government in November 2023 — the month before the Helena World Chronicle class action was filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. on 2023-12-15 — the search giant will pay Canadian media for use of their content. qid: Does the TechCrunch article discussing Meta's moderation bias problem suggest a similar impact on users compared to the TechCrunch article on Meta's proposed legislation for teen app downloads, with the former affecting Palestinian voices and the latter concerning parental oversight of teen social media usage?
context:
# Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." That denial of motive does not reach the documented record: a lengthy history of incidents reflecting inherent bias in Meta's processes, from both inside and outside the company, plus a third-party report Meta commissioned after the 2021 Hamas-Israel violence finding an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Calling removals a "bug" localizes harm to a single defect, while the bias here is distributed across language coverage, policy architecture, and escalation channels.


---


# Meta's suppression of Palestinian content is structural bias, not a bug — TechCrunch, 19 Oct 2023

TechCrunch's claim on 19 Oct 2023: Instagram's shadowbanning of Palestine-related content is "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes," not the technical error Meta invokes. Meta says it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated 18 Oct, insists "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." The assembled warrants make intent beside the point. Meta cannot navigate Arabic's over 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversifying language resources. Its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuance, such as content discussing violence without condoning it. Partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Enforcement tracks user reports: filmmaker Khitam Jabr lost 24 hours of posting on West Bank travel Reels she says drew anti-Palestine comments and reports. And during the 2021 Hamas–Israel outbreak, a report Meta commissioned from a third party concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation.


---


# Hypothesis: Meta's government agency partnerships bias moderation against Palestinian expression

A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

The hypothesis is falsified if removal and restriction rates for comparable Palestine-related content show no association with escalation in those agency channels: more reports or referrals routed through partner agencies, but unchanged enforcement rates, would sever the claimed link.

Scope: Meta's platforms, notably Instagram, in the period following Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade of Gaza.


---


# Index: Meta's Moderation of Palestinian Voices (TechCrunch, 19 October 2023)

This document (doc_0106) is TechCrunch's 19 October 2023 report that Instagram users suspect Meta of shadowbanning — that is, limiting the visibility of — content about Palestine. Its definitional material covers shadowbanning and black-and-white policy design. Its structural-bias mechanisms include Meta's thin Arabic language resources (a language with over 25 dialects) and partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, set against Meta's ban on content supporting Hamas, designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union. Case material covers filmmaker Khitam Jabr's 24-hour restrictions and Bella Hadid's Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Counter-argument material carries Meta communications director Andy Stone's rebuttals and the Oct. 18 newsroom statement, plus the 2021 third-party human rights report behind the bias-versus-bug dispute.


---


# Meta's "bug" explanation cannot account for a multi-year pattern of restrictions on Palestinian content

Meta attributed the October 2023 Instagram shadowbanning complaints to a bug affecting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts. That single-incident technical account doesn't fit the pattern TechCrunch described on Oct. 19, 2023: the accusations were "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents" on Meta platforms reflecting an inherent bias against Palestinian users, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company, and involving restrictions on content that never supported Hamas. Meta's own commissioned third-party report, issued during the 2021 Hamas–Israel violence, concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. Meta also blamed technical errors for removing posts about Palestine during that 2021 conflict.


---


# Meta's Counter: Andy Stone Attributes Reduced Story Reach to a Bug, Not Bias

Against the accusation that Instagram shadowbanned Stories about Palestine in October 2023, Meta communications director Andy Stone attributed the reduced reach to a technical fault rather than moderation policy. In a Threads post, he wrote, "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts" — meaning the limitation reached every account doing that, wherever located, irrespective of subject matter, and was corrected quickly. Stone declined to comment on the record for TechCrunch's story, dated 2023-10-19, and pointed to Meta's newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, which stated that Meta applies its policies "equally around the world" and that "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." Meta had likewise blamed technical errors for removals of Palestine posts during the 2021 conflict.


---


# Meta-Commissioned Third-Party Report Found Adverse Human Rights Impact on Palestinian Users in 2021

During the 2021 Hamas-Israel escalation, a third-party report commissioned by Meta concluded that the company's own actions had produced an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation. The finding, cited in a TechCrunch article published Oct. 19, 2023, is significant because Meta itself paid for the assessment, making it an internally sourced acknowledgment rather than an external allegation. Meta separately attributed its 2021 content removals to technical errors.


---


# Meta's rebuttal to deliberate suppression of Palestinian voices: equal policy application and appeals

In its 19 October 2023 TechCrunch report on suspected Instagram shadowbanning of Palestine content, Meta's counter-argument came via communications director Andy Stone, who declined to comment on the record and pointed instead to Meta's newsroom post on the conflict, updated 18 October 2023. That post states: "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice … We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it." Meta added that it may inadvertently flag content but never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."


---


# Black-and-White Moderation Policy

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it." Content that describes violence without endorsing it fits neither the "allowed" nor the "banned" category cleanly, so it tends to be mis-flagged or removed. Meta was additionally criticized in the article for struggling with Arabic's cultural and linguistic nuances, a language with over 25 dialects.

# "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." In *US v. Google* on September 26, 2023, Meagan Bellshaw, a Justice Department lawyer, pressed Eddy Cue on Apple's defence that iPhone setup covers "just critical stuff" and that showing people a bunch of search engines would be a bad user experience. Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:

Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, Eddy Cue testified on 2023-09-26 about what a "default search engine" means in practice: the engine preselected on a device, which a user must actively change rather than choose. qid: Has the perspective on the US economy's risk of entering a recession as reported by The Sydney Morning Herald changed between the article published on October 1, 2023, and the one published on December 5, 2023?
context:
# Fed's data-dependence at risk if US economic reports get postponed

Stated as a hypothesis: postponements of scheduled US economic reports could undermine the Federal Reserve's insistence that it will make its upcoming interest-rate decisions based on what incoming data say about the economy.

Testable because of the reporting calendar itself, per The Sydney Morning Herald on 2023-10-01: the latest monthly update on the US jobs market is due the week after that date, with a couple of important inflation reports coming the following week, and the Fed's next meeting on rates ends on November 1.

Falsification condition: if the Fed's October–November guidance tracks the published data cleanly, the postponements have not impaired its stated data-dependent approach, and the hypothesis fails.


---


# US Economic Data Calendar After 1 October 2023: Jobs, Inflation, and the Fed Meeting

As reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 1 October 2023, the latest monthly update on the US jobs market was due the following week, with a couple of important reports on inflation coming the week after that. The Federal Reserve's next meeting on interest rates ends on 1 November 2023. The Fed has insisted it will make upcoming rate decisions based on what incoming data say about the economy.


---


# Jacobsen's three drags on US consumer spending, October 2023

Brian Jacobsen, chief economist at Annex Wealth Management, identified three factors that in combination depressed the growth of US consumer spending in late 2023: higher energy prices, student loan debt repayments, and "real disposable incomes that have been on a declining trajectory since June". His verdict on the trio was blunt — it "doesn't bode well". He described the slowdown of US consumer spending growth as having "come to a boil during a hot summer, and the temperature is really starting to come down". The written opinion was reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 1 October 2023. Supporting the first factor, US crude settled at $US90.79 a barrel on the Friday before, down 92¢ that day but far above the $US70 of June, at the highest level in more than a year. The article dated this assessment to the 29 September 2023 close, when August data showed US consumer spending growth cooler than expected alongside slightly cooler inflation — a reading positive for inflation but a risk to the spending that had kept the US economy out of recession, since resumed US student-loan repayments diverted dollars away from purchases.


---


# Cooler US consumer spending cuts both ways: easing inflation, weakening growth

Economic data released Friday and reported on 1 October 2023 showed growth in spending by US consumers was cooler than expected in August, alongside inflation that was also a touch cooler than expected. That slowdown runs in two opposing directions. Fewer dollars pouring into purchases eases demand-pull pressure, giving companies less encouragement to try to raise prices further and supporting the Federal Reserve's attempt to push still-high inflation down to its target. But softer consumption may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession. Brian Jacobsen, chief economist at Annex Wealth Management, said spending growth had "come to a boil during a hot summer" and was cooling, citing higher energy prices, student-loan repayments and real disposable incomes declining since June.


---


# ASX set to open lower, 1 October 2023 briefing: contents index

The Sydney Morning Herald market briefing of 1 October 2023, "ASX set to open lower as Wall Street closes September with more losses", opens with the day's largest local decliners — Treasury Wine Estates (down 1.9 per cent), Woolworths (down 1.2 per cent) in a consumer staples sector down 1.1 per cent, Pilbara Minerals (down 2.1 per cent) and Qantas (down 1.5 per cent) — then its "The lowdown" section covers iron ore strength, the RBA's Tuesday meeting and NAB's November hike forecast to 4.35 per cent. Follow-on sections track Wall Street's September close, the Treasury-yield mechanism, US inflation and consumer-spending data, oil, the US economic calendar and single stocks. The trailing "Tweek of the day" and "Quote of the day" placeholders are empty in the source.


---


# Hypothesis: resumed US student-loan repayments divert household dollars from consumption

Hypothesis, as reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 2023-10-01: the resumption of US student-loan repayments may funnel dollars away from the consumer spending that has helped keep the US economy afloat, so post-September retail and personal-consumption data should decelerate in a way attributable to debt repayment. It would be falsified if those releases show no such deceleration. Supporting logic in the source: spending growth cooled in August alongside cooler inflation, and Brian Jacobsen of Annex Wealth Management cited student loan debt repayments among factors slowing a hot summer.

Word count check: ~95 words.


---


# NAB's forecast of an RBA hike to 4.35 per cent in November 2023

In a report covered by The Sydney Morning Herald on 2023-10-01, the National Australia Bank forecasts the Reserve Bank of Australia will lift the cash rate again in November 2023, to 4.35 per cent. The forecast sits against the market expectation cited in the same article that the RBA will keep rates on hold at its October meeting, with interest-rate sensitive sectors such as healthcare and consumer companies among the weakest on that view.

The proposition is falsifiable by the RBA's November 2023 decision: either the cash rate moves to 4.35 per cent, or it does not.


---


# Treasury yield as the anchor for what investors pay for stocks

Treasury bonds are regarded as some of the safest investments available, so the yield they pay is the return investors can obtain without taking equity risk. That makes the Treasury yield the reference price for risk assets: when that yield rises, investors are less likely to pay high prices for stocks and other riskier investments, and equity prices fall. The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 1 October 2023 that this mechanism was a big reason the S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent. In the session described, the 10-year Treasury yield returned to 4.58 per cent after dipping to 4.52 per cent, again near its highest level since 2007.


---


# S&P 500 fell 4.9 per cent in September 2023, leaving 2023 up only 11.7 per cent

The S&P 500 dropped 4.9 per cent in September 2023, dragging what had been a big gain for the year down to 11.7 per cent, according to a Sydney Morning Herald report filed on 1 October 2023. Wall Street closed out its worst month and quarter of the year. Rising US Treasury yields were cited as a big reason: the 10-year returned to 4.58 per cent, near its highest level since 2007.


---


# European indexes modestly higher as Asian exchanges closed, 29 September 2023

In overseas sharemarkets on 29 September 2023, indexes finished modestly higher in Europe, while exchanges were closed across much of Asia. The European gain sat in contrast to Wall Street, which had closed the month with further losses after its worst month and quarter of the year. The report was published by The Sydney Morning Herald on 1 October 2023.


---


# Oil prices at a one-year-plus high in early October 2023 despite a 92-cent US crude fall

Oil prices jumped to their highest level in more than a year as of 1 October 2023, according to The Sydney Morning Herald, pressuring the US economy by raising fuel costs for everyone. A barrel of US crude sank 92¢ on Friday 29 September 2023 to settle at $US90.79, but that price remained up sharply from about $US70 in June 2023. Brent crude, the international standard, also weakened on 29 September 2023. S&P 500 energy stocks fell 2 per cent that day, more than double the loss of any other sector.

# Hypothesis: Meta's government agency partnerships bias moderation against Palestinian expression

A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

Scope: Meta's platforms, notably Instagram, in the period following Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade of Gaza.

"Featured Snippets" are a Google search feature in which Google algorithmically extracts answers directly from webpages and surfaces them above ordinary results. In the class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C., reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, these Snippets are cited alongside older question-and-answer tools like the Knowledge Graph (launched May 2012) as technologies shifting traffic away from publishers' websites rather than sending readers to them.

# Silva's vegan-keyword search and his light bulb moment about Google presence

Felix Silva, owner of Barber Shop Near Me in Coral Springs, Florida, frequently searches Google for keywords like "vegan" to find restaurants. One time, Google returned results for a restaurant that wasn't vegan but had a customer review containing the keyword, highlighted.

"It was a light bulb moment… like, 'Okay, this is the path I need to take. I really need to dial in and focus on the online presence, specifically Google, because that is going to be the foundation of the business," Silva said, as reported by The Verge on 2023-10-26.

The anecdote is his own demonstration that a business's Google presence, not its actual offering, decides what turns up in search.

# SEO's Spread Has Made Ordinary Searches commercially Shaped (The Verge, 2023)

Reporting for The Verge on 2023-11-01 argues that the harm from search engine optimization is no longer confined to sites built for it. The article states that "over time, SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up 'sneaker' in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike." By 2023, users described Google Search results as "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." Since Google holds a 90 percent market share for online search, that commercial shaping reaches nearly every informational query, destroying "the illusion that the internet was ever about anything other than selling stuff."

# Meta's suppression of Palestinian content is structural bias, not a bug — TechCrunch, 19 Oct 2023

TechCrunch's claim on 19 Oct 2023: Instagram's shadowbanning of Palestine-related content is "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes," not the technical error Meta invokes. Meta says it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated 18 Oct, insists "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." The assembled warrants make intent beside the point. Meta cannot navigate Arabic's over 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversifying language resources. Its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuance, such as content discussing violence without condoning it. Partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Enforcement tracks user reports: filmmaker Khitam Jabr lost 24 hours of posting on West Bank travel Reels she says drew anti-Palestine comments and reports. And during the 2021 Hamas–Israel outbreak, a report Meta commissioned from a third party concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation.


---


# The "winter break hypothesis" for ChatGPT's December performance decline

The "winter break hypothesis" is a user-proposed explanation, circulating in December 2023, for why ChatGPT appeared to worsen in quality at year's end. It argues that AI is worse in December because it "learned" to do less work over the holidays, having absorbed seasonal patterns of reduced human labor from its training data.

The hypothesis arose because, starting in November 2023, ChatGPT users noticed the chatbot felt "lazier" than normal, citing instances of simpler answers and refusing to complete requested tasks. OpenAI confirmed on December 8, 2023 that it was aware of the complaints about GPT-4 getting lazier, stated it hadn't updated the model since November 11, 2023, and said the behavior "certainly isn't intentional" and unpredictable, and that it was looking into fixing it. Sporting News' December 5, 2023 guidance on NFL award longshots (MVP, OPOY, DPOY, Coach of the Year, Comeback Player of the Year) is to keep the stake small, or to use a promotional bonus bet if one is available at the sportsbook. The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.

# Futures Odds Diverge Across Sportsbooks Because of Liability, So Timing Matters

In a guide to line shopping published by Sporting News on 2023-11-06, a model of sportsbook pricing explains why futures are the exception to the usual uniformity of odds. Most game lines are similar at different sportsbooks, but the odds in futures markets can vary significantly. The mechanism is liability: sportsbooks sometimes have higher liabilities for specific teams and offer better odds on others to lay that off. Timing is everything. Getting it right lets a bettor take advantage of changes in different futures markets due to liability, and the only way to find these opportunities is shopping lines.

# Market Definition in Epic v. Google: Narrow Android Market vs. All Smartphones

In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, "market definition" is the name The Verge gives to the question that decides the case: a monopoly on what? Epic claims Google holds illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing", so anyone who buys or develops for Android phones is stuck paying the "Google tax". Google answers that the real competition is Apple, because people can choose to buy an iPhone instead. The same conduct is lawful or unlawful depending on the boundary drawn: if the court holds the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, Google is "on the road to victory"; if it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic is in better shape. The court could also pick a different market definition entirely, as the judge in Epic's Apple case did.

# Google argues its Play commission pays for more than billing

In Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began November 6, 2023, Google contests the framing that the 15% to 30% commission it charges app developers on the sales it processes through Google Play's required first-party billing system is payment-processing markup. Its argument is that the commission instead funds other features and controls that keep Android users safe and guide them toward discovering new applications, plus the tools and services developers need to build and grow their apps. Google claims credit for reach beyond the mobile phone too: Android support across platforms, ranging from tablets to TVs to autos and more. In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, the trial's outcome turns on the market definition the court adopts — the line of argument The Verge names "market definition." If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google's on the road to victory, since Google argues the real competition is Apple and buyers can choose an iPhone instead. If it accepts that Android apps are their own market, Epic will be in better shape; Epic claims illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." Epic Games' claim against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, rests on one argument: Google's agreements with Android device manufacturers and app developers are anticompetitive restraints under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act and under California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law, regardless of whether Android permits sideloading.

That sideloading point matters because it distinguishes this case from Epic's suit against Apple, where Epic alleged there was no other way to load apps. Here Android does allow sideloading, so Epic contends those agreements — not the absence of alternatives — are what restrain competition in two markets: distribution of apps to Android users, and payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps. Epic cites Anti-Fragmentation Agreements blocking OEMs from modifying Android for frictionless downloading outside Google Play, through which 90% of apps are still downloaded.

He offered a figure jurors would hear often — "$360 million" — described as an alleged payment that kept Activision from opening an app store that could compete with Google Play, alongside payments to game developers not to build their own app stores or standalone app launchers like Epic did with Fortnite. The result, in his framing: a status quo where the vast, vast majority of Android app installs are from Google Play, with only a tiny sliver attributable to the Galaxy Store preinstalled on every Samsung phone.

Google plans to push back against Epic's claim that it faces no competition in the app store business. Beyond that, Google will point out that Android also supports competitive app stores, specifically Samsung's Galaxy Store and Amazon's Appstore. This counters Epic's assertion that Google restrains competition in the market for distributing apps to Android users. Epic's anticipated response is that Google makes it hard for those alternative app stores to succeed and reach consumers.

Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued — Epic Games names two markets in which it alleges Google holds illegal monopolies: "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." # Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. # NAB's forecast of an RBA hike to 4.35 per cent in November 2023

The forecast sits against the market expectation cited in the same article that the RBA will keep rates on hold at its October meeting, with interest-rate sensitive sectors such as healthcare and consumer companies among the weakest on that view.

The proposition is falsifiable by the RBA's November 2023 decision: either the cash rate moves to 4.35 per cent, or it does not.

# Fed's data-dependence at risk if US economic reports get postponed

Stated as a hypothesis: postponements of scheduled US economic reports could undermine the Federal Reserve's insistence that it will make its upcoming interest-rate decisions based on what incoming data say about the economy.

Testable because of the reporting calendar itself, per The Sydney Morning Herald on 2023-10-01: the latest monthly update on the US jobs market is due the week after that date, with a couple of important inflation reports coming the following week, and the Fed's next meeting on rates ends on November 1.

Falsification condition: if the Fed's October–November guidance tracks the published data cleanly, the postponements have not impaired its stated data-dependent approach, and the hypothesis fails.

# "Higher-for-longer": the market's assumption that central banks hold rates elevated rather than cut quickly

"Higher-for-longer" names the market's assumption that a central bank keeps policy rates elevated well past the near term instead of cutting quickly — as Sydney Morning Herald reporting on 2023-10-01 put it, "Wall Street accepts a new normal where the Federal Reserve is likely to keep interest rates high for longer."

The concept describes expectations, not announced policy. Anchors cited then: the US Federal Reserve's main rate at its highest level since 2001, with the central bank signalling in the week before that it may cut in 2024 by less than earlier expected, and its next rate meeting ending November 1. In Australia, the RBA was expected to hold at its Tuesday meeting, with National Australia Bank forecasting another hike to 4.35 per cent in November.

As reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 1 October 2023, the latest monthly update on the US jobs market was due the following week, with a couple of important reports on inflation coming the week after that. # The Fed's transmission mechanism: high rates slow the economy and depress asset prices

As of October 1, 2023, the Federal Reserve is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target. Its main tool, high interest rates, does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated in the week before October 1, 2023 that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The associated rate-holding stance is described as "higher for longer."

# Interest-rate-sensitive sectors: equities priced off the policy rate

An interest-rate-sensitive sector is an equity grouping whose share prices move more than the market when the policy rate changes, because its cash flows are long-dated or its customers depend on credit. Rates rising compress valuations in both cases, since higher yields on government debt make riskier assets less attractive at any price.

In The Sydney Morning Herald's reporting of 1 October 2023, healthcare and consumer companies were named among the weakest sectors on the ASX as markets expected the RBA to keep rates on hold, with National Australia Bank forecasting another hike to 4.35 per cent in November. Economic data released Friday and reported on 1 October 2023 showed growth in spending by US consumers was cooler than expected in August, alongside inflation that was also a touch cooler than expected. Fewer dollars pouring into purchases eases demand-pull pressure, giving companies less encouragement to try to raise prices further and supporting the Federal Reserve's attempt to push still-high inflation down to its target. Guidance issued by the U.K. Judicial Office permits judges in the United Kingdom to use ChatGPT, along with other AI tools, to write legal rulings and perform court duties. TechCrunch records the item in the December 2023 section of its running ChatGPT timeline, in an article dated 2023-09-28 and updated afterward. The guidance also lays out ways to use AI responsibly in the courts; the two measures TechCrunch names are being aware of potential bias and upholding privacy. TechCrunch's account is abbreviated: it does not reproduce the full set of conditions the Judicial Office attached to the permission, so the boundaries of what a U.K. judge may automate in a ruling cannot be settled from this source alone.


---


# Black-and-White Moderation Policy

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it." Content that describes violence without endorsing it fits neither the "allowed" nor the "banned" category cleanly, so it tends to be mis-flagged or removed. Meta was additionally criticized in the article for struggling with Arabic's cultural and linguistic nuances, a language with over 25 dialects.


---


# Axel Springer licenses its news content to OpenAI, week of 15 December 2023

In the week of 15 December 2023, German publisher Axel Springer signed a deal with OpenAI to license its news for AI model training, a TechCrunch article on that date reported. The agreement was cited as one example of publishers "trying to get ahead of" the threat that AI-powered search poses to their traffic. In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.

# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.

Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. In the U.S. antitrust trial over Google's search dominance, CEO Sundar Pichai defended what Google spends on default placement with a self-reinforcing account of why the money is justified. Being the default on other companies' browsers, phones and platforms produces more searches; more searches mean more data taken in; more data make Google the best engine across those devices; and being the best explains why partners choose it and why further default payments are reasonable. TechCrunch reported this on 2023-10-31, describing Pichai's testimony that Monday, two days after search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on 2023-10-28 that Google had paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default placement. Pichai added that the decision was made with the consumer in mind. The loop is Google's own testimony about its motives, not an independently established causal finding, and the government contests its premise.

# Index — Five revelations from the Google antitrust trial, 30–31 October 2023

A breakdown published by TechCrunch on 30–31 October 2023, anchored on Google CEO Sundar Pichai's Monday testimony in the U.S. government's antitrust trial over Google's 2020-era search dominance, organizes the week's disclosures into five points.

1. Default-payment totals: $26.3 billion paid in 2021 across browsers, phones and platforms including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, roughly $18 billion of it to Apple, per search head Prabhakar Raghavan's 28 October testimony.
2. The Chrome-promotion ban: Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users.
3. The iPhone preinstall bid: Pichai's 2018 attempt to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device.
4. Deleted chat logs: history-off default vs. the DOJ's litigation hold.
5. Google's early letter on defaults: a 2007 email citing 15% and 27% swings.

# Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

# 2024 AI industry consolidation hypothesis: most 2023 AI products will not survive

TechCrunch's 2023-12-19 predictions piece "8 predictions for AI in 2024" hypothesizes that 2023's AI products "will not all survive by a long shot," even while underlying capabilities "continue to grow and advance." # AI Tool Customer Withdrawal Predicted for 2024 as Marketing Claims Face Review

In an article published 2023-12-19 on TechCrunch, the hypothesis is advanced that a considerable customer withdrawal from AI tools will occur during 2024. The reasoning is that marketing claims made for machine learning systems—often adopted by companies merely to avoid falling behind—will face their quarterly and yearly reviews, and will very likely be found wanting. The measurable benefits will fail to justify the costs and risks involved. On the far end of this spectrum, lawsuits and regulatory action against AI service providers that cannot back up their claims are anticipated as a consequence of the same dynamic.

Publishers believe they will lose somewhere between 20-40% of their website traffic when Google's AI products fully roll out, according to The Wall Street Journal's report as relayed in a TechCrunch article dated 2023-12-15. # AI's Central Debate Framed as Control or Freedom

In "How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence" (The Age, 9 December 2023), the argument about AI is framed as a single either/or question: whether the technology "should be controlled or set free." That choice rests on a prior uncertainty — whether AI "will elevate the world or destroy it – or at least inflict grave damage." The framing organises an ongoing debate among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators, and pits some of the world's richest men against one another: Musk, Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI.


---


# OpenAI as the pivot of AI's control-versus-freedom argument

In *The Age*'s report of 2023-12-09, "How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence," the argument over whether AI "should be controlled or set free" is shown to run through OpenAI rather than through the abstract idea of the technology. The reason is ChatGPT: thanks to that chatbot, OpenAI "has fundamentally changed the technology industry and has introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence." A lab valued at more than $US80 billion ($A123 billion) thereby became the shared reference point for a debate conducted among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators, and one that pits Elon Musk, Larry Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI against one another.

The claim is tested by what happened inside that same company months later, when rebel board members tried to force out Altman on the belief they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity. Over five chaotic days, the control-versus-freedom argument stopped being a policy abstractions and turned into a single boardroom confrontation, one whose outcome giant investors and employees threatening to follow Altman out the door ultimately reversed when the board backed down. That episode "gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI" — and confirms the argument's logic: because OpenAI made both the promise and the hazard legible at once, every contest over AI's direction is now conducted by reference to it.


---


# Hypothesis: Apple ships its AI under the Siri brand, not a new one

Testable claim drawn from a TechCrunch predictions piece dated 2023-12-19: Apple will release its AI in 2024 under the existing Siri brand rather than launching a separately named service such as "Apple AI", because the incumbency of "hey Siri" voice habits outweighs that assistant's reputation for mediocrity. The reasoning sits on the article's observation that Apple has an established pattern of waiting, watching and learning from other companies' failures, then arriving with a refined and polished take that puts others to shame, and that the timing is right partly because waiting too long risks competitors eating up the market. Falsified if Apple introduces a distinct AI brand.


---


# Big Tech will push AI into existing product lines in 2024, but less aggressively than OpenAI

Hypothesis (TechCrunch, 2023-12-19): the trend of embedding AI directly into established product lines, expected at OpenAI after Sam Altman took fuller control following the November leadership shake-up, will also spread to other major companies running AI programs in 2024. The cited example: Gemini/Bard predicted to "horn in on a ton of Google products."

The prediction carries a bound — the author suspects the AI-into-products push "will be more pronounced in this case," meaning OpenAI, whose caution and academic reserve, worn down by the previous board, give way to an unseemly lust for markets and customers.

---


# Altman: Ego and Conflict Grow With Shared Purpose, Not Opposition

Sam Altman's argument is that disagreement, mistrust and ego intensify with proximity of purpose rather than fading as people agree more. "There is disagreement, mistrust, egos," Altman said in The Age's survey of AI's founders published 9 December 2023. "The closer people are to being pointed in the same direction, the more contentious the disagreements are. You see this in sects and religious orders. There are bitter fights between the closest people." The consequence for artificial intelligence: its sharpest disputes should be expected among collaborators pursuing the same goal, not between the camps that openly oppose each other. That claim's own test case arrived in November 2023, when rebel OpenAI board members tried to force Altman out over trust, and the fight lasted five chaotic days at a company valued at more than $US80 billion ($A123 billion).


---


# 2024 ROI Reviews Will Find Hyped Machine-Learning Purchases Wanting

Hypothesis from TechCrunch's "8 predictions for AI in 2024" (published 2023-12-19): the hype built up in 2023 will be very hard for companies to follow through on. Machine-learning systems that enterprises adopted specifically in order to not fall behind carry vendor marketing claims, and those claims will face their quarterly and yearly reviews during 2024 — where, the authors expect, they will very likely be found wanting. The mechanism is reassessment, not a sudden drop in capability.

Falsified if enterprise reassessments broadly validate the vendors' 2023 claims and the purchased ML features pass their quarterly and yearly ROI reviews.


---


# Contents of the supplied excerpt of TechCrunch's "8 predictions for AI in 2024" (2023-12-19)

The supplied excerpt of TechCrunch's 2023-12-19 article "8 predictions for AI in 2024" carries six prediction sections, not the eight its title promises. Comparing NBA Rookie of the Year odds across every "online sportsbook" reachable on the open internet is unsound. # Steps to Open a Funded US Sportsbook Account Before Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures

Precondition (per Sporting News, 2023-10-04): you are in a US jurisdiction where online sportsbooks are legal. The source warns that offshore sportsbooks advertise widely but are illegal and offer no protection against fraud.

# Some Sports Betting Apps Copy Lines Rather Than Set Their Own

As of Sporting News' line-shopping guide dated 2023-11-06, sportsbook pricing is not uniform across the market. The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services, which use computer models and algorithms weighing analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps, by contrast, simply copy those lines rather than produce prices of their own.

# NBA Futures Markets Span the Whole Season, Including Rookie of the Year

NBA Rookie of the Year is one of the NBA futures markets, so wagering opens before the start of the NBA regular season and continues throughout the year, as with other NBA futures odds. # Sportsbook Opening Lines Come From Computer Models Run by Oddsmakers

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), the best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and dedicated oddsmaking services to produce their lines and odds. Those oddsmakers and oddsmaking services run computer models and algorithms that weigh analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, among other inputs, to develop the lines and odds before betting opens. Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. # The Fed's transmission mechanism: high rates slow the economy and depress asset prices

As of October 1, 2023, the Federal Reserve is trying to push still-high inflation down to its target. Its main tool, high interest rates, does that by trying to slow the economy and hurting prices for investments. The Fed's main interest rate is at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated in the week before October 1, 2023 that it may cut interest rates next year by less than it earlier expected. The associated rate-holding stance is described as "higher for longer."


---


# "Higher-for-longer": the market's assumption that central banks hold rates elevated rather than cut quickly

"Higher-for-longer" names the market's assumption that a central bank keeps policy rates elevated well past the near term instead of cutting quickly — as Sydney Morning Herald reporting on 2023-10-01 put it, "Wall Street accepts a new normal where the Federal Reserve is likely to keep interest rates high for longer."

The concept describes expectations, not announced policy. Anchors cited then: the US Federal Reserve's main rate at its highest level since 2001, with the central bank signalling in the week before that it may cut in 2024 by less than earlier expected, and its next rate meeting ending November 1. In Australia, the RBA was expected to hold at its Tuesday meeting, with National Australia Bank forecasting another hike to 4.35 per cent in November.

# Fed policy rate at highest since 2001 as 2024 cut expectations trimmed

As at the end of September 2023, the Federal Reserve's main interest rate stood at its highest level since 2001, and the central bank indicated the week before it may cut interest rates in 2024 by less than it had earlier expected. The forecast sits against the market expectation cited in the same article that the RBA will keep rates on hold at its October meeting, with interest-rate sensitive sectors such as healthcare and consumer companies among the weakest on that view.

The proposition is falsifiable by the RBA's November 2023 decision: either the cash rate moves to 4.35 per cent, or it does not.

# Rate-hold bets and higher-for-longer pricing weigh on ASX healthcare and consumer stocks

On 1 October 2023, *The Sydney Morning Herald* reported that most ASX sectors traded lower, but interest-rate-sensitive sectors — healthcare and consumer companies — were among the weakest, as the market priced in expectations that the Reserve Bank of Australia would keep rates on hold at its October meeting, with the RBA due to meet on Tuesday. # Interest-rate-sensitive sectors: equities priced off the policy rate

An interest-rate-sensitive sector is an equity grouping whose share prices move more than the market when the policy rate changes, because its cash flows are long-dated or its customers depend on credit. Rates rising compress valuations in both cases, since higher yields on government debt make riskier assets less attractive at any price.

In The Sydney Morning Herald's reporting of 1 October 2023, healthcare and consumer companies were named among the weakest sectors on the ASX as markets expected the RBA to keep rates on hold, with National Australia Bank forecasting another hike to 4.35 per cent in November. The 10-year US Treasury yield sat at 4.58 per cent, near its highest since 2007.

# Once a Bet Is Locked, a Moving Line Can Only Be Answered With New Action

Sporting News (November 6, 2023) states that when you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted. A wager already placed cannot be repriced if the market later moves in your favour, so the available procedure is to respond with fresh action rather than to revisit the original ticket. Because lines shift when the public bets heavily on one side, and because each sportsbook's book differs, a subsequent move usually appears as improved odds or a more favorable line somewhere else. The step is to place additional action there, at that new price.

# Why Line Shopping Pays for the Time It Costs

The argument for line shopping is a mismatch between what it gains and what it costs. Sporting News's guide "Line Shopping in Sports Betting – How to Find the Best Odds" (2023-11-06) puts the cost at "just seconds" when a bettor uses a live odds feed showing differences between sportsbooks, or longer when working manually by installing more than one sports betting app on a phone and tapping among them to compare.

The gain is larger. Betting volume is rarely the same at every sportsbook, so one may be forced to move a line or change odds while another is not; prices may also differ from the opening. Caesars Sportsbook's point spreads can be "a half-point to two points better than the competition's," and its moneyline odds may be more favorable. A half-point at that size changes which side of a posted number a spread wager settles on. As the guide puts it, shopping around lets a bettor "lay less, win more, and improve your chances."

# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.

The reasoning is that a player or several players have relatively short odds because they have been the best at their position all season, and there is just as good a reason why longshots carry odds as long as the ones they do. So the longshot's price reflects a genuine, not merely overlooked, case against it.

Sizing down, or staking money the bettor did not deposit, caps the loss on a low-probability outcome while leaving the payout upside intact: if the longshot goes on to win, the bettor collects the full odds on the original price rather than a shorter one obtained by waiting, since with five weeks left in the 2023 regular season a longshot can still become a contender, and the payout falls the longer the bet is deferred.

The class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 alleges evidence of improper spoliation by Google — specifically the destruction of chat messages. The complaint ties that allegation to a known precedent: the same issue of destroyed chat messages was raised in Epic Games' recent lawsuit against Google over app-store antitrust conduct, a case Epic won. The spoliation claim sits alongside the suit's other concerns, including allegedly changed AdSense rates, and appears among the counts supporting its requests for damages and injunctive relief against Google.

The Epic Games v. Google antitrust proceeding reads as a dated four-year chain rather than a single lawsuit. Its causal origin is a September 2019 email surfaced in discovery, describing Epic's plan to draw Google into a legal battle over antitrust — the document that predates and sets up everything after it. That plan became a four-week federal antitrust trial before a nine-person jury, which found on Monday, December 11, 2023 that Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems and illegally tied Google Play billing to its app store. - U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.

Epic v. Google went to trial on 2023-11-06, "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued," according to The Verge's 2023-11-05 explainer. This TechCrunch roundup of November 13, 2023 indexes five sections. First, why US v Google matters and the remedies at stake before Judge Amit Mehta: sharing APIs, bans on anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, and surrendering data — the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. Second, Google's concurrent antitrust matters: the Match Group settlement and the November 6 trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games over Google Play. # Epic's Google case rests on the Microsoft browser-monopoly precedent

Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google, which began on November 6, 2023 and concerns Google Play's app distribution and its 15% to 30% commissions, is analogically dependent on the Microsoft antitrust rulings, as reported by TechCrunch. In those earlier cases, courts found that Microsoft had a monopoly over the operating system and was abusing it by making it hard for users to download alternative browsers, like Netscape, on Windows devices. The analogy carries weight because Android, unlike Apple's iOS, permits sideloading — so Epic's theory of the case runs on a dominant platform owner's agreements constraining rivals rather than on the absence of any alternative.


---


# US v Google's ripple effect on parallel Big Tech antitrust cases

A ruling in US v Google may have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases, since enforcers need one landmark judgment to demonstrate antitrust law remains relevant. The parallel matters named in a TechCrunch roundup dated 2023-11-13: the FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power; the DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products; and there's an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, wherein the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp. The proposition is falsified if those cases proceed and settle unaffected by the Google judgment. Judge Amit Mehta hears the Google case.

# Sherman Act: the U.S. antitrust statute behind Epic's claims against Google

The Sherman Act is the U.S. antitrust statute Epic Games planned to invoke against Google at the trial that began November 6, 2023, taking Section 1 and Section 2 claims alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. Section 1 concerns restraints of competition; Section 2 concerns monopolization. Epic's case rested on arguing that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.

The Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021, and a ruling came down that September mostly in Apple's favor, with both parties still waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in. The Google suit never got its day in court during those years, delayed again and again, so that Epic v. Google trial beginning November 6th, 2023 arrived "a mere 1,180 days" after Epic filed, per The Verge's article dated 2023-11-05.

A Sporting News article on NFL award longshots, published December 5, 2023, names Demar Hamlin the current favorite for Comeback Player of the Year while stating the objection to that position. Returning from a life-threatening injury like a cardiac arrest makes Hamlin "a great candidate," the piece grants, but it then concedes voters could look elsewhere, since Hamlin has seldom been active on game day and has rarely seen the field. # Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

Sporting News applied this on 2023-12-12, reviewing the UEFA Champions League group stage ahead of its final match night and examining what teams from each group needed to qualify for the Round of 16, of which 16 places were at stake.

Group A shows the method at its simplest. Bayern Munich had already qualified, but Copenhagen, Galatasaray and Manchester United all entered the final matchweek with a chance of joining them. Galatasaray knew that if they beat Copenhagen at Parken they would go through. Copenhagen won 1-0 through Lukas Lerager's only goal, which took Copenhagen into the knockout rounds and left Galatasaray on 5 points from 6 games. Manchester United were eliminated after a 1-0 defeat to Bayern at Old Trafford, Kingsley Coman scoring, leaving them bottom of the group on 4 points.

NFL Network's Rich Eisen added a slew of lyric references to a preshow — "shake it off," "anti-hero" and "all too well" — and Kelce answered the Instagram montage with "Well played Rich … Well played." The CBSSports.com timeline dated 2023-10-12 supports its claim of a "rumored romance" between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce by accumulation rather than by proof. What makes the case, in the article's framing, is that the entries chain: Kelce's June 29 and September 22 Swift-bracelet gestures, Swift's attendance at five Chiefs games this season including the September 24 Week 3 game against the Bears and the article's present-day Sunday game against the Chargers, her cheering a three-yard touchdown in a 41-10 win, and being seen chatting with his mother, Donna Kelce. # Google Summit Notebooks Printed a Racially Insensitive "Cotton" Phrase, August 2023

Attendees of Google's K&I Black Summit, held in August 2023, were handed third-party notebooks whose inside pages were printed with the phrase "I was just cotton the moment, but I came back to take your notes," a play on "cotton" reported by TechCrunch's Dominic-Madori. # Black-and-White Moderation Policy

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it." Content that describes violence without endorsing it fits neither the "allowed" nor the "banned" category cleanly, so it tends to be mis-flagged or removed. Meta was additionally criticized in the article for struggling with Arabic's cultural and linguistic nuances, a language with over 25 dialects.


---


# The Age's Own Caveat: Arrowhead Sighting Does Not Confirm a Romance

The Age concedes, in its own words, that "none of this actually confirms Swift and Kelce are actually dating." Every datapoint the timeline marshals in its favour of romance is equally consistent with friendship. Swift's presence at Arrowhead Stadium on Monday September 2023, her cheering No. 87, the stadium's 1989-era references, Kelce's post-game outfit allegedly labelled the "1989 bedroom painting set", and Swifties capturing the two "leaving the stadium together" — each has a plainer reading: a supporter at a football game, a wardrobe coincidence, two people sharing a ride. # NFL Award Longshots: High Play, Long Odds, Little Credit

In a Sporting News betting piece dated 2023-12-05, an NFL award longshot is defined as a player or coach whose betting odds are very long despite performing at a high level, overlooked because other players have commanded the spotlight and the voters' narrative. The article's reasoning: short odds reflect being the best at a position all season, so equally long odds reflect the opposite perception, not necessarily the opposite play. The stated example: Vikings defensive end Danielle Hunter leads the league in tackles for loss and ranks third in sacks at 13.5, yet trails Micah Parsons, Myles Garrett and T.J. Watt in name recognition. With five weeks left in the regular season, a longshot can still become a contender, and a bet placed later pays less than one placed at that moment.

Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning, she thought it "impossible" Google could lose, reasoning that if Epic couldn't prove Apple's walled iOS garden was a monopoly, the comparatively open Android was harder still to convict. # Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.

# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

The article states that "over time, SEO techniques have spread and become insidious, such that googling anything can now feel like looking up 'sneaker' in the dictionary and finding a definition that sounds both incorrect and suspiciously as though it were written by someone promoting Nike." By 2023, users described Google Search results as "absolutely unusable," "garbage," and "a nightmare" because "a lot of the content doesn't feel authentic." His counter-argument: Google's travel listings are one of the most popular experiences the company has built, so those results serve users rather than merely taxing rivals. In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.

# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told
