# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.

In 2005, after Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, Google legal chief David Drummond wrote to Microsoft arguing that the default was anticompetitive, according to a TechCrunch report dated 2023-10-31 on the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google. Drummond's letter rested on a claim about user behavior: most end users "do not change defaults," so the engine picked at the outset keeps the searches.

Gary Wang's account of his own FTX criminality reached past himself to named others. Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos on Thursday 5 October 2023, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?", Wang answered "Yes," and said those crimes — wire and commodities fraud — were carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research. When Roos asked whether he saw any of those people in the courtroom, Wang stood, looked around, said "Yes," and identified "Sam Bankman-Fried." The argument's force is a sworn guilty plea, tempered by his six-page cooperation agreement and the up to 50 years in prison he still faces at sentencing.


---


# Gary Wang — CTO of FTX, co-owner of FTX and Alameda

Gary Wang is the chief technology officer of FTX, the failed cryptocurrency exchange, and co-owner of both FTX and Alameda Research. Wang testified against FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who stood trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy, saying Alameda received a special credit line and an option to take its balance into the negative without triggering liquidation — something he alleged other FTX accounts didn't get. On 2023-10-10, defense attorney Christian Everdell cross-examined Wang the same day as Caroline Ellison.


---


# FTX Co-Defendants Wang and Ellison Pleaded Guilty December 2022, Set as Trial Witnesses

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang and Alameda Research’s former CEO Caroline Ellison both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges tied to the FTX collapse. They also face civil penalties from the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) alongside the criminal charges. Wang and Ellison plan to cooperate with prosecutors and will be major witnesses in the trial, given their close ties to Bankman-Fried, FTX and Alameda. Source: TechCrunch, 2023-10-01.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda Research head and prosecution's star witness in the FTX trial

Caroline Ellison ran Alameda Research, the sister hedge fund of the crypto exchange FTX, and had been a girlfriend of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Per a CNBC report dated 2023-10-06 covering Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, she and FTX co-founder Gary Wang were integral members of Bankman-Fried's personal and professional inner circles, and both pleaded guilty in December 2022. Ellison is considered the prosecution's star witness and was expected to take the stand under a cooperation arrangement similar to Wang's.


---


# Index: The Seven People Closest to Sam Bankman-Fried in the October 2023 FTX Trial Record

This index scopes the individuals named in a The Verge article dated 2023-10-26 as the people who loved or worked with Sam Bankman-Fried and appeared in the FTX trial record. The source lists them in order of testimony and relationship: Adam Yedidia and Gary Wang (college roommates), Nishad Singh (longtime family friend), Caroline Ellison (ex-girlfriend), his parents Joe Bankman and Barbara Fried, and his brother Gabe Bankman-Fried. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are felons; the article's closing paragraph covers their sentencing exposure, restitution, job bars, and reputational damage.


---


# FTX's Collapse Traced to Alameda Research Drawing on Customer Funds

In The Verge's 2023-10-26 account of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, FTX collapsed as the result of Bankman-Fried's trading firm Alameda Research purloining the exchange's customers' funds. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, testified that Alameda took customer funds and that Bankman-Fried knew about it and even invested them against her advice; she also described the seven phony balance sheets she had created. Gary Wang, co-founder of FTX and Alameda Research, testified about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code. Customers who had money trapped on the FTX exchange when it collapsed lost access to funds that should have been available at any time they wanted it, even if the bankruptcy proceedings later make them whole.


---


# The FTX Trial's Real Story: Fraud Plus a Destroyed Inner Circle

The Verge's argument on 2023-10-26, as the prosecution's case neared its end, is that the FTX trial matters on two tracks at once. The first is familiar: the prosecution made a strong case that Sam Bankman-Fried presided over the frauds at FTX and his trading firm Alameda Research, which purloined customers' funds, and he faces seven counts, two of wire fraud and five conspiracy charges. What gives the trial its weight, however, is "a simultaneous drama of ruined lives playing out in the courtroom" among the people closest to him. Adam Yedidia, his college roommate, testified with immunity after having texted "I love you Sam… I'm not going anywhere." Gary Wang, co-founder of FTX and Alameda, "sang like a canary"; Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, pleaded guilty to six charges; Caroline Ellison, his ex-girlfriend, described the seven phony balance sheets she created. Wang, Singh, and Ellison are now felons. The Verge reads all of it as Greek tragedy, precipitated by one man's character flaw: the arrogance of Sam Bankman-Fried.


---


# Gary Wang: FTX's lesser-known co-founder and technology chief

Gary Wang, aged 30 when he testified against Sam Bankman-Fried in Manhattan federal court on October 5–6, 2023, is the lesser-known co-founder of FTX and served as its technology chief. The source identifies him as a former friend of Bankman-Fried's from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where the two met, and it also places Wang among those who worked at the crypto exchange while living with the founder in the Bahamas.


---


# Gary Wang Testifies on Alameda's Hidden Privileges in FTX Code

Gary Wang, co-founder of both FTX and Alameda Research and a second college roommate of Sam Bankman-Fried, testified in Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, which The Verge reported on 2023-10-26. Wang took the stand after fellow engineer Adam Yedidia and, per The Verge, "sang like a canary" about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda inside the FTX code. As a co-founder of both the exchange and the trading firm, Wang was positioned to describe how that code favored Alameda. Wang, Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison are now felons.


---


# Wang's "FTX Was Not Fine" Rebuts the Nov. 7, 2022 Reassurance Tweets

At Sam Bankman-Fried's Manhattan fraud trial on Oct. 6, 2023, FTX co-founder Gary Wang rebutted the reassurance record prosecutors put before the jury: a series of tweets beginning Nov. 7, 2022, in which FTX blamed bank hours for slow withdrawals while Bankman-Fried assured customers from his personal account that all was fine. "FTX was not fine and assets were not fine," Wang testified.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda CEO at the Centre of Both Sides' FTX Trial Story

Caroline Ellison is the figure both sides leaned on in the opening statements of Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, as reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04. She was the CEO of Alameda Research, the crypto hedge fund Bankman-Fried also owned, and his on-again off-again girlfriend. Prosecutor Thane Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried used Ellison as a front to get "secret access" to customer money — both cash and crypto. Defence lawyer Mark Cohen answered that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and pointed the finger at Ellison, who, he said, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. By then she was a former lieutenant turned government cooperator, which is why she was not among the prosecution's first two witnesses.

qid: Which company, featured in articles by TechCrunch, The Verge, and Fortune, had significant holdings in "unlocked FTT" and "FTT collateral," was able to maintain a negative balance without liquidation on FTX, and was involved in taking losses to present a better financial image for FTX, all while acting within its legal boundaries as a customer, payment processor, and market maker?
context:
# Alameda's balance sheet listed more FTT than existed, 193% above total market cap

CoinDesk's publication of Alameda Research's balance sheet — showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022 — revealed an anomaly. Alameda's largest asset was $3.66 billion of "unlocked FTT" plus $2.16 billion of "FTT collateral": $5.82 billion of FTT, the token behind FTX. That was 193% higher than the total FTT market cap, then about $3 billion, meaning Alameda purported to hold more FTT than existed. Reported by TechCrunch, 2023-10-01.


---


# Spot margin (FTX program)

Spot margin was a program at the cryptocurrency exchange FTX that let users lend each other assets for margin trading. Its distinguishing feature: in those cases, it was possible to have a negative balance in a specific coin. It was not, however, possible for spot margin accounts to avoid liquidation, nor to hold an overall negative balance. The term surfaced on 2023-10-10 at Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal trial, when defense attorney Christian Everdell raised spot margin in cross-examining FTX chief technology officer Gary Wang. Wang had testified that Alameda Research could take its balance negative without triggering liquidation, an option he alleged other FTX accounts did not get.


---


# FTX's Spot Margin Program Was Not Equivalent to Alameda's Credit Line

During cross-examination of FTX chief technology officer Gary Wang on 2023-10-10, at Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, defense attorney Christian Everdell raised FTX's spot margin program as a counter to Wang's claim that Alameda Research received a special credit line. The two arrangements look alike but are not equivalent. Wang had testified that Alameda got access to a special credit line and an option to take its balance into the negative without triggering liquidation — something he alleged other accounts at FTX didn't get. The spot margin program let users lend each other assets for margin trading, and in those cases it was possible to have a negative balance in a specific coin. It was not, however, possible for those accounts to avoid liquidation, as Wang testified Alameda could do, or to have an overall negative balance.


---


# FTX's "Special Credit Line" for Alameda Research (Gary Wang's October 2023 Testimony)

In testimony described by The Verge on 2023-10-10 during Sam Bankman-Fried's criminal fraud trial, Gary Wang — chief technology officer of FTX and co-owner of both FTX and Alameda Research — said Alameda had been given access to a special credit line, defined as the Alameda-only arrangement permitting the firm to take its balance into the negative without triggering liquidation. Wang alleged that other accounts at FTX received neither element of that arrangement. Defense attorney Christian Everdell tried to undercut the claim by pointing to FTX's spot margin program, which let users lend each other assets for margin trading and could leave a balance negative in a specific coin. But per Wang, spot margin accounts could not avoid liquidation or hold an overall negative balance — so the credit line's boundary is the combination of both privileges, which Wang said belonged to Alameda alone.


---


# Everdell's spot-margin cross of Gary Wang was confusion strategy, not rebuttal — The Verge, 2023-10-10

Writing about the FTX trial on 2023-10-10 for The Verge, the author argues that defense attorney Christian Everdell's cross-examination of Gary Wang — chief technology officer of FTX and co-owner of both FTX and Alameda — was a credibility play, not a substantive rebuttal. Last week Wang testified that Alameda received a special credit line plus an option to take its balance into the negative without triggering liquidation, which he alleged other FTX accounts did not get. Everdell's response was to steer into the spot margin program, which let users lend each other assets for margin trading and could produce a negative balance in a specific coin. That comparison fails on its own terms, the author notes: spot-margin accounts could neither avoid liquidation nor hold an overall negative balance. So the questioning's only real function was drowning the jury in confusing technicalities — and even that held as a sideshow, because it "couldn't undo the damage of last week's code review."


---


# FTX and Alameda Research filed for Chapter 11 in mid-November 2022

FTX's collapse came after CoinDesk published Alameda Research's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022, and after Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022 (TechCrunch, 2023-10-01).

[Provenance caveat: the assigned thought's wider industry-contagion element — BlockFi's November 2022 Chapter 11 filing and Genesis Global Trading's January 2023 filing — is not present in the source text supplied, so it is omitted rather than attributed to this article. If those facts appear in the full TechCrunch piece, they can be restored.]


---


# Full FTX Restitution Cannot Undo the Harm of Trapped Customer Funds

When the FTX exchange collapsed in late 2022 because Sam Bankman-Fried's trading firm Alameda Research had purloined its customers' funds, everyone with money trapped on the platform had their life altered, The Verge argued on 2023-10-26 during Bankman-Fried's trial. The courtroom reporting's central claim: even if the bankruptcy proceedings make those customers financially whole, the entitlement already destroyed was access — money that should have been available at any time they wanted it. That lost liquidity translates into concrete harms no restitution reverses: houses that weren't purchased, medical procedures that were left undone, and life savings lost. Compensation restores a balance, not the life that delay forecloses.


---


# Gary Wang — CTO of FTX, co-owner of FTX and Alameda

Gary Wang is the chief technology officer of FTX, the failed cryptocurrency exchange, and co-owner of both FTX and Alameda Research. Wang testified against FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, who stood trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy, saying Alameda received a special credit line and an option to take its balance into the negative without triggering liquidation — something he alleged other FTX accounts didn't get. On 2023-10-10, defense attorney Christian Everdell cross-examined Wang the same day as Caroline Ellison.


---


# Cohen's Competing Model: Alameda and FTX as Lawful, Ordinary Businesses

In his opening statement on Oct 4, 2023, as reported by Fortune, defence lawyer Mark Cohen offered a model of the FTX–Alameda relationship at odds with the prosecution's two-entity structure. Alameda was not subterranean or shady but a successful hedge fund, he said; FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, Cohen argued: Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor and market maker, a financial entity acting as a trading partner for customers buying and selling cryptocurrencies. "Sam didn't defraud anyone," he said.


---


# FTX's Collapse Traced to Alameda Research Drawing on Customer Funds

In The Verge's 2023-10-26 account of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, FTX collapsed as the result of Bankman-Fried's trading firm Alameda Research purloining the exchange's customers' funds. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, testified that Alameda took customer funds and that Bankman-Fried knew about it and even invested them against her advice; she also described the seven phony balance sheets she had created. Gary Wang, co-founder of FTX and Alameda Research, testified about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code. Customers who had money trapped on the FTX exchange when it collapsed lost access to funds that should have been available at any time they wanted it, even if the bankruptcy proceedings later make them whole.


---


# Prosecution's claim beyond diversion: concealed money flows and forged documents

In the opening statement reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04, prosecutor Thane Rehn pushed the government's case past the taking of FTX customer funds: Bankman-Fried allegedly directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers and forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged.

# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.

qid: Does the article from The Verge suggest that Sam Bankman-Fried was aware of the financial discrepancies at FTX, while the TechCrunch article alleges that he knowingly committed fraud, or do both articles imply a level of awareness and intent by Sam Bankman-Fried regarding the financial issues at FTX?

# Sam Bankman-Fried: FTX founder and criminal fraud defendant

Sam Bankman-Fried is defined here as the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX and the defendant in a criminal fraud trial, as reported by The Verge on 2023-10-10. He was on trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Those characterizations come from the government's allegations, not from findings the article reports as settled.


---

# The Paradox at the Heart of the AI Race: Fear and Ambition Entangled

As reported by The Age on 2023-12-09, the competition among Silicon Valley's leading AI builders contains what the article calls a "brain-stretching paradox": the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches. They have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The founders caught in this contradiction are Elon Musk, Larry Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI. In an interview published by TechCrunch on 2023-11-30, Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, separated an "AI breakthrough" from what she called a bonafide "user experience breakthrough." ChatGPT, released a year earlier as a "low-key research preview," was that: a free, web-based, chat-focused interface on top of OpenAI's existing model GPT-3.5, taking generative AI mainstream. # Meta's suppression of Palestinian content is structural bias, not a bug — TechCrunch, 19 Oct 2023

TechCrunch's claim on 19 Oct 2023: Instagram's shadowbanning of Palestine-related content is "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes," not the technical error Meta invokes. Meta says it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated 18 Oct, insists "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." The assembled warrants make intent beside the point. Meta cannot navigate Arabic's over 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversifying language resources. Its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuance, such as content discussing violence without condoning it. Partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Enforcement tracks user reports: filmmaker Khitam Jabr lost 24 hours of posting on West Bank travel Reels she says drew anti-Palestine comments and reports. And during the 2021 Hamas–Israel outbreak, a report Meta commissioned from a third party concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation.


---


# Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." That denial of motive does not reach the documented record: a lengthy history of incidents reflecting inherent bias in Meta's processes, from both inside and outside the company, plus a third-party report Meta commissioned after the 2021 Hamas-Israel violence finding an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Calling removals a "bug" localizes harm to a single defect, while the bias here is distributed across language coverage, policy architecture, and escalation channels.


---


# Index: Meta's Moderation of Palestinian Voices (TechCrunch, 19 October 2023)

This document (doc_0106) is TechCrunch's 19 October 2023 report that Instagram users suspect Meta of shadowbanning — that is, limiting the visibility of — content about Palestine. Its definitional material covers shadowbanning and black-and-white policy design. Its structural-bias mechanisms include Meta's thin Arabic language resources (a language with over 25 dialects) and partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, set against Meta's ban on content supporting Hamas, designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union. Case material covers filmmaker Khitam Jabr's 24-hour restrictions and Bella Hadid's Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Counter-argument material carries Meta communications director Andy Stone's rebuttals and the Oct. 18 newsroom statement, plus the 2021 third-party human rights report behind the bias-versus-bug dispute.


---


# Meta's "bug" explanation cannot account for a multi-year pattern of restrictions on Palestinian content

Meta attributed the October 2023 Instagram shadowbanning complaints to a bug affecting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts. That single-incident technical account doesn't fit the pattern TechCrunch described on Oct. 19, 2023: the accusations were "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents" on Meta platforms reflecting an inherent bias against Palestinian users, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company, and involving restrictions on content that never supported Hamas. Meta's own commissioned third-party report, issued during the 2021 Hamas–Israel violence, concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. Meta also blamed technical errors for removing posts about Palestine during that 2021 conflict.


---


# Hypothesis: Meta's government agency partnerships bias moderation against Palestinian expression

A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

The hypothesis is falsified if removal and restriction rates for comparable Palestine-related content show no association with escalation in those agency channels: more reports or referrals routed through partner agencies, but unchanged enforcement rates, would sever the claimed link.

Scope: Meta's platforms, notably Instagram, in the period following Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade of Gaza.


---


# Meta's rebuttal to deliberate suppression of Palestinian voices: equal policy application and appeals

In its 19 October 2023 TechCrunch report on suspected Instagram shadowbanning of Palestine content, Meta's counter-argument came via communications director Andy Stone, who declined to comment on the record and pointed instead to Meta's newsroom post on the conflict, updated 18 October 2023. That post states: "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice … We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it." Meta added that it may inadvertently flag content but never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."


---


# Meta-Commissioned Third-Party Report Found Adverse Human Rights Impact on Palestinian Users in 2021

During the 2021 Hamas-Israel escalation, a third-party report commissioned by Meta concluded that the company's own actions had produced an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation. The finding, cited in a TechCrunch article published Oct. 19, 2023, is significant because Meta itself paid for the assessment, making it an internally sourced acknowledgment rather than an external allegation. Meta separately attributed its 2021 content removals to technical errors.


---


# Report Volume, Not Rule Breach, Can Trigger Meta Account Restrictions

A 2023-10-19 TechCrunch report on Instagram moderation describes a mechanism in which enforcement output tracks how hard users mobilize against a post rather than whether the post breached a rule: Instagram users "complained that they've been harassed and reported for posting content about Palestine, regardless of whether or not it violates Meta's policies." Under that pattern, a report threshold can itself be the trigger, so a mass-reported post on innocuous subject matter can produce the same restriction as a genuine violation. Palestinian-American filmmaker Khitam Jabr suspects precisely this: she believes Instagram restricted her account for 24 hours because users reported her Reels about a family trip to the West Bank — travel vlogs showing Palestinian meals and a wedding dance, with nothing about the occupation.


---


# Meta's Counter: Andy Stone Attributes Reduced Story Reach to a Bug, Not Bias

Against the accusation that Instagram shadowbanned Stories about Palestine in October 2023, Meta communications director Andy Stone attributed the reduced reach to a technical fault rather than moderation policy. In a Threads post, he wrote, "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts" — meaning the limitation reached every account doing that, wherever located, irrespective of subject matter, and was corrected quickly. Stone declined to comment on the record for TechCrunch's story, dated 2023-10-19, and pointed to Meta's newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, which stated that Meta applies its policies "equally around the world" and that "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." Meta had likewise blamed technical errors for removals of Palestine posts during the 2021 conflict.

# Shang: Conversational Interface Research Explains ChatGPT's "Convincingly Real" Dialogue

Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction, named ChatGPT's ability to conduct conversations that are "convincingly real" as one reason for the chatbot's enduring popularity, in TechCrunch's coverage of its first anniversary on 2023-11-30.

Shang grounded that explanation in earlier work: "Human-computer interaction researchers have studied how conversational interfaces can improve understandability of information, and the socialization aspects of chatbots bring increased engagement." She continued: "Now, AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues."

The contrast Shang drew is with chatbots that had existed for decades but ran on models much less sophisticated than those powering ChatGPT, so the same two interface properties now operate at far higher fidelity.


---


# Shang: ChatGPT's target shifted from domain-specific chatbots to general-purpose systems via prompting

Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction, attributes part of ChatGPT's enduring popularity in a TechCrunch article published 2023-11-30 to a change in what such systems were built to be. Chatbots had existed for decades, but the models behind ChatGPT were far more sophisticated than what users were accustomed to. Training on vast data moved the design target away from specialized, domain-specific chatbots toward general-purpose systems that people drive through instruction prompting, on the condition that users need learn no new interaction language. Shang notes that "AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues."


---


# Hyland: ChatGPT's "feel" difference from ELIZA lies in the model, not the psychology

Adam Hyland, a PhD student studying AI at the University of Washington, draws out the emotional component of ChatGPT: conversations with it have a palpably different "feel" than with more rudimentary chatbots. He points back to ELIZA, the chatbot created by MIT computer scientist Joseph Weizenbaum in 1966. "In the 1960s, ELIZA offered a chatbot, the response to which was very similar to how people reacted to ChatGPT," Hyland said. "Humans interacting with the system inferred emotional content and a narrative through line in chat messages." The parallel locates the difference between ELIZA and ChatGPT in the sophistication of the underlying model, not in the psychology of the interaction: users in 1966 were already supplying the emotion and the story themselves.


---


# ChatGPT's research preview launch as a data-harvesting strategy

When OpenAI released ChatGPT "a year ago" — i.e. a year before TechCrunch's retrospective of 2023-11-30 — it did so as a "low-key research preview," reportedly spurred in part by an intense rivalry with the AI startup Anthropic. OpenAI leadership told the OpenAI rank-and-file at the time that the goal was to gather more data on how people use and interact with generative AI, in order to inform the development of OpenAI's future models. ChatGPT was not a new model at all in that framing: initially a basic free-to-use, web-based, chat-focused interface on top of one of OpenAI's existing models, GPT-3.5.


---

In October 2023, Wired published, then removed for not meeting its standards, an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates search queries for ad revenue — for example replacing "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". # Google's rebuttal to Megan Gray's Wired query-rewrite allegation

# Wired removed Megan Gray's article alleging Google rewrites search queries for ad revenue

In October 2023, Wired published an opinion piece by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". Google rejected the piece as misleading and inaccurate, denying it ever alters search terms. # The reporter's gator fantasy implicates journalism too

In "The people who ruined the internet" (The Verge, 2023-11-01), the reporter's self-description of what he hoped to witness at a South Florida rooftop bar functions as the piece's central argument: the drive to dress up reality for engagement is not a defect peculiar to SEO professionals. He booked a plane ticket after hearing that a 10-foot alligator would be released at a party for the digital marketers accused of ruining the internet, conceding that a link reading "WATCH: 10-foot Gator Prepares to Maul Digital Marketers" would have gotten his click. Then he names the fuller fantasy — an SEO professional attacked by a "gigantic, prehistoric-looking reptile" in front of him, which he could "repackage such a tragedy into a sensationalized anecdote for a viral article," implying nature punished the bad guy while "assuming the ethical high ground." His stated vulnerabilities: he uses Google, wants reliable results, and enjoys "the sweet taste of revenge." The alligator measured five and a half feet, not 10 — "Classic clickbait!"

# Hypothesis: OpenAI's leadership fallout could redirect attention and funding to Meta's LLaMA and AI startups

A hypothesis in TechCrunch's ChatGPT explainer (published 2023-09-28, updated through OpenAI's November 2023 leadership crisis) is that the turmoil may shift advantage to OpenAI's rivals. CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return "raised concerns about its direction and opened the door for competitors," and two beneficiary groups are named: established rivals such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, and independent AI startups, which the article suggests may more easily "get attention and funding as the industry watches OpenAI implode and put itself back together." The mechanism is reputational and financial rather than technical, unfolding while ChatGPT already had 100 million weekly active users and use inside more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies. # Adoption and Investment as Grounds for AI Chatbots Outlasting OpenAI's Leadership Crisis

TechCrunch's ChatGPT coverage (published 2023-09-28, updated through December 2023) argues that AI chatbots are not going away anytime soon, resting the claim on two grounds: measured adoption and OpenAI's continued investment.

Adoption: ChatGPT reached 100 million weekly active users since its initial launch nearly a year ago, and is used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Investment: OpenAI announced GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API and a GPT store at its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, on November 6; connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users; integrated DALL-E 3; and re-enabled ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.

In UEFA Champions League Group A on 12 December 2023, FC Copenhagen beat Galatasaray 1-0 at Parken, Lukas Lerager scoring the only goal. # Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

Sporting News applied this on 2023-12-12, reviewing the UEFA Champions League group stage ahead of its final match night and examining what teams from each group needed to qualify for the Round of 16, of which 16 places were at stake.

Group A shows the method at its simplest. Bayern Munich had already qualified, but Copenhagen, Galatasaray and Manchester United all entered the final matchweek with a chance of joining them. Galatasaray knew that if they beat Copenhagen at Parken they would go through. Copenhagen won 1-0 through Lukas Lerager's only goal, which took Copenhagen into the knockout rounds and left Galatasaray on 5 points from 6 games. Manchester United were eliminated after a 1-0 defeat to Bayern at Old Trafford, Kingsley Coman scoring, leaving them bottom of the group on 4 points.


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Copenhagen 1-0 Galatasaray, Parken, 12 December 2023: Group A's decider went the hosts' way

In UEFA Champions League Group A on 12 December 2023, FC Copenhagen beat Galatasaray 1-0 at Parken, Lukas Lerager scoring the only goal. Going into that final matchweek Galatasaray knew that a win over Copenhagen would take them through; the defeat ended that route. Copenhagen instead finished second in the group on 8 points, behind Bayern Munich on 16, with Galatasaray on 5.

*Source: Sporting News, "Champions League permutations, scenarios: What teams need to qualify from groups for 2023/24 Round of 16 stage," 2023-12-12.*

# OpenAI's December 2023 Axel Springer Deal Covered Both Model Training and Live ChatGPT Answers

In December 2023, OpenAI announced a content agreement with Axel Springer, the Berlin-based news publisher that owns Business Insider and Politico, which OpenAI framed as helping "provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools." That combination — a licensing deal that pays for a publisher's archive as training data while also giving that publisher's newest work privileged placement in a chatbot's responses — made the deal notable beyond the parties involved, and it was reported in TechCrunch's running ChatGPT timeline alongside other December 2023 OpenAI news, including the reopening of ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.

# The Availability Objection to Demar Hamlin as Comeback Player of the Year Favorite

A Sporting News article on NFL award longshots, published December 5, 2023, names Demar Hamlin the current favorite for Comeback Player of the Year while stating the objection to that position. Returning from a life-threatening injury like a cardiac arrest makes Hamlin "a great candidate," the piece grants, but it then concedes voters could look elsewhere, since Hamlin has seldom been active on game day and has rarely seen the field. The objection is that his on-field contribution is minimal beside an award meant to recognize a playing comeback. The article leaves the outcome resting on how vital voters deem playing to be.

# Google Bard trained on news publisher content, Helena World Chronicle complaint alleges

In the class action antitrust complaint Helena World Chronicle filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023, the Arkansas publisher alleges that Google's Bard AI chatbot was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications." # Similarweb data: Google drives nearly 40% of news publishers' web traffic (December 2023)

# Atlético Madrid's 13 December 2023 win over Lazio settled Group E's top spot

On 13 December 2023, Atlético Madrid beat Lazio 2-0 in the Spanish capital to claim first place in their UEFA Champions League Group E. # The SEO Business Model: Ranking High to Convert Google's Objectivity Into Ad Traffic

According to a 2023-11-01 Verge report on search engine optimization, the SEO business model works by borrowing the appearance of neutrality that Google lends to organic results. The practitioner's goal is to tell the algorithm whatever it needs to hear for a site to appear as high up as possible in search results, then use that placement — Google's supposed objectivity — to lure people in and, usually, show them some kind of advertising. The article distinguishes this from simply buying the advertising space labeled "Sponsored" above organic results, comparing SEO instead to the Wizard of Oz projecting his voice to magnify his authority. The scheme is contingent on ranking: it pays only insofar as the site actually reaches the top of results, against a backdrop in which Google holds a 90 percent market share for online search.

# Google's behavioural data as the personalisation engine across Search, mobile widgets and other services

In a search-engine comparison published in The Age on 2023-10-22, the author writes that the test "did remind me how much data Google collects — not just my searches but anything I say to a smart speaker, any search result or ad that I click." That accumulated behavioural data is the mechanism the article names for relevance: it "does also mean that Google (not just search but also mobile widgets and other services) personalises to me more effectively." The competing service in the same test, DuckDuckGo, collects less but "didn't perform as well and is harder to read." Personalisation in the article's account is therefore compounded across surfaces rather than confined to the search results page.

qid: Does the TechCrunch article on Meta's moderation bias suggest the same kind of issue affecting Palestinians as the TechCrunch article on Norway's push to extend the ban on Meta's tracking ads, with the former discussing suppression of voices and the latter addressing unlawful user tracking?
context:
# Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." That denial of motive does not reach the documented record: a lengthy history of incidents reflecting inherent bias in Meta's processes, from both inside and outside the company, plus a third-party report Meta commissioned after the 2021 Hamas-Israel violence finding an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Calling removals a "bug" localizes harm to a single defect, while the bias here is distributed across language coverage, policy architecture, and escalation channels.


---


# Meta's suppression of Palestinian content is structural bias, not a bug — TechCrunch, 19 Oct 2023

TechCrunch's claim on 19 Oct 2023: Instagram's shadowbanning of Palestine-related content is "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes," not the technical error Meta invokes. Meta says it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated 18 Oct, insists "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." The assembled warrants make intent beside the point. Meta cannot navigate Arabic's over 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversifying language resources. Its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuance, such as content discussing violence without condoning it. Partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Enforcement tracks user reports: filmmaker Khitam Jabr lost 24 hours of posting on West Bank travel Reels she says drew anti-Palestine comments and reports. And during the 2021 Hamas–Israel outbreak, a report Meta commissioned from a third party concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation.


---


# Index: Meta's Moderation of Palestinian Voices (TechCrunch, 19 October 2023)

This document (doc_0106) is TechCrunch's 19 October 2023 report that Instagram users suspect Meta of shadowbanning — that is, limiting the visibility of — content about Palestine. Its definitional material covers shadowbanning and black-and-white policy design. Its structural-bias mechanisms include Meta's thin Arabic language resources (a language with over 25 dialects) and partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, set against Meta's ban on content supporting Hamas, designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union. Case material covers filmmaker Khitam Jabr's 24-hour restrictions and Bella Hadid's Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Counter-argument material carries Meta communications director Andy Stone's rebuttals and the Oct. 18 newsroom statement, plus the 2021 third-party human rights report behind the bias-versus-bug dispute.


---


# Hypothesis: Meta's government agency partnerships bias moderation against Palestinian expression

A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

The hypothesis is falsified if removal and restriction rates for comparable Palestine-related content show no association with escalation in those agency channels: more reports or referrals routed through partner agencies, but unchanged enforcement rates, would sever the claimed link.

Scope: Meta's platforms, notably Instagram, in the period following Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade of Gaza.


---


# Meta's rebuttal to deliberate suppression of Palestinian voices: equal policy application and appeals

In its 19 October 2023 TechCrunch report on suspected Instagram shadowbanning of Palestine content, Meta's counter-argument came via communications director Andy Stone, who declined to comment on the record and pointed instead to Meta's newsroom post on the conflict, updated 18 October 2023. That post states: "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice … We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it." Meta added that it may inadvertently flag content but never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."


---


# Meta's "bug" explanation cannot account for a multi-year pattern of restrictions on Palestinian content

Meta attributed the October 2023 Instagram shadowbanning complaints to a bug affecting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts. That single-incident technical account doesn't fit the pattern TechCrunch described on Oct. 19, 2023: the accusations were "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents" on Meta platforms reflecting an inherent bias against Palestinian users, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company, and involving restrictions on content that never supported Hamas. Meta's own commissioned third-party report, issued during the 2021 Hamas–Israel violence, concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. Meta also blamed technical errors for removing posts about Palestine during that 2021 conflict.


---


# Meta's Counter: Andy Stone Attributes Reduced Story Reach to a Bug, Not Bias

Against the accusation that Instagram shadowbanned Stories about Palestine in October 2023, Meta communications director Andy Stone attributed the reduced reach to a technical fault rather than moderation policy. In a Threads post, he wrote, "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts" — meaning the limitation reached every account doing that, wherever located, irrespective of subject matter, and was corrected quickly. Stone declined to comment on the record for TechCrunch's story, dated 2023-10-19, and pointed to Meta's newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, which stated that Meta applies its policies "equally around the world" and that "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." Meta had likewise blamed technical errors for removals of Palestine posts during the 2021 conflict.


---


# Linguistic Under-Coverage in Platform Moderation of Arabic

Linguistic under-coverage is a moderation capacity condition in which a platform's language resources treat Arabic as a single variety, even though it has over 25 dialects, so dialectal and cultural nuance falls outside the reach of both automated classifiers and human reviewers. TechCrunch described this on 2023-10-19 in "Meta has a moderation bias problem, not just a 'bug,' that's suppressing Palestinian voices" (publisher: TechCrunch, dated 2023-10-19), noting that Meta struggles to navigate the cultural and linguistic nuances of Arabic and has been criticized for neglecting to adequately diversify its language resources.

The concept names a capability gap rather than an intent: content in a given variety sits beyond what the resources can parse.


---


# Meta-Commissioned Third-Party Report Found Adverse Human Rights Impact on Palestinian Users in 2021

During the 2021 Hamas-Israel escalation, a third-party report commissioned by Meta concluded that the company's own actions had produced an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation. The finding, cited in a TechCrunch article published Oct. 19, 2023, is significant because Meta itself paid for the assessment, making it an internally sourced acknowledgment rather than an external allegation. Meta separately attributed its 2021 content removals to technical errors.

qid: Which company, scrutinized in articles from both 'The Age' and 'TechCrunch', is not only accused of potentially unfair practices to maintain its dominance as a default search engine but also faces allegations of harming news publishers' revenues and audiences through its operations?

# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Wired removed Megan Gray's article alleging Google rewrites search queries for ad revenue

In October 2023, Wired published an opinion piece by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had accidentally revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue. The example given was replacing a search for "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". Google rejected the piece as misleading and inaccurate, denying it ever alters search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Google Search Antitrust Trial: the 2020 Dominance Claim

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. It is distinct from the separate claim filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado, which seeks to break Google's monopoly in digital advertising, not search.


---


# Reach of the retracted Wired piece on Google query manipulation, October 2023

In October 2023, Wired published, then removed for not meeting its standards, an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates search queries for ad revenue — for example replacing "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". The Age reports that the extent of its sharing on social media and boosting in write-ups at other outlets shows how willing people are to accept foul play by Google, amid a standing suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling.

SOURCE: The Age, "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", 2023-10-22.


---


# Google's rebuttal to Megan Gray's Wired query-rewrite allegation

In October 2023, in response to the Wired opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray — which alleged, on the example of a search for "children's clothing" being replaced with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear", that Google manipulates people's search queries for maximum ad revenue — Google rejected the piece in very strong terms, calling it misleading and inaccurate while denying ever altering search terms. Wired removed the article for not meeting its standards.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Revenue-ranked queries as evidence of Google's vertical search dominance

In TechCrunch's 2023-11-13 roundup of the US v Google trial, the reporter interprets a publicly released list of the 20 search terms that made Google the most money during the week of September 22, 2018 — a list Judge Amit Mehta ruled to make public, with per-term revenue and query counts redacted — as proof of Google's dominance of vertical search, meaning search in very specific market categories. The warrant is saturation: the terms are concentrated in the categories where advertisers pay most — "Auto Insurance," "Car Insurance," "Car Insurance Quotes," "Cheap Car Insurance," "Insurance Quotes," "Cheap Flights," "DirecTV," "AT&T," "Spectrum," "Comcast," "Xfinity," "Hulu," "Free Credit Report," "LifeLock." The iPhone 8 aside concedes the list is unsurprising, since "September 22, 2017 was the official release date of the iPhone 8" and Google and Apple maintain a mutually beneficial relationship even while competing. The reporter also attributes "LifeLock" to the 2017 Equifax breach. The whole reading rests on one week in 2018.

qid: Does 'The Age' article suggest that Taylor Swift's interaction with Travis Kelce during her NFL takeover involves a different type of exchange than the one mentioned in 'The Independent - Life and Style' articles, with one discussing a friendship bracelet and the other an invitation to a game and openness about a personal relationship?
context:
# Index: The Age's timeline of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce, 26 September 2023

This index covers The Age's chronology "When pop culture and sport collide: A timeline of Taylor Swift's NFL takeover" (26 September 2023), which runs eight dated beats under Swift song-title headings. In order: the 2016 "Kiss, Marry, Kill" choice on AfterBuzz TV; Travis Kelce's July friendship-bracelet attempt at the Kansas City Eras Tour; his August moustache remark; that month's New York City trip; September's report that the two had been "quietly hanging out" for months; the 17 September broadcast lyric references by CBS's Ian Eagle and NFL Network's Rich Eisen; Kelce's 21 September game invitation on The Pat McAfee Show; and the Monday Arrowhead Stadium sighting.


---


# The Kelce–Swift Timeline Argues by Accumulation, Not by Any Single Act

The CBSSports.com timeline dated 2023-10-12 supports its claim of a "rumored romance" between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce by accumulation rather than by proof. Individually, each entry is ambiguous: Kelce's July 26 friendship bracelet with "my number on it" could be a jersey number, his September 21 invitation on the Pat McAfee show was spoken as a joke, and Jason Kelce's September 14 response "did not confirm them, but he also did not deny them." What makes the case, in the article's framing, is that the entries chain: Kelce's June 29 and September 22 Swift-bracelet gestures, Swift's attendance at five Chiefs games this season including the September 24 Week 3 game against the Bears and the article's present-day Sunday game against the Chargers, her cheering a three-yard touchdown in a 41-10 win, and being seen chatting with his mother, Donna Kelce. The inference holds only while the acts are read as coordinated.


---


# Kelce Told Listeners the Friendship Bracelet He Meant for Swift Never Reached Her

On the July 2023 episode of *New Heights*, the podcast Travis Kelce shares with his brother, Kelce said he had intended to give Taylor Swift a friendship bracelet with his phone number on it during her Eras Tour concert in Kansas City. The bracelet never made it to her wrist, and Kelce likewise never got her digits. This is the first documented contact attempt in the timeline The Age published on 26 September 2023 under the section heading "Cruel Summer."


---


# Travis Kelce made a friendship bracelet for NFL tight end camp newcomers, June 29, 2023

On June 29, 2023, Travis Kelce made a friendship bracelet to give to the newcomers at a camp for NFL tight ends, saying he was "taking a page out of Taylor Swift's book." CBSSports.com reported the episode on 2023-10-12 inside its timeline of the rumored Swift–Kelce romance, and flags the June 29 date as the candidate origin point of the whole sequence: "Is this where it all begin?" The friendship bracelet tradition comes from Swift's Eras Tour.


---


# Swift's Eagles fandom makes her Chiefs cheering a signal — but only of affiliation

In The Age's 2023-09-26 timeline of Taylor Swift's NFL takeover, the evidential weight of Swift's Arrowhead appearance rests on a fandom conflict. Swift is known as an Eagles supporter: she is originally from Pennsylvania and references the team in "Gold Rush". So her visible backing of the Kansas City Chiefs — shouting "let's f—ing go" after Travis Kelce's touchdown, then chest-bumping other Chiefs fans, at the game following his 2023-09-21 invitation on The Pat McAfee Show — reads as abandoning her own civic team, which points to personal affiliation with Kelce. The warrant reaches fan behaviour only. It does not establish relationship status: a supporter switching teams signals affinity, not romance.


---


# Kelce's moustache line implies contact with Swift the record has not granted

In The Age's 2023-09-26 timeline, Travis Kelce says of the moustache he grows every year in honour of Chiefs head coach Andy Reid: "We're not going to bring up Taylor Swift in this episode… But something tells me she's going to like it." The warrant for reading this as evidence of contact is the audience he names but never accounts for: in July, on New Heights, he reported the friendship bracelet with his number never reached her, and that "she doesn't meet anybody, or at least she didn't want to meet me." A confident prediction about a person he had not met therefore suggests prior contact, and a planned meeting. The status is suggestion, not proof.


---


# The Bracelet Dead-End: July 2023's Asymmetric Swift–Kelce Outreach

Between Travis Kelce's friendship-bracelet attempt on the New Heights podcast in July 2023 and the September 2023 reports that he and Taylor Swift had been "quietly hanging out" for months, the only outreach he described ran through a channel that was closed by design. Kelce planned to give Swift a bracelet bearing his number at her Eras Tour concert in Kansas City. His grievance was Swift's performance-vocal-preservation routine: "she doesn't talk before or after her shows because she has to save her voice for the 44 songs she sings." "She doesn't meet anybody, or at least she didn't want to meet me, so I took it personal[sic]." The bracelet, as he put it, "never made it to her wrist or his digits to her phone." The Age's own timeline reads this as one-sided — "Was she just not that into him?" — but the venue was the constraint, not the signal: a no-contact rule built for 44 songs yields no evidence either way about him.


---


# Hard-Launch: The Deliberate Public Debut of a Couple

To "hard-launch" a relationship is to appear publicly as a couple for the first time, by design rather than by accident, thereby ending whatever speculation preceded it. In The Age's 26 September 2023 timeline of Taylor Swift's NFL takeover, the phrase asks whether Swift and Travis Kelce, on the day Kelce invited her to a game (announced 21 September 2023), were "finally about to hard-launch their friendship/potential romance to the world, laying all speculation to rest". The term distinguishes that intentional reveal from the ambiguous proximity before it: Kelce's New York trip during her 1989 re-recording, and September reports of "quietly hanging out" for months.


---

# Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." That denial of motive does not reach the documented record: a lengthy history of incidents reflecting inherent bias in Meta's processes, from both inside and outside the company, plus a third-party report Meta commissioned after the 2021 Hamas-Israel violence finding an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Calling removals a "bug" localizes harm to a single defect, while the bias here is distributed across language coverage, policy architecture, and escalation channels.


---


# Hypothesis: Meta's government agency partnerships bias moderation against Palestinian expression

A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

The hypothesis is falsified if removal and restriction rates for comparable Palestine-related content show no association with escalation in those agency channels: more reports or referrals routed through partner agencies, but unchanged enforcement rates, would sever the claimed link.

Scope: Meta's platforms, notably Instagram, in the period following Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade of Gaza.


---


# Gaza's devastation and Meta's stated Hamas content rules after October 2023

In the aftermath of Hamas' attack on Israelis, Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade — cutting access to electricity, water and vital supplies — have devastated Gaza, according to a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19. In response to the escalating violence, Meta said it is closely monitoring its platforms for violations and may inadvertently flag certain content, but never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view." Content praising or supporting Hamas, which governs Gaza and is designated as a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union, is expressly forbidden on Meta's platforms.


---


# Meta's suppression of Palestinian content is structural bias, not a bug — TechCrunch, 19 Oct 2023

TechCrunch's claim on 19 Oct 2023: Instagram's shadowbanning of Palestine-related content is "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes," not the technical error Meta invokes. Meta says it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated 18 Oct, insists "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." The assembled warrants make intent beside the point. Meta cannot navigate Arabic's over 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversifying language resources. Its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuance, such as content discussing violence without condoning it. Partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Enforcement tracks user reports: filmmaker Khitam Jabr lost 24 hours of posting on West Bank travel Reels she says drew anti-Palestine comments and reports. And during the 2021 Hamas–Israel outbreak, a report Meta commissioned from a third party concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation.


---


# Index: Meta's Moderation of Palestinian Voices (TechCrunch, 19 October 2023)

This document (doc_0106) is TechCrunch's 19 October 2023 report that Instagram users suspect Meta of shadowbanning — that is, limiting the visibility of — content about Palestine. Its definitional material covers shadowbanning and black-and-white policy design. Its structural-bias mechanisms include Meta's thin Arabic language resources (a language with over 25 dialects) and partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, set against Meta's ban on content supporting Hamas, designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union. Case material covers filmmaker Khitam Jabr's 24-hour restrictions and Bella Hadid's Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Counter-argument material carries Meta communications director Andy Stone's rebuttals and the Oct. 18 newsroom statement, plus the 2021 third-party human rights report behind the bias-versus-bug dispute.

# Meta's "bug" explanation cannot account for a multi-year pattern of restrictions on Palestinian content

Meta attributed the October 2023 Instagram shadowbanning complaints to a bug affecting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts. That single-incident technical account doesn't fit the pattern TechCrunch described on Oct. 19, 2023: the accusations were "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents" on Meta platforms reflecting an inherent bias against Palestinian users, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company, and involving restrictions on content that never supported Hamas. Meta's own commissioned third-party report, issued during the 2021 Hamas–Israel violence, concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. Meta also blamed technical errors for removing posts about Palestine during that 2021 conflict.


---


# Black-and-White Moderation Policy

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it." Content that describes violence without endorsing it fits neither the "allowed" nor the "banned" category cleanly, so it tends to be mis-flagged or removed. Meta was additionally criticized in the article for struggling with Arabic's cultural and linguistic nuances, a language with over 25 dialects.


---


# Meta-Commissioned Third-Party Report Found Adverse Human Rights Impact on Palestinian Users in 2021

The Sherman Act is the U.S. antitrust statute Epic Games planned to invoke against Google at the trial that began November 6, 2023, taking Section 1 and Section 2 claims alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, leads with an agreement theory, because Android allows sideloading and Epic cannot claim, as it did against Apple, that no other way exists to load apps. TechCrunch reported this on 2023-10-31, describing Pichai's testimony that Monday, two days after search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on 2023-10-28 that Google had paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default placement. In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. # "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

Read as a single structure rather than two verdicts, the findings a federal jury returned against Google — reported by Tim Sweeney of Epic Games in The Verge, 2023-12-12 — describe one loop with two ends.

One end is the monopolised product: Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems. The other end is the tied product: Google illegally tied its Google Play billing system to its app store.

The relation between the ends is the model. Whichever product a developer must accept to reach Android users also becomes the channel through which that developer's money moves, so control of distribution converts into control of payment — and the payment share Sweeney calls "huge taxes" paid to a few gatekeepers reinforces the distribution hold. Two holdings, one circuit.

In Epic Games' antitrust suit against Google, whose trial began on November 6th, 2023, Epic's core argument concerns Android app distribution. Epic argues that Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store's standard fees, that Google has created an illegal monopoly. The claimed harms are twofold: the monopoly unjustly enriches Google, and it artificially drives up app prices, because other app stores can't compete. Epic calls the standard in-app payment fees the "Google tax". The remedy Epic seeks is to break up Google's alleged monopoly on Android app stores and payment methods, so that developers aren't stuck paying that tax or passing the fee along to players.
