Epic Games' interest in Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023 — 1,180 days after Epic first sued — is the break-up of what it calls Google's illegal monopolies in "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing." Epic charges up to ten times more per transaction than you pay with PayPal. The theory is straightforward: if those two monopolies are dismantled, developers buying or selling on Android are no longer stuck paying the "Google tax," the 30%-style in-app payment fee critics named — and therefore no longer pass that fee along to consumers in higher app prices. In Epic v. Google, which went to trial on November 6th, 2023, the trial's outcome turns on the market definition the court adopts — the line of argument The Verge names "market definition." # Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Google's Drummond Called Microsoft's Search Default Anticompetitive in 2005

In 2005, after Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, Google legal chief David Drummond wrote to Microsoft arguing that the default was anticompetitive, according to a TechCrunch report dated 2023-10-31 on the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google. Drummond's letter rested on a claim about user behavior: most end users "do not change defaults," so the engine picked at the outset keeps the searches.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---

An interest-rate-sensitive sector is an equity grouping whose share prices move more than the market when the policy rate changes, because its cash flows are long-dated or its customers depend on credit. In *The Age*'s report of 2023-12-09, "How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence," the argument over whether AI "should be controlled or set free" is shown to run through OpenAI rather than through the abstract idea of the technology. The claim is tested by what happened inside that same company months later, when rebel board members tried to force out Altman on the belief they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity. Over five chaotic days, the control-versus-freedom argument stopped being a policy abstractions and turned into a single boardroom confrontation, one whose outcome giant investors and employees threatening to follow Altman out the door ultimately reversed when the board backed down. That episode "gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI" — and confirms the argument's logic: because OpenAI made both the promise and the hazard legible at once, every contest over AI's direction is now conducted by reference to it.

qid: Does the Sporting News article suggest that bettors earn a fixed profit when betting on the Red Sox, while the CBSSports.com article indicates that Spread betting involves wagering on the margin of victory rather than a fixed outcome?
context:
# A Placed Bet Locks In the Odds or Line Posted at Wagering

Sporting News (2023-11-06), in its guide to line shopping, states the rule in one sentence: "When you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted." A ticket is priced at the moment it is accepted. Subsequent moves — a spread shifting because the public bet heavily on one side, or odds changing on fresh injury and roster news — apply to bets still to come, not to the wager already placed, whether those later changes would have helped or hurt.


---


# Why Line Shopping Pays for the Time It Costs

The argument for line shopping is a mismatch between what it gains and what it costs. Sporting News's guide "Line Shopping in Sports Betting – How to Find the Best Odds" (2023-11-06) puts the cost at "just seconds" when a bettor uses a live odds feed showing differences between sportsbooks, or longer when working manually by installing more than one sports betting app on a phone and tapping among them to compare.

The gain is larger. Betting volume is rarely the same at every sportsbook, so one may be forced to move a line or change odds while another is not; prices may also differ from the opening. Caesars Sportsbook's point spreads can be "a half-point to two points better than the competition's," and its moneyline odds may be more favorable. A half-point at that size changes which side of a posted number a spread wager settles on. As the guide puts it, shopping around lets a bettor "lay less, win more, and improve your chances."


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.


---

# Lewis's unverified claim that SBF considered paying Trump ~$5B to skip a re-run

Michael Lewis, author of "Going Infinite" (debuting 2023-10-02, day one of Sam Bankman-Fried's Manhattan Federal Court trial), claimed in a 60 Minutes interview broadcast 2023-10-01 that Sam Bankman-Fried had concocted a plan to buy off Donald Trump to get him not to run again for president. Lewis recounted the reasoning as: "Like how much would it take to get an answer? There was a number that was kicking around… this was $5 billion."

The hypothesis remains unproven on two counts Lewis himself supplied. First, Bankman-Fried was never sure whether the $5 billion figure came directly from Trump. Those outlays were purchases of legitimacy and "edge," made while the company was still raising roughly $2 billion, including $1 billion in 2021, from Sequoia, Temasek and Tiger Global rather than earning solvency. Exchange volume peaking at $15 billion/day measured speculation, not stability. A counter-argument sits inside TechCrunch's Week in Review of 2023-10-07 on X's publicly stated post volume. In the opening statement reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04, prosecutor Thane Rehn pushed the government's case past the taking of FTX customer funds: Bankman-Fried allegedly directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers and forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. # Manchester United and Newcastle United Out of Europe After Finishing Bottom of Their 2023/24 Champions League Groups

Manchester United and Newcastle United will play no further part in European competition in 2023/24, having been eliminated by finishing bottom of their UEFA Champions League groups, Sporting News reported on 12 December 2023. Manchester United ended Group A last on 4 points from six matches, with one win, one draw and four defeats.


---


# Bayern's 1-0 at Old Trafford on 12 December 2023 ended Manchester United's European season

Manchester United 0-1 Bayern Munich at Old Trafford on 12 December 2023, the final matchweek of the 2023/24 UEFA Champions League Group A: Kingsley Coman scored the only goal for Thomas Tuchel's side, in what the Sporting News described as "a limp display" from the hosts. The defeat left Manchester United on 4 points from six games — one win, one draw, four losses, goal difference -3 — bottom of Group A and out of Europe altogether, while Bayern Munich finished top with 16 points from five wins and no losses.


---


# Navigating Sporting News' Champions League group-stage permutations review (12 December 2023)

Sporting News' 12 December 2023 article "Champions League permutations, scenarios: What teams need to qualify from groups for 2023/24 Round of 16 stage" is organised Group A through Group D onward, each section pairing a standings table (GP, W, D, L, GD, P, with qualifiers marked "(Q)") with prose on the decisive fixtures and what each club needed in the final matchweek of the 2023/24 UEFA Champions League group stage. The standfirst frames Manchester City's bid for back-to-back titles and the eliminations of Manchester United and Newcastle United. Two "MORE:" cross-links branch out: the Champions League Round of 16 schedule, draw & qualified teams, and Jude Bellingham's incredible stats for Real Madrid this season.

# 2023/24 Champions League Group A final standings after six matchdays

After six matchdays of 2023/24 UEFA Champions League Group A, Bayern Munich led on 16 points from 6 games (5 wins, 0 draws, 0 losses, goal difference +6). FC Copenhagen, also qualified, had 8 points (2 wins, 2 draws, 2 losses, GD 0), ahead of Galatasaray on 5 points (1 win, 2 draws, 3 losses, GD -3) and Manchester United on 4 points (1 win, 1 draw, 4 losses, GD -3). An unusual record sits behind Manchester City looking to go back-to-back after their triumph in last season's Champions League: they would be the first English club since Nottingham Forest in 1980 to successfully defend the trophy, per Sporting News' group-stage review dated 2023-12-12. The claim's scope is only English clubs, so it says nothing about the competition's wider history — Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and Barcelona, whom the same review credits with "strong group-stage campaigns" and places "in the mix towards the sharp end of the competition," fall outside it. # Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

Sporting News applied this on 2023-12-12, reviewing the UEFA Champions League group stage ahead of its final match night and examining what teams from each group needed to qualify for the Round of 16, of which 16 places were at stake.

Group A shows the method at its simplest. Bayern Munich had already qualified, but Copenhagen, Galatasaray and Manchester United all entered the final matchweek with a chance of joining them. Galatasaray knew that if they beat Copenhagen at Parken they would go through. Copenhagen won 1-0 through Lukas Lerager's only goal, which took Copenhagen into the knockout rounds and left Galatasaray on 5 points from 6 games. # Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:

- **The ISA**: the Information Services Agreement making Google default search on all Apple devices, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016.
- **The 2016 revenue-share renegotiation**: Apple sought a larger share of Google's search revenue from Apple-directed users; specific numbers were reserved for closed court sessions.
- **The no-alternative defence**: "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — Cue never considered switching providers or building Apple's own search.
- **Setup-choice arguments**: DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's iPhone setup screenshots (Appearance, location tracking, App Tracking Transparency) against Cue's "Setup is just critical stuff," plus the disputed ease of changing defaults.
- **Privacy versus payments**: Apple's privacy claims set against emails in which Cue railed at Google's privacy policies.


---


# Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

In its 2023-10-31 report on the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, TechCrunch stated that "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.


---


# Cue's rebuttal to the DOJ: Apple does not measure the Google ISA as a share of its profits

On September 26, 2023, in the US v. Google antitrust trial before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed Apple's senior vice president of Internet Services, Eddy Cue, on the Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the default-search deal with Google, in place since 2002, that pays Apple billions of dollars a year and which Cue renegotiated with CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Against her point that the ISA accounts for a significant portion of Apple's profits, Cue replied that Apple does not look at the money that way: the profits figure omits the work Apple did to make its platform attractive enough for the deal to perform. He had already argued the deal was about more than economics, and that "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time."


---


# US v Google's ripple effect on parallel Big Tech antitrust cases

A ruling in US v Google may have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases, since enforcers need one landmark judgment to demonstrate antitrust law remains relevant. The parallel matters named in a TechCrunch roundup dated 2023-11-13: the FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power; the DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products; and there's an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, wherein the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp. The proposition is falsified if those cases proceed and settle unaffected by the Google judgment. # Sweeney: Google's trillion-dollar size was no guardrail

Tim Sweeney's reaction to the Epic v. Google verdict, published in The Verge on 12 December 2023, undercuts the very expectation he voices: that a firm of Google's scale necessarily runs respectable processes and leadership checks against misconduct. "It was really disconcerting to see the extent of bad faith efforts that were going on in a company of Google's size," he said of the assumption that "you'd think a trillion-dollar company" would restrain itself. What he listed instead was wrongdoing diffused through routine commercial channels, not policed by them: leaking Epic's conversations to reporters to prompt negative stories; paying other developers off so they would not launch their own stores; secretly paying carriers and OEMs not to carry competing stores. When Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with makers such as OnePlus and with "carriers of all sorts", they said Google had already done a secret deal with them.


---

TechCrunch's 2023-10-31 account of the U.S. antitrust trial against Google records the observed effect of the Apple search deal in place since 2003: Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, and during that agreement Apple never switched to a Google search competitor and never let iPhone users choose a browser when setting up their iPhones.

# Why Line Shopping Pays for the Time It Costs

The argument for line shopping is a mismatch between what it gains and what it costs. Caesars Sportsbook's point spreads can be "a half-point to two points better than the competition's," and its moneyline odds may be more favorable. # Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

The suit's plaintiff, Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle, describes SGE as offering web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode, with answers delivered inside the results page rather than through a click to the source. In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.

The argument for line shopping is a mismatch between what it gains and what it costs. Caesars Sportsbook's point spreads can be "a half-point to two points better than the competition's," and its moneyline odds may be more favorable. # Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.

# Line Shopping: Checking Odds Across Multiple Sportsbooks

Line shopping is the practice of checking the lines and odds for a prospective bet at multiple online sports betting sites. Sporting News' guide to line shopping, published 6 Nov 2023, defines the process this way and describes its result as "quite often better odds and improved lines." # AI Tool Customer Withdrawal Predicted for 2024 as Marketing Claims Face Review

In TechCrunch's predictions article "8 predictions for AI in 2024" (TechCrunch, published 2023-12-19), the term "agent" is defined by capability of access rather than by output quality. An AI qualifies as an agent, the article argues, only when it can reach things like a user's spreadsheets, ticket buying interfaces, and transportation apps — the step beyond merely summarizing text or making lists of things, which the article treats as the baseline any model can already do. It dates the first tentative attempts at this "agent" approach to 2023, and notes none of them caught on.

TechCrunch's claim on 19 Oct 2023: Instagram's shadowbanning of Palestine-related content is "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes," not the technical error Meta invokes. Meta says it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated 18 Oct, insists "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." The assembled warrants make intent beside the point. Meta cannot navigate Arabic's over 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversifying language resources. Its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuance, such as content discussing violence without condoning it. Partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Enforcement tracks user reports: filmmaker Khitam Jabr lost 24 hours of posting on West Bank travel Reels she says drew anti-Palestine comments and reports. Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction, attributes part of ChatGPT's enduring popularity in a TechCrunch article published 2023-11-30 to a change in what such systems were built to be. Chatbots had existed for decades, but the models behind ChatGPT were far more sophisticated than what users were accustomed to. Training on vast data moved the design target away from specialized, domain-specific chatbots toward general-purpose systems that people drive through instruction prompting, on the condition that users need learn no new interaction language. Shang notes that "AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues."

TechCrunch's 2023-12-19 predictions piece "8 predictions for AI in 2024" hypothesizes that 2023's AI products "will not all survive by a long shot," even while underlying capabilities "continue to grow and advance." A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

The hypothesis is falsified if removal and restriction rates for comparable Palestine-related content show no association with escalation in those agency channels: more reports or referrals routed through partner agencies, but unchanged enforcement rates, would sever the claimed link.

Scope: Meta's platforms, notably Instagram, in the period following Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade of Gaza.

Hypothesis from TechCrunch's "8 predictions for AI in 2024" (published 2023-12-19): the hype built up in 2023 will be very hard for companies to follow through on. Machine-learning systems that enterprises adopted specifically in order to not fall behind carry vendor marketing claims, and those claims will face their quarterly and yearly reviews during 2024 — where, the authors expect, they will very likely be found wanting. Against the accusation that Instagram shadowbanned Stories about Palestine in October 2023, Meta communications director Andy Stone attributed the reduced reach to a technical fault rather than moderation policy. Stone declined to comment on the record for TechCrunch's story, dated 2023-10-19, and pointed to Meta's newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, which stated that Meta applies its policies "equally around the world" and that "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." # Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.


---


# Default placement, not search quality, sets rivals' scale — the testable counterfactual from Google antitrust testimony

A testable proposition emerging from testimony in the U.S. government's Google antitrust trial (TechCrunch, 2023-10-31): a search engine of comparable product quality given equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale in online search. The evidence base is rival executives' own accounts. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make deals with Apple like Google's — a deal in place since 2003. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. The proposition is falsified if a rival granted default placement of that kind failed to grow share, and it is the direct negation of Google's defense that it is default because it is the best.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---


# Google's Drummond Called Microsoft's Search Default Anticompetitive in 2005

In 2005, after Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, Google legal chief David Drummond wrote to Microsoft arguing that the default was anticompetitive, according to a TechCrunch report dated 2023-10-31 on the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google. Drummond's letter rested on a claim about user behavior: most end users "do not change defaults," so the engine picked at the outset keeps the searches.

# Some Sports Betting Apps Copy Lines Rather Than Set Their Own

As of Sporting News' line-shopping guide dated 2023-11-06, sportsbook pricing is not uniform across the market. The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services, which use computer models and algorithms weighing analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps, by contrast, simply copy those lines rather than produce prices of their own.


---


# "Higher-for-longer": the market's assumption that central banks hold rates elevated rather than cut quickly

"Higher-for-longer" names the market's assumption that a central bank keeps policy rates elevated well past the near term instead of cutting quickly — as Sydney Morning Herald reporting on 2023-10-01 put it, "Wall Street accepts a new normal where the Federal Reserve is likely to keep interest rates high for longer."

The concept describes expectations, not announced policy. Anchors cited then: the US Federal Reserve's main rate at its highest level since 2001, with the central bank signalling in the week before that it may cut in 2024 by less than earlier expected, and its next rate meeting ending November 1. In Australia, the RBA was expected to hold at its Tuesday meeting, with National Australia Bank forecasting another hike to 4.35 per cent in November.

Consequences observed: the 10-year US Treasury yield back at 4.58 per cent, near its highest since 2007; interest-rate-sensitive healthcare and consumer stocks weakest; the S&P 500 down 4.9 per cent in September.


---


# Sportsbook Opening Lines Come From Computer Models Run by Oddsmakers

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), the best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and dedicated oddsmaking services to produce their lines and odds. Those oddsmakers and oddsmaking services run computer models and algorithms that weigh analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, among other inputs, to develop the lines and odds before betting opens. Not every operator does this work itself: other sports betting apps simply copy the lines that the oddsmakers and oddsmaking services set. The models' inputs are therefore the origin point for the prices that later move on public betting.


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Futures Odds Diverge Across Sportsbooks Because of Liability, So Timing Matters

In a guide to line shopping published by Sporting News on 2023-11-06, a model of sportsbook pricing explains why futures are the exception to the usual uniformity of odds. Most game lines are similar at different sportsbooks, but the odds in futures markets can vary significantly. The mechanism is liability: sportsbooks sometimes have higher liabilities for specific teams and offer better odds on others to lay that off. Timing is everything. # Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.

Google, the antitrust trial over Google's search business, Eddy Cue testified on 2023-09-26 about what a "default search engine" means in practice: the engine preselected on a device, which a user must actively change rather than choose. # Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.

# Google–Apple Search Deal: Payment for Default Placement, Restraint on Chrome

Under the Google–Apple search deal, in place since 2003, Google pays Apple for default search placement in Safari: of the $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults across browsers, phones and platforms in 2021, about $18 billion went to Apple, according to testimony in the U.S. antitrust trial reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.

The consideration flowing back to Apple is restraint. Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, per Bloomberg, though Google had the means to do so through banners, pop-ups and similar prompts inside its other applications. That term's effect on Apple's own conduct: Apple never switched to a Google competitor as its search engine and never let iPhone users choose a browser when setting up their devices.

# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."

The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. # The Epic v. Google hypothesis: paid exclusion, not consumer preference, kept rival app stores off Android

Testable proposition from the Epic v. Google trial record, stated by Epic CEO Tim Sweeney in his interview with The Verge published 2023-12-12: rival Android app stores failed to reach devices because Google paid for that outcome — paying "other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores" and "paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores." Sweeney says he suspected these practices since 2018, early enough that critics called him a conspiracy theorist, and says the testimony confirmed them; when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with manufacturers like OnePlus and carriers of all sorts, they told him Google had already done a secret deal with them. Falsified if carriers, OEMs or developers declined competition for reasons documented independently of Google payments.


---


# Apple Never Switched Search Providers or Prompted Browser Choice Under Its Google Deal

TechCrunch's 2023-10-31 account of the U.S. antitrust trial against Google records the observed effect of the Apple search deal in place since 2003: Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, and during that agreement Apple never switched to a Google search competitor and never let iPhone users choose a browser when setting up their iPhones.


---


# Apple's wait-then-polish pattern as the model for its 2024 AI entry

TechCrunch's 2023-12-19 piece "8 predictions for AI in 2024" models Apple's likely AI entry on a repeated competitive pattern rather than on any announced product. According to the article, Apple has an established pattern of waiting, watching and learning from other companies' failures, then arriving with a refined and polished take that puts those earlier entrants to shame.

The prediction is that this pattern repeats in AI, for two reasons the article treats as the model's drivers. First, the timing rationale is defensive: if Apple waits too long, its competition may eat up the market. Second, and more importantly, the technology is described as ripe for Apple's particular kind of improvement — polish applied to rivals' rough prototypes — rather than as a frontier Apple must discover itself.


---


# Engadget's verdict: the Steam Deck OLED is a refinement, not a successor

In its 2023-11-09 review, Engadget scored the Steam Deck OLED 89 and concluded it "isn't the Steam Deck 2 some are waiting for, it's just a welcome improvement on an already good device" — a mid-cycle refresh from Valve, comparable to the Switch OLED. The evidence it marshals points one way: a 7.4-inch OLED at 1,000 nits peak and 90Hz replacing the original's 7-inch, 400-nit, 60Hz LCD; roughly 30 grams less weight; better thermals; and a Hades run of 4 hours 23 minutes against 2 hours 42 minutes on the LCD model, a 62 percent gain exceeding Valve's own 30 to 50 percent estimate. The single counterweight is the unchanged chassis — both listed cons, "Still ridiculously large" and "Seriously it's so big," say the same thing. Priced at $549 on Steam, the device reads as better, not new.


---


# Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

In its 2023-10-31 report on the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, TechCrunch stated that "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.

qid: Who is the individual that, according to reports from The Verge and TechCrunch, faced challenges managing the growth of FTX and Alameda Research, allegedly used FTX customer funds to buy out Binance, was informed about a financial discrepancy after a judge's intervention, and is accused by the prosecution of committing fraud for personal gain?
context:
# SEC alleges FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a multi-billion-dollar shortfall from customer funds

The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX, the cryptocurrency exchange Sam Bankman-Fried founded in 2019, was a fraud "from the start," diverting customers' funds to his crypto trading firm Alameda Research, with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds," according to reporting by The Verge on 2023-09-28, shortly before Bankman-Fried's trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy began.


---


# SBF Faces Seven Counts of Fraud and Money Laundering from FTX and Alameda Leadership

Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO and co-founder of the collapsed crypto exchange FTX, faces seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering allegedly committed while leading FTX and its sister trading firm Alameda Research. As of October 6, 2023, the trial was entering the defense phase after the prosecution had concluded its case and Bankman-Fried was set to testify in his own defense.


---


# Notre Dame professor Easton traced billions between Alameda Research and FTX to customer deposits

In week three of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, University of Notre Dame professor Peter Easton, who helped the government prosecutions of Enron and WorldCom, testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX (TechCrunch, Oct. 6, 2023). Easton testified that much of that funding came from customers, and that user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments, or direct funding toward political causes and charities. The reported coverage placed his testimony early in that week of proceedings.


---


# FTX's Collapse Traced to Alameda Research Drawing on Customer Funds

In The Verge's 2023-10-26 account of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, FTX collapsed as the result of Bankman-Fried's trading firm Alameda Research purloining the exchange's customers' funds. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, testified that Alameda took customer funds and that Bankman-Fried knew about it and even invested them against her advice; she also described the seven phony balance sheets she had created. Gary Wang, co-founder of FTX and Alameda Research, testified about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code. Customers who had money trapped on the FTX exchange when it collapsed lost access to funds that should have been available at any time they wanted it, even if the bankruptcy proceedings later make them whole.


---


# Binance's $2.1 billion redemption triggered the bank run on FTX

Around the time CoinDesk exposed Alameda Research's balance sheet in early November 2022, Binance — then the world's largest crypto exchange — began pulling out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash held in BUSD and FTT. Per TechCrunch (2023-10-01), this essentially triggered a bank run on FTX. Binance had held an equity position in FTX from 2019 to 2021.


---


# Caroline Ellison: Alameda Research head and prosecution's star witness in the FTX trial

Caroline Ellison ran Alameda Research, the sister hedge fund of the crypto exchange FTX, and had been a girlfriend of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried. Per a CNBC report dated 2023-10-06 covering Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, she and FTX co-founder Gary Wang were integral members of Bankman-Fried's personal and professional inner circles, and both pleaded guilty in December 2022. Ellison is considered the prosecution's star witness and was expected to take the stand under a cooperation arrangement similar to Wang's.


---


# FTX and Alameda Research filed for Chapter 11 in mid-November 2022

FTX's collapse came after CoinDesk published Alameda Research's balance sheet showing $14.6 billion in assets and $8 billion in liabilities as of June 30, 2022, and after Binance pulled out its remaining $2.1 billion equivalent of cash in BUSD and FTT, triggering a bank run. FTX and Alameda filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in the U.S. in mid-November 2022 (TechCrunch, 2023-10-01).

[Provenance caveat: the assigned thought's wider industry-contagion element — BlockFi's November 2022 Chapter 11 filing and Genesis Global Trading's January 2023 filing — is not present in the source text supplied, so it is omitted rather than attributed to this article. If those facts appear in the full TechCrunch piece, they can be restored.]


---


# Prosecution's claim beyond diversion: concealed money flows and forged documents

In the opening statement reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04, prosecutor Thane Rehn pushed the government's case past the taking of FTX customer funds: Bankman-Fried allegedly directed employees to conceal the flow of money into FTX's coffers and forged financial documents distributed to lenders and investors. "The defendant lied to the world," Rehn alleged.


---


# Index: "Sam Bankman-Fried didn't ask where the $8 billion went" (The Verge, Oct 31, 2023)

Navigation index for The Verge's October 31, 2023 courtroom report on the June 2022 thread of Sam Bankman-Fried's self-testimony at his fraud trial — seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The decomposition entries attach to these parts of the article: the software bug overestimating Alameda's debt to FTX by about $8 billion, found by Adam Yedidia; Bankman-Fried's discovery of the fiat@ftx account in June 2022 but not its purpose until October; staff telling him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting"; his "no, no, and no" on directions, policies and measures protecting FTX customer money; Yedidia's padel tennis court exchange in June or July, and Judge Lewis Kaplan's intervention; and the Alameda balance sheet of June 13, 2022 listing the borrowed money as "ftx borrows."


---


# Wang's testimony: FTX platform code as the mechanism behind Alameda's access

Gary Wang's testimony at Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial in a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday, Oct. 5 and Friday, Oct. 6, 2023, put software at the center of the exposure: code baked into FTX's exchange platform gave sister hedge fund Alameda Research special access, including unlimited withdrawals on the exchange. Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, and those privileges, held while he ran the technology, are what he said allowed Alameda to withdraw and transfer funds derived from customers. Wang, who pleaded guilty in December and testified under a six-page cooperation agreement, faces up to 50 years in prison.


---


# Wang's courtroom admission named Bankman-Fried, Singh and Ellison in his FTX frauds

Gary Wang's account of his own FTX criminality reached past himself to named others. Asked by Assistant U.S. Attorney Nicolas Roos on Thursday 5 October 2023, "Did you commit financial crimes while working at FTX?", Wang answered "Yes," and said those crimes — wire and commodities fraud — were carried out with the help of Sam Bankman-Fried, FTX ex-engineering head Nishad Singh, and Caroline Ellison, who ran sister hedge fund Alameda Research. When Roos asked whether he saw any of those people in the courtroom, Wang stood, looked around, said "Yes," and identified "Sam Bankman-Fried." The argument's force is a sworn guilty plea, tempered by his six-page cooperation agreement and the up to 50 years in prison he still faces at sentencing.


---


# Cohen's Competing Model: Alameda and FTX as Lawful, Ordinary Businesses

In his opening statement on Oct 4, 2023, as reported by Fortune, defence lawyer Mark Cohen offered a model of the FTX–Alameda relationship at odds with the prosecution's two-entity structure. Alameda was not subterranean or shady but a successful hedge fund, he said; FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, Cohen argued: Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor and market maker, a financial entity acting as a trading partner for customers buying and selling cryptocurrencies. "Sam didn't defraud anyone," he said.

qid: Which company, reported by TechCrunch, has both invested $26.3 billion to maintain its default search engine status across devices and platforms in 2021, and has been accused in a class action lawsuit of harming news publishers' revenues and readership through anticompetitive practices?
context:
# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Apple took roughly $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default payments

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Index — Five revelations from the Google antitrust trial, 30–31 October 2023

A breakdown published by TechCrunch on 30–31 October 2023, anchored on Google CEO Sundar Pichai's Monday testimony in the U.S. government's antitrust trial over Google's 2020-era search dominance, organizes the week's disclosures into five points.

1. Default-payment totals: $26.3 billion paid in 2021 across browsers, phones and platforms including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, roughly $18 billion of it to Apple, per search head Prabhakar Raghavan's 28 October testimony.
2. The Chrome-promotion ban: Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users.
3. The iPhone preinstall bid: Pichai's 2018 attempt to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device.
4. Deleted chat logs: history-off default vs. the DOJ's litigation hold.
5. Google's early letter on defaults: a 2007 email citing 15% and 27% swings.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Google–Apple Search Deal: Payment for Default Placement, Restraint on Chrome

Under the Google–Apple search deal, in place since 2003, Google pays Apple for default search placement in Safari: of the $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults across browsers, phones and platforms in 2021, about $18 billion went to Apple, according to testimony in the U.S. antitrust trial reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.

The consideration flowing back to Apple is restraint. Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, per Bloomberg, though Google had the means to do so through banners, pop-ups and similar prompts inside its other applications. That term's effect on Apple's own conduct: Apple never switched to a Google competitor as its search engine and never let iPhone users choose a browser when setting up their devices.

context:

This page maps the internal structure of the CBSSports.com article "Taylor Swift-Travis Kelce timeline: Everything to know about rumored romance between pop star, Chiefs TE," published 2023-10-12. It has three parts: undated lede paragraphs (reporting Swift's attendance at five Chiefs games so far this season, including a Sunday game against the Chargers, with her last-week visit for Week 6 vs. the Denver Broncos on "Thursday Night Football"), dated timeline entries, and the break where the text ends.

# Jason Kelce Neither Confirmed Nor Denied Swift-Kelce Rumors, Sept 14, 2023

In CBSSports.com's Taylor Swift–Travis Kelce timeline (published 2023-10-12), the Sept. 14, 2023 entry is titled "Rumors aren't denied." Jason Kelce, the Philadelphia Eagles center who is Travis Kelce's brother and podcast partner on "New Heights" and whom the article describes as very close with his brother, was asked whether rumors of the two hanging out were true. He did not confirm them, and he did not deny them. The entry's stated substance is that non-denial — the source records no statement from Swift or from Travis Kelce at that date.

# The Kelce–Swift Timeline Argues by Accumulation, Not by Any Single Act

The CBSSports.com timeline dated 2023-10-12 supports its claim of a "rumored romance" between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce by accumulation rather than by proof. Individually, each entry is ambiguous: Kelce's July 26 friendship bracelet with "my number on it" could be a jersey number, his September 21 invitation on the Pat McAfee show was spoken as a joke, and Jason Kelce's September 14 response "did not confirm them, but he also did not deny them." On the Pat McAfee show on Sept 21, 2023, Travis Kelce addressed romance speculation with Taylor Swift: "It is hilarious how much traction this has actually got," comparing it to "that old game in school called telephone where everybody is just whispering in each others ear." In CBSSports.com's timeline (published 2023-10-12), speculation and public signal reinforce one another rather than resolve into fact. Kelce's dated gestures generate coverage, and the coverage raises the stakes of the next gesture: June 29, a friendship bracelet for fellow tight ends, "taking a page out of Taylor Swift's book"; July 26, a bracelet with his number for Swift after her concert ("12-time Grammy winner," "44 songs"); Aug. 5, a named celebrity crush; Sept. 14, Jason Kelce neither confirming nor denying; Sept. 17, Ian Eagle calling a touchdown "Kelce finds a blank space for the score"; Sept. 21, an on-air invite on the Pat McAfee show ("I threw the ball in her court"); Sept. 22, a "Vigilante Sh--" bracelet; Sept. 24, Swift at Arrowhead for the Week 3 Bears game, Kelce's three-yard catch making it 41-0 in a 41-10 win. The loop holds only while nothing is confirmed, so its output is escalating attention — five Chiefs games attended — not established fact.


---


# Travis Kelce made a friendship bracelet for NFL tight end camp newcomers, June 29, 2023

On June 29, 2023, Travis Kelce made a friendship bracelet to give to the newcomers at a camp for NFL tight ends, saying he was "taking a page out of Taylor Swift's book." CBSSports.com reported the episode on 2023-10-12 inside its timeline of the rumored Swift–Kelce romance, and flags the June 29 date as the candidate origin point of the whole sequence: "Is this where it all begin?" The friendship bracelet tradition comes from Swift's Eras Tour.

# Taylor Swift at the Chiefs–Broncos Week 6 "Thursday Night Football" Game (CBSSports.com Timeline)

CBSSports.com's 2023-10-12 timeline of the rumored Taylor Swift–Travis Kelce romance gives, as its second dated attendance record, that "last week, she was in attendance to watch the Chiefs as they defeated the Denver Broncos in Week 6 on 'Thursday Night Football.'" This follows the first, her appearance at the Chiefs' Week 3 game against the Chicago Bears on Sept. 24. The same article's lede counts five Chiefs games Swift attended that season, including the Sunday matchup against the Los Angeles Chargers at Arrowhead Stadium.


---


# Hard-Launch: The Deliberate Public Debut of a Couple

To "hard-launch" a relationship is to appear publicly as a couple for the first time, by design rather than by accident, thereby ending whatever speculation preceded it. In The Age's 26 September 2023 timeline of Taylor Swift's NFL takeover, the phrase asks whether Swift and Travis Kelce, on the day Kelce invited her to a game (announced 21 September 2023), were "finally about to hard-launch their friendship/potential romance to the world, laying all speculation to rest". The term distinguishes that intentional reveal from the ambiguous proximity before it: Kelce's New York trip during her 1989 re-recording, and September reports of "quietly hanging out" for months.

# Five Chiefs Games as the Swift-Kelce Speculation Marker

In a Taylor Swift–Travis Kelce timeline published by CBSSports.com on 2023-10-12, the article attributed intensified dating speculation to Swift attending five Kansas City Chiefs games so far in the 2023 regular season, including the Sunday game against the Los Angeles Chargers. The article also placed her first attendance at a Chiefs game in the month before its publication.
