# Kelce's August 2023 New York trip overlapped Swift's 1989 re-recording sessions

Travis Kelce took a week off Chiefs training to visit New York City in August 2023 and, per Vulture, this happened to be while Taylor Swift was re-recording her 1989 tracks in that city. The hypothesis, set out in a timeline published by The Age on 26 September 2023: the overlap is not coincidence but private time together, before either publicly acknowledged meeting. The article calls this a "suspicion" reportedly confirmed in September 2023, when it was reported the two had been "quietly hanging out" for months. # Week in Review (WiR): TechCrunch's Weekly Tech News Digest

Week in Review, abbreviated WiR, is TechCrunch's weekly email digest of the past week in tech news. TechCrunch describes it as its column that highlights the major stories over the past few days, and pitches it as "a darn useful resource for folks on the go." The newsletter arrives in subscribers' inboxes every Saturday, and readers not yet subscribed are invited to sign up through a link in the email. # Legacy-Media Confirmation, Not Fan Detection, Converted Swift–Kelce Claims Into the Zeitgeist

The Age's 2023-09-26 timeline of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce describes a two-stage pipeline. Stage one — social-media fan detection — produced the claims: amateur "Swiftie sleuths" inferred a relationship, fed by Kelce's own remarks on the New Heights podcast in July and August 2023. Stage two converted those claims into shared fact: in September 2023 it was reported the two had been "quietly hanging out" for months, which the article names "the first, albeit tentative, confirmation from the media rather than from amateur Swiftie sleuths on social media". # Hypothesis: Meta's government agency partnerships bias moderation against Palestinian expression

A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

The hypothesis is falsified if removal and restriction rates for comparable Palestine-related content show no association with escalation in those agency channels: more reports or referrals routed through partner agencies, but unchanged enforcement rates, would sever the claimed link.

TechCrunch's Week in Review (WiR) edition of 2023-10-07, titled "Sam Altman backs teens' startup, Google unveils the Pixel 8 and TikTok tests an ad-free tier," indexes its stories in a fixed order. # More than 92% of Fortune 500 Companies Use ChatGPT (TechCrunch, 2023)

# Google Bard trained on news publisher content, Helena World Chronicle complaint alleges

In the class action antitrust complaint Helena World Chronicle filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023, the Arkansas publisher alleges that Google's Bard AI chatbot was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications." # Post/Allen Institute finding: News and Media sites are the third-largest category of AI training data

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Bellshaw's Internal Google Documents Turn Google's Own Default-Setting Criticism Against Its Consumer-Preference Defence

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google on 2023-10-31 (TechCrunch), Google's defence to paying for default search placement is consumer preference: everybody wants Google as the default engine because it is the best, so the practice is lawful business. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's exhibits undercut that position from inside Google. She showed CEO Sundar Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting recording that people who changed their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away saw Google searches drop 27% — the meeting summary told Pichai and other Google leaders that "focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The accompanying $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults in 2021, about $18 billion of it to Apple, is the budget version of that logic.


---


# Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

In its 2023-10-31 report on the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, TechCrunch stated that "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.


---


# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.

# Index: Eddy Cue testifies for Apple in US v. Google (The Verge, 2023-09-26)

Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:

- **The ISA**: the Information Services Agreement making Google default search on all Apple devices, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016.
- **The 2016 revenue-share renegotiation**: Apple sought a larger share of Google's search revenue from Apple-directed users; specific numbers were reserved for closed court sessions.
- **The no-alternative defence**: "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — Cue never considered switching providers or building Apple's own search.
- **Setup-choice arguments**: DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's iPhone setup screenshots (Appearance, location tracking, App Tracking Transparency) against Cue's "Setup is just critical stuff," plus the disputed ease of changing defaults.
- **Privacy versus payments**: Apple's privacy claims set against emails in which Cue railed at Google's privacy policies.

# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Sweeney: Google's trillion-dollar size was no guardrail

Tim Sweeney's reaction to the Epic v. Google verdict, published in The Verge on 12 December 2023, undercuts the very expectation he voices: that a firm of Google's scale necessarily runs respectable processes and leadership checks against misconduct. "It was really disconcerting to see the extent of bad faith efforts that were going on in a company of Google's size," he said of the assumption that "you'd think a trillion-dollar company" would restrain itself. What he listed instead was wrongdoing diffused through routine commercial channels, not policed by them: leaking Epic's conversations to reporters to prompt negative stories; paying other developers off so they would not launch their own stores; secretly paying carriers and OEMs not to carry competing stores. When Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with makers such as OnePlus and with "carriers of all sorts", they said Google had already done a secret deal with them.

In his courtroom account that The Verge described on 2023-10-28 as "the story of FTX, from his point of view," Sam Bankman-Fried began by informing the jury he is "somewhat introverted, naturally," then launched into a prolonged tour of his pre-Alameda Research life that the reporter skipped. Only after that detour did he reach 2017. The same morning included explanations of "Amazon Web Services" and "database."


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried: FTX founder and criminal fraud defendant

Sam Bankman-Fried is defined here as the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX and the defendant in a criminal fraud trial, as reported by The Verge on 2023-10-10. He was on trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Those characterizations come from the government's allegations, not from findings the article reports as settled.

# Google's Drummond Called Microsoft's Search Default Anticompetitive in 2005

In 2005, after Microsoft made Internet Explorer the default search engine, Google legal chief David Drummond wrote to Microsoft arguing that the default was anticompetitive, according to a TechCrunch report dated 2023-10-31 on the U.S. government's antitrust case against Google. Drummond's letter rested on a claim about user behavior: most end users "do not change defaults," so the engine picked at the outset keeps the searches.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Default placement, not search quality, sets rivals' scale — the testable counterfactual from Google antitrust testimony

A testable proposition emerging from testimony in the U.S. government's Google antitrust trial (TechCrunch, 2023-10-31): a search engine of comparable product quality given equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale in online search. The evidence base is rival executives' own accounts. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make deals with Apple like Google's — a deal in place since 2003. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. The proposition is falsified if a rival granted default placement of that kind failed to grow share, and it is the direct negation of Google's defense that it is default because it is the best.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Pichai's Loop: Default Payments, Data Intake, Search Quality

In the U.S. antitrust trial over Google's search dominance, CEO Sundar Pichai defended what Google spends on default placement with a self-reinforcing account of why the money is justified. Being the default on other companies' browsers, phones and platforms produces more searches; more searches mean more data taken in; more data make Google the best engine across those devices; and being the best explains why partners choose it and why further default payments are reasonable. TechCrunch reported this on 2023-10-31, describing Pichai's testimony that Monday, two days after search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified on 2023-10-28 that Google had paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default placement. Pichai added that the decision was made with the consumer in mind. The loop is Google's own testimony about its motives, not an independently established causal finding, and the government contests its premise.


---


# Microsoft and DuckDuckGo CEOs Tied Their Search Shortfalls to Missing Apple Default Deals

Earlier in October 2023, in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. Reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, citing The Information.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. qid: After TechCrunch reported on Meta's moderation issues affecting Palestinian voices on October 19, 2023, and again on Meta's ad-free subscription service being potentially illegal and unfair on November 30, 2023, was there consistency in the news source's critical perspective towards Meta's policies and practices?
context:
# Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." That denial of motive does not reach the documented record: a lengthy history of incidents reflecting inherent bias in Meta's processes, from both inside and outside the company, plus a third-party report Meta commissioned after the 2021 Hamas-Israel violence finding an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Calling removals a "bug" localizes harm to a single defect, while the bias here is distributed across language coverage, policy architecture, and escalation channels.


---


# Index: Meta's Moderation of Palestinian Voices (TechCrunch, 19 October 2023)

This document (doc_0106) is TechCrunch's 19 October 2023 report that Instagram users suspect Meta of shadowbanning — that is, limiting the visibility of — content about Palestine. Its definitional material covers shadowbanning and black-and-white policy design. Its structural-bias mechanisms include Meta's thin Arabic language resources (a language with over 25 dialects) and partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, set against Meta's ban on content supporting Hamas, designated a terrorist organization by the United States and the European Union. Case material covers filmmaker Khitam Jabr's 24-hour restrictions and Bella Hadid's Story views dropping by "almost 1 million." Counter-argument material carries Meta communications director Andy Stone's rebuttals and the Oct. 18 newsroom statement, plus the 2021 third-party human rights report behind the bias-versus-bug dispute.


---


# Meta's "bug" explanation cannot account for a multi-year pattern of restrictions on Palestinian content

Meta attributed the October 2023 Instagram shadowbanning complaints to a bug affecting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts. That single-incident technical account doesn't fit the pattern TechCrunch described on Oct. 19, 2023: the accusations were "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents" on Meta platforms reflecting an inherent bias against Palestinian users, documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company, and involving restrictions on content that never supported Hamas. Meta's own commissioned third-party report, issued during the 2021 Hamas–Israel violence, concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. Meta also blamed technical errors for removing posts about Palestine during that 2021 conflict.


---


# Meta's suppression of Palestinian content is structural bias, not a bug — TechCrunch, 19 Oct 2023

TechCrunch's claim on 19 Oct 2023: Instagram's shadowbanning of Palestine-related content is "the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes," not the technical error Meta invokes. Meta says it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated 18 Oct, insists "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." The assembled warrants make intent beside the point. Meta cannot navigate Arabic's over 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversifying language resources. Its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuance, such as content discussing violence without condoning it. Partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Enforcement tracks user reports: filmmaker Khitam Jabr lost 24 hours of posting on West Bank travel Reels she says drew anti-Palestine comments and reports. And during the 2021 Hamas–Israel outbreak, a report Meta commissioned from a third party concluded its actions had an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation.


---


# Meta's rebuttal to deliberate suppression of Palestinian voices: equal policy application and appeals

In its 19 October 2023 TechCrunch report on suspected Instagram shadowbanning of Palestine content, Meta's counter-argument came via communications director Andy Stone, who declined to comment on the record and pointed instead to Meta's newsroom post on the conflict, updated 18 October 2023. That post states: "Our policies are designed to keep people safe on our apps while giving everyone a voice … We apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice … We can make errors and that is why there is an appeals process for people to tell us when they think we have made the wrong decision, so we can look into it." Meta added that it may inadvertently flag content but never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view."


---


# Hypothesis: Meta's government agency partnerships bias moderation against Palestinian expression

A hypothesis drawn from a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: advocacy groups have raised concerns that Meta's partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform's policy decisions. Extending that concern into a testable claim, the partnerships shift content-policy outcomes against Palestinian expression — the same user group reported for posting Palestine-related content regardless of whether it violates Meta's policies, and restricted from features such as posting or commenting for 24 hours.

The hypothesis is falsified if removal and restriction rates for comparable Palestine-related content show no association with escalation in those agency channels: more reports or referrals routed through partner agencies, but unchanged enforcement rates, would sever the claimed link.

Scope: Meta's platforms, notably Instagram, in the period following Hamas' attack on Israelis and Israel's retaliatory airstrikes and total blockade of Gaza.


---


# Meta's Counter: Andy Stone Attributes Reduced Story Reach to a Bug, Not Bias

Against the accusation that Instagram shadowbanned Stories about Palestine in October 2023, Meta communications director Andy Stone attributed the reduced reach to a technical fault rather than moderation policy. In a Threads post, he wrote, "We identified a bug impacting all Stories that re-shared Reels and Feed posts" — meaning the limitation reached every account doing that, wherever located, irrespective of subject matter, and was corrected quickly. Stone declined to comment on the record for TechCrunch's story, dated 2023-10-19, and pointed to Meta's newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, which stated that Meta applies its policies "equally around the world" and that "there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." Meta had likewise blamed technical errors for removals of Palestine posts during the 2021 conflict.


---


# Black-and-White Moderation Policy

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it." Content that describes violence without endorsing it fits neither the "allowed" nor the "banned" category cleanly, so it tends to be mis-flagged or removed. Meta was additionally criticized in the article for struggling with Arabic's cultural and linguistic nuances, a language with over 25 dialects.


---


# Meta-Commissioned Third-Party Report Found Adverse Human Rights Impact on Palestinian Users in 2021

During the 2021 Hamas-Israel escalation, a third-party report commissioned by Meta concluded that the company's own actions had produced an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' right to freedom of expression and political participation. The finding, cited in a TechCrunch article published Oct. 19, 2023, is significant because Meta itself paid for the assessment, making it an internally sourced acknowledgment rather than an external allegation. Meta separately attributed its 2021 content removals to technical errors.

# Cue's rebuttal to the DOJ: Apple does not measure the Google ISA as a share of its profits

On September 26, 2023, in the US v. Google antitrust trial before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed Apple's senior vice president of Internet Services, Eddy Cue, on the Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the default-search deal with Google, in place since 2002, that pays Apple billions of dollars a year and which Cue renegotiated with CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Against her point that the ISA accounts for a significant portion of Apple's profits, Cue replied that Apple does not look at the money that way: the profits figure omits the work Apple did to make its platform attractive enough for the deal to perform. He had already argued the deal was about more than economics, and that "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time."


---


# Google's Top-20 Revenue Search Terms, Week of September 22, 2018

In the US v Google antitrust trial, Judge Amit Mehta ruled to make public a list of the 20 search terms that earned Google the most revenue during the week of September 22, 2018. Ordered by revenue, the terms were: iPhone 8, iPhone 8 plus, Auto insurance, Car insurance, Cheap flights, Car insurance quotes, DirecTV, Online colleges, AT&T, Hulu, iPhone, Uber, Spectrum, Comcast, Xfinity, Insurance quotes, Free credit report, Cheap car insurance, AARP, LifeLock. Redacted were revenue per search term, query counts per term, and a separate list ordered by queries rather than revenue. TechCrunch dated the report November 13, 2023 and noted its own date slip, tying iPhone 8 revenue to the device's release on September 22, 2017.


---


# Google's behavioural data as the personalisation engine across Search, mobile widgets and other services

In a search-engine comparison published in The Age on 2023-10-22, the author writes that the test "did remind me how much data Google collects — not just my searches but anything I say to a smart speaker, any search result or ad that I click." That accumulated behavioural data is the mechanism the article names for relevance: it "does also mean that Google (not just search but also mobile widgets and other services) personalises to me more effectively." The competing service in the same test, DuckDuckGo, collects less but "didn't perform as well and is harder to read." Personalisation in the article's account is therefore compounded across surfaces rather than confined to the search results page.


---


# Epic's price-harm claim rests on monopoly-set app store and payment fees

Epic's case against Google depends on one relation: that Google's app-store and payment-processing terms are set by monopoly power rather than by competition, and that the consequence is consumers pay more for apps than they would in a contested market. Epic's earlier legal filings suggested this upshot for consumers — higher prices for apps than there would be "if there were more competition and / or lower app store and payment processing fees." Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein argued the same structure at the opening described by The Verge on 2023-11-07, showing jurors 70 percent app profit margins on $12 billion in revenue a year, per Epic, and Google "pay[ing] actual and potential competitors not to compete." Epic sued Google in 2020 over in-app purchase fees. The claim fails if the fee levels would persist under competition.


---


# Vendor capability claims and user outcomes are weakly coupled — Gemini Pro, December 2023

The weakness of benchmark-derived vendor claims as evidence about real use shows up sharply in the Gemini Pro launch. In blog posts and press materials released the week of 2023-12-07, according to TechCrunch's "Early impressions of Google's Gemini aren't great," Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities and claimed the model meets or exceeds the performance of leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4. The end-user evidence that a "lite" version, Gemini Pro, began rolling out to Bard on 2023-12-06 does not refute those claims, and that is precisely the problem. Users posting on X reported wrong 2023 Oscar winners, a seven-letter answer to a request for a six-letter French word, stale Ukraine summaries, and failed Python and HTML coding attempts. Blog-asserted capability and observed outcome are only weakly related.


---


# Epic's day-one chart put Google's Play margins at 70 percent on $12 billion

During Epic's opening argument on day one of the Epic v. Google trial, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's app profit margins: 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, per Epic's figure. Bornstein used those charts to frame Google's alleged payments to competitors as protection of that margin.


---


# The Article's Argument: The Burden of Proof Makes the Google Case an Uphill Battle

In "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", published by The Age on 22 October 2023, the author argues that the US antitrust suit against Google "could be an uphill battle" because the government "has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo" — that is, show that Google's dominance as the default search provider was unlawfully won rather than earned by being, as Google contends, simply the best product. The same paragraph grants the case a countervailing value: for everyone outside the courtroom it "offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share," specifically whether Google is still focused on being the best, or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money even at the expense of product quality, and how "organic" its results are.


---


# Gatekeeper Commission Tax Model: Higher Consumer Prices and Unviable Product Categories

In a The Verge interview published 2023-12-12, after a federal jury found that Google holds an illegal monopoly over Android app distribution and in-app payment systems, Epic Games CEO and controlling shareholder Tim Sweeney described the market structure he was challenging. He called for change in an "industry which is being strangled by a few gatekeepers imposing insane amounts of control and extracting huge taxes." The model: concentration of distribution and billing power in a few hands acts as a tax levy. That tax has two linked effects, in Sweeney's account — it "raise[s] prices for consumers" and it makes "a lot of kinds of products just unviable," since categories whose margins cannot absorb the levy never get built.

# Contents index: TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup of US v Google

This TechCrunch roundup of November 13, 2023 indexes five sections. First, why US v Google matters and the remedies at stake before Judge Amit Mehta: sharing APIs, bans on anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, and surrendering data — the DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. Second, Google's concurrent antitrust matters: the Match Group settlement and the November 6 trial with Fortnite maker Epic Games over Google Play. Third, the declassified list of 20 search terms ordered by revenue for the week of September 22, 2018, and vertical search. Fourth, Jamie Rosenberg's November 8 testimony on MADA (11 pre-loaded Google apps) and RSA mechanics. Fifth, Expedia and Barry Diller on ad load.

# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.

# Black-and-White Moderation Policy

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it." Content that describes violence without endorsing it fits neither the "allowed" nor the "banned" category cleanly, so it tends to be mis-flagged or removed. Meta was additionally criticized in the article for struggling with Arabic's cultural and linguistic nuances, a language with over 25 dialects.

"Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.

# Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

Sporting News applied this on 2023-12-12, reviewing the UEFA Champions League group stage ahead of its final match night and examining what teams from each group needed to qualify for the Round of 16, of which 16 places were at stake.

Group A shows the method at its simplest. Bayern Munich had already qualified, but Copenhagen, Galatasaray and Manchester United all entered the final matchweek with a chance of joining them. Galatasaray knew that if they beat Copenhagen at Parken they would go through. Copenhagen won 1-0 through Lukas Lerager's only goal, which took Copenhagen into the knockout rounds and left Galatasaray on 5 points from 6 games. Manchester United were eliminated after a 1-0 defeat to Bayern at Old Trafford, Kingsley Coman scoring, leaving them bottom of the group on 4 points.

Sporting News (2023-11-06) describes the manual route to line shopping as installing several sportsbook apps on one phone and comparing odds by hand. The procedure: download and install more than one sports betting app on your phone, then tap around among the sportsbooks to compare lines and odds for the bets you plan. In each app, pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs to find the odds and line for that bet; moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets can all be shopped this way. Bet when you see an opportunity at better odds or an improved line compared to the competition. The trade-off: the manual task takes longer than an aggregated live odds feed, but you can check more sportsbooks, or the chosen few you feel consistently offer the best lines and odds.

context:
# The Rosewood dinner and the founding of OpenAI (2015)

OpenAI was the laboratory created later in 2015 out of a private dinner in a room at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, a favoured deal-making spot close to the venture capital offices of Sand Hill Road. There Elon Musk dined with Sam Altman, who was then running a tech incubator, and several researchers. The dinner came a few weeks after Musk and Google's Larry Page stopped speaking following a summer party in Napa Valley. Backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Musk and other funders, the new lab promised to protect the world from Page's vision. Per The Age, 9 Dec 2023, OpenAI later became valued at more than US$80 billion (A$123 billion), though the Musk-Altman partnership ended and the two stopped speaking.


---


# Hypothesis: OpenAI's leadership fallout could redirect attention and funding to Meta's LLaMA and AI startups

A hypothesis in TechCrunch's ChatGPT explainer (published 2023-09-28, updated through OpenAI's November 2023 leadership crisis) is that the turmoil may shift advantage to OpenAI's rivals. CEO and co-founder Sam Altman's firing and swift return "raised concerns about its direction and opened the door for competitors," and two beneficiary groups are named: established rivals such as Meta and its LLaMA family of large language models, and independent AI startups, which the article suggests may more easily "get attention and funding as the industry watches OpenAI implode and put itself back together." The mechanism is reputational and financial rather than technical, unfolding while ChatGPT already had 100 million weekly active users and use inside more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies. The article calls the outcome unsettled: "The fallout is still settling."


---


# OpenAI never published a research paper on ChatGPT itself

Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, observes pointedly that OpenAI — despite having released dozens of research papers on its models — never published one on ChatGPT. She made that remark in a TechCrunch article dated November 30, 2023, marking ChatGPT's first anniversary, while stopping short of calling ChatGPT an AI breakthrough per se.


---


# TechCrunch contrasts ChatGPT's minimal launch with an unsourced "fastest-growing consumer app" claim

TechCrunch's case for ChatGPT's significance on its first birthday (November 30, 2023) rests on a contrast between an unpromising origin and a superlative outcome. The chatbot shipped a year earlier as a "low-key research preview" — initially only a basic free-to-use, web-based, chat-focused interface on top of GPT-3.5, one of OpenAI's existing models. From that, the article asserts, it became OpenAI's most popular product ever and "the fastest-growing consumer app in history," a record stated without naming the data behind it. Sam Altman's retrospective tweet that evening — "a year ago tonight we were probably just sitting around the office putting the finishing touches on chatgpt … what a year it's been…" (@sama, November 30, 2023) — supplies the humble-origin half of the argument.


---


# OpenAI connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users

OpenAI connected ChatGPT to the live internet for all users, according to TechCrunch's running explainer on the chatbot (dated 2023-09-28). The rollout is notable for who it covered. Unlike GPT-4, which the article says "remains largely exclusive to paying ChatGPT users" — reachable free of charge only through Microsoft's Bing Chat in the Edge, Google Chrome and Safari browsers — the internet connection went to the entire user base rather than to subscribers alone. It arrived alongside a slew of updates announced around OpenAI DevDay, the company's first developer conference, held November 6.


---


# OpenAI as the pivot of AI's control-versus-freedom argument

In *The Age*'s report of 2023-12-09, "How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence," the argument over whether AI "should be controlled or set free" is shown to run through OpenAI rather than through the abstract idea of the technology. The reason is ChatGPT: thanks to that chatbot, OpenAI "has fundamentally changed the technology industry and has introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence." A lab valued at more than $US80 billion ($A123 billion) thereby became the shared reference point for a debate conducted among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators, and one that pits Elon Musk, Larry Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI against one another.

The claim is tested by what happened inside that same company months later, when rebel board members tried to force out Altman on the belief they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity. Over five chaotic days, the control-versus-freedom argument stopped being a policy abstractions and turned into a single boardroom confrontation, one whose outcome giant investors and employees threatening to follow Altman out the door ultimately reversed when the board backed down. That episode "gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI" — and confirms the argument's logic: because OpenAI made both the promise and the hazard legible at once, every contest over AI's direction is now conducted by reference to it.


---


# Adoption and Investment as Grounds for AI Chatbots Outlasting OpenAI's Leadership Crisis

TechCrunch's ChatGPT coverage (published 2023-09-28, updated through December 2023) argues that AI chatbots are not going away anytime soon, resting the claim on two grounds: measured adoption and OpenAI's continued investment.

Adoption: ChatGPT reached 100 million weekly active users since its initial launch nearly a year ago, and is used by more than 92% of Fortune 500 companies.

Investment: OpenAI announced GPT-4 Turbo, a multimodal API and a GPT store at its first developer conference, OpenAI DevDay, on November 6; connected ChatGPT to the internet for all users; integrated DALL-E 3; and re-enabled ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.

The reasoning is that a user base that large and a product roadmap that active do not reverse because CEO and co-founder Sam Altman was fired and swiftly returned — a turmoil the article says may instead empower Meta's LLaMA models and rival AI startups.

In December 2023, OpenAI announced a content agreement with Axel Springer, the Berlin-based news publisher that owns Business Insider and Politico, which OpenAI framed as helping "provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools." The agreement had two distinct limbs. First, OpenAI would train its generative AI models on Axel Springer's journalism. Second, it would add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT, so the reporting surfaces inside answers rather than only shaping the underlying model. That combination — a licensing deal that pays for a publisher's archive as training data while also giving that publisher's newest work privileged placement in a chatbot's responses — made the deal notable beyond the parties involved, and it was reported in TechCrunch's running ChatGPT timeline alongside other December 2023 OpenAI news, including the reopening of ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.


---


# OpenAI valued at more than US$80 billion in its latest funding round

OpenAI is valued at more than US$80 billion (A$123 billion), according to two people familiar with the company's latest funding round, as reported by The Age on 2023-12-09. That valuation attaches to the startup created in 2015 from a dinner between Elon Musk and Sam Altman at the Rosewood hotel in Menlo Park, California, and backed by hundreds of millions of dollars from Musk and other funders.

TechCrunch's predictions piece of 2023-12-19 reports that OpenAI's GPT store was originally planned for launch in December but was "understandably delayed due to the C-suite fracas" — the leadership shake-up of November 2023. The article describes the store as an "app store for AI" that OpenAI will push hard as the platform for AI tools.

In a guide to line shopping published by Sporting News on 2023-11-06, a model of sportsbook pricing explains why futures are the exception to the usual uniformity of odds. Most game lines are similar at different sportsbooks, but the odds in futures markets can vary significantly. # The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.

Sporting News (2023-11-06) describes the manual route to line shopping as installing several sportsbook apps on one phone and comparing odds by hand. The procedure: download and install more than one sports betting app on your phone, then tap around among the sportsbooks to compare lines and odds for the bets you plan. In each app, pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs to find the odds and line for that bet; moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets can all be shopped this way. Bet when you see an opportunity at better odds or an improved line compared to the competition. The trade-off: the manual task takes longer than an aggregated live odds feed, but you can check more sportsbooks, or the chosen few you feel consistently offer the best lines and odds.

# Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

Sporting News applied this on 2023-12-12, reviewing the UEFA Champions League group stage ahead of its final match night and examining what teams from each group needed to qualify for the Round of 16, of which 16 places were at stake.

Group A shows the method at its simplest. Bayern Munich had already qualified, but Copenhagen, Galatasaray and Manchester United all entered the final matchweek with a chance of joining them. The 2023 article *How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence* (The Age, 2023-12-09) describes Eliezer Yudkowsky as an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher rather than a credentialed computer scientist, and as a leader of a community who called themselves Rationalists and, in later years, effective altruists. They believed AI could cure cancer or solve climate change but worried bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Yudkowsky ran a Thiel-funded AI lab and an annual conference on the singularity, and Demis Hassabis's two British co-founders were among those connected to him.


---


# The Paradox at the Heart of the AI Race: Fear and Ambition Entangled

As reported by The Age on 2023-12-09, the competition among Silicon Valley's leading AI builders contains what the article calls a "brain-stretching paradox": the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches. They have justified their ambition with their strong belief that they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth. The founders caught in this contradiction are Elon Musk, Larry Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI. All have fought for a piece of a business that one day could be worth trillions of dollars, and for the power to shape it, even as the question of whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it frames their public debate.


---


# Episodes in The Age's account of AI's rise — index

Four scenes anchor The Age's 9 December 2023 account of AI's rise.

- **2015, Napa Valley:** Elon Musk and Larry Page argue over whether AI will elevate the world or destroy it — or at least inflict grave damage. They stop speaking soon after that party.
- **A few weeks later, Rosewood hotel, Menlo Park, California:** Musk dines with Sam Altman, then running a tech incubator, and several researchers in a private room — the dinner that led to OpenAI later in the year.
- **2010, Peter Thiel's San Francisco town house:** Demis Hassabis, a 34-year-old neuroscientist, finds a chessboard overlooking the Palace of Fine Arts and a swan pond; the birth of DeepMind follows.
- **November 2023, OpenAI's boardroom:** rebel board members try to force out Altman over five chaotic days, then back down.


---


# Artificial general intelligence (AGI): a machine that could do anything the brain could do

Artificial general intelligence, or AGI, is defined as a machine that could do anything the brain could do — general capability matching human cognition, rather than a tool built for one task. In 2010, Demis Hassabis, then a 34-year-old neuroscientist, and two colleagues who all lived in Britain were looking for money to start building it, pitching Peter Thiel at Thiel's San Francisco town house. The definition matters as a benchmark: at the time, after a half-century of research, the AI field had failed to deliver anything remotely close to the human brain, and few people were interested in funding AI at all.

(Source: "How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence," The Age, 2023-12-09.)

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.

Epic Games sued Apple and Google on the same day, August 13th, 2020, both over in-app payment fees critics call the "Apple tax" and "Google tax," but the two cases then moved at wildly different speeds. The Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021, and a ruling came down that September mostly in Apple's favor, with both parties still waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in. The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. # Epic v. Google after openings: what the evidence phase must settle

Following both sides' opening statements to the jury in early November 2023 — Epic Games' on Monday, 2023-11-06, and Google's later the same week, lasting 45 minutes — the Epic v. Google antitrust trial moves to its evidence phase, with several disputes deferred to later weeks. Testimony must first settle Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein's claim that "Google pays actual and potential competitors not to compete," including the alleged $360 million payment that kept Activision from opening an app store competing with Google Play; Activision told The Verge in 2022 it "never entered into an agreement that Activision would not open its own app store." The Sherman Act is the U.S. antitrust statute Epic Games planned to invoke against Google at the trial that began November 6, 2023, taking Section 1 and Section 2 claims alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. Epic's case rested on arguing that Google restrains competition within two separate markets: the distribution of apps to Android users, and the market for payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps.

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. # Apple took roughly $18 billion of Google's $26.3 billion in 2021 default payments

Of the $26.3 billion Google paid in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms — including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla — to be the default search engine, about $18 billion went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier in October 2023. TechCrunch reported the figure on October 31, 2023, during the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google; the Google–Apple default deal had been in place since 2003.


---


# Google's default-search deal with Apple dates to 2003

In its 2023-10-31 report on the U.S. antitrust trial against Google, TechCrunch stated that "Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003." That is the agreement making Google the default search engine on Apple devices, so it had been running roughly twenty years by the time the deal's cost came under scrutiny in court in late October 2023.


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Google–Apple Search Deal: Payment for Default Placement, Restraint on Chrome

Under the Google–Apple search deal, in place since 2003, Google pays Apple for default search placement in Safari: of the $26.3 billion Google spent on defaults across browsers, phones and platforms in 2021, about $18 billion went to Apple, according to testimony in the U.S. antitrust trial reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.

The consideration flowing back to Apple is restraint. Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users, per Bloomberg, though Google had the means to do so through banners, pop-ups and similar prompts inside its other applications. That term's effect on Apple's own conduct: Apple never switched to a Google competitor as its search engine and never let iPhone users choose a browser when setting up their devices.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. Recipients included the companies Apple, Samsung and Mozilla. Of that $26.3 billion total, roughly $18 billion went directly to Apple, under a Google–Apple search deal in place since 2003.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 for default search status, per US v Google disclosures

In the previous TechCrunch roundup from the US v Google antitrust trial, disclosures showed Google spent $26.3 billion in 2021 making itself the default search engine across platforms. That same roundup reported Google had tried to have Chrome preinstalled on iPhones. Both facts were carried into TechCrunch's roundup published on November 13, 2023.


---


# Microsoft and DuckDuckGo CEOs Tied Their Search Shortfalls to Missing Apple Default Deals

Earlier in October 2023, in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. Reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, citing The Information.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Default placement, not search quality, sets rivals' scale — the testable counterfactual from Google antitrust testimony

A testable proposition emerging from testimony in the U.S. government's Google antitrust trial (TechCrunch, 2023-10-31): a search engine of comparable product quality given equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale in online search. The evidence base is rival executives' own accounts. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make deals with Apple like Google's — a deal in place since 2003. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. The proposition is falsified if a rival granted default placement of that kind failed to grow share, and it is the direct negation of Google's defense that it is default because it is the best.


---


# Index — Five revelations from the Google antitrust trial, 30–31 October 2023

A breakdown published by TechCrunch on 30–31 October 2023, anchored on Google CEO Sundar Pichai's Monday testimony in the U.S. government's antitrust trial over Google's 2020-era search dominance, organizes the week's disclosures into five points.

1. Default-payment totals: $26.3 billion paid in 2021 across browsers, phones and platforms including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, roughly $18 billion of it to Apple, per search head Prabhakar Raghavan's 28 October testimony.
2. The Chrome-promotion ban: Google agreed not to promote Chrome to Safari users.
3. The iPhone preinstall bid: Pichai's 2018 attempt to get Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device.
4. Deleted chat logs: history-off default vs. the DOJ's litigation hold.
5. Google's early letter on defaults: a 2007 email citing 15% and 27% swings.


---


# The Apple–Google ISA revenue-share: a percentage of Google's search ad revenue from Apple users

Under the Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the deal that makes Google the default search engine on Apple's products, in place since 2002 and renegotiated in its current form in 2016 by Eddy Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai — Google pays Apple a share of the advertising revenue Google earns from Apple users it directs toward Google Search. The model is a percentage, not a fixed sum. At the 2016 renegotiation, Apple pressed for a higher percentage of that revenue; Pichai wanted to keep the deal as it was. They compromised on a figure neither disclosed in open court: on 26 September 2023, in US v. Google before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Cue testified that discussion of specific numbers was reserved for closed court sessions. Google has paid Apple that percentage ever since, a sum the reporting describes as billions of dollars a year.

# Caroline Ellison: Alameda CEO at the Centre of Both Sides' FTX Trial Story

Caroline Ellison is the figure both sides leaned on in the opening statements of Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, as reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04. She was the CEO of Alameda Research, the crypto hedge fund Bankman-Fried also owned, and his on-again off-again girlfriend. Prosecutor Thane Rehn alleged that Bankman-Fried used Ellison as a front to get "secret access" to customer money — both cash and crypto. Defence lawyer Mark Cohen answered that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and pointed the finger at Ellison, who, he said, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. By then she was a former lieutenant turned government cooperator, which is why she was not among the prosecution's first two witnesses.


---


# Alameda Research: The Hedge Fund at the Centre of the FTX Trial

Alameda Research, the crypto hedge fund also owned by Sam Bankman-Fried, was named in both 2023-10-04 opening statements as central to the case. Prosecutor Thane Rehn called it the key to the alleged scheme, through which Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money. Defence lawyer Mark Cohen countered that Alameda was not "subterranean or shady" but "a successful hedge fund", acting legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker.


---


# Wang's testimony: FTX platform code as the mechanism behind Alameda's access

Gary Wang's testimony at Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial in a Manhattan courtroom on Thursday, Oct. 5 and Friday, Oct. 6, 2023, put software at the center of the exposure: code baked into FTX's exchange platform gave sister hedge fund Alameda Research special access, including unlimited withdrawals on the exchange. Wang, 30, was technology chief for FTX, and those privileges, held while he ran the technology, are what he said allowed Alameda to withdraw and transfer funds derived from customers. Wang, who pleaded guilty in December and testified under a six-page cooperation agreement, faces up to 50 years in prison.


---


# Defence's counter: Alameda's risk failure lay with CEO Caroline Ellison, not Bankman-Fried's design

Countering the prosecution's Alameda-centred account, Mark Cohen, one of Sam Bankman-Fried's lawyers, told the jury on Oct. 4, 2023 at the FTX founder's trial that Caroline Ellison, the former chief executive of Alameda Research, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. Alameda, he said, was a successful hedge fund, not a subterranean or shady front, and business practices between it and FTX were reasonable; Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor and market maker. Locating the failure in Ellison's risk management, rather than in Bankman-Fried's design, Cohen framed working at a startup as "like building a plane as you're flying it," adding that businesses sometimes fail.


---


# Can Sun testified SBF sought a "legal justification" for using consumer funds days before FTX's bankruptcy

Can Sun, FTX's former general counsel, testified in the third week of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud and money-laundering trial, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-06. Sun, who opted to cooperate with authorities as several of Bankman-Fried's former colleagues did, said Bankman-Fried asked him to create a theoretical "legal justification" for the use of billions in consumer funds. That request came just days before FTX filed for bankruptcy, and Sun's testimony was one of the prosecution's noteworthy moments that week.


---


# Notre Dame professor Easton traced billions between Alameda Research and FTX to customer deposits

In week three of Sam Bankman-Fried's fraud trial, University of Notre Dame professor Peter Easton, who helped the government prosecutions of Enron and WorldCom, testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX (TechCrunch, Oct. 6, 2023). Easton testified that much of that funding came from customers, and that user deposits were used by both FTX and Alameda to purchase real estate, make investments, or direct funding toward political causes and charities. The reported coverage placed his testimony early in that week of proceedings.


---


# FTX's Collapse Traced to Alameda Research Drawing on Customer Funds

In The Verge's 2023-10-26 account of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial, FTX collapsed as the result of Bankman-Fried's trading firm Alameda Research purloining the exchange's customers' funds. Caroline Ellison, Bankman-Fried's ex-girlfriend, testified that Alameda took customer funds and that Bankman-Fried knew about it and even invested them against her advice; she also described the seven phony balance sheets she had created. Gary Wang, co-founder of FTX and Alameda Research, testified about the secret privileges he had created for Alameda in the FTX code. Customers who had money trapped on the FTX exchange when it collapsed lost access to funds that should have been available at any time they wanted it, even if the bankruptcy proceedings later make them whole.


---


# Alameda's privileges left the hedge fund owing FTX $8 billion of customer deposits, Wang testified

Testifying in Manhattan federal court on 6 October 2023, FTX co-founder and technology chief Gary Wang told jurors that the special privileges granted to Alameda Research ultimately resulted in the hedge fund owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits. Wang gave his evidence under a cooperation agreement with the government, having pleaded guilty in December.


---


# Cohen's Competing Model: Alameda and FTX as Lawful, Ordinary Businesses

In his opening statement on Oct 4, 2023, as reported by Fortune, defence lawyer Mark Cohen offered a model of the FTX–Alameda relationship at odds with the prosecution's two-entity structure. Alameda was not subterranean or shady but a successful hedge fund, he said; FTX was no Ponzi scheme but a "very innovative, successful company." The business practices between the two were reasonable, Cohen argued: Alameda acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor and market maker, a financial entity acting as a trading partner for customers buying and selling cryptocurrencies. "Sam didn't defraud anyone," he said.


---


# Bankman-Fried Answered "No" to All Three Control Questions on FTX Customer Deposits

During his October 2023 trial testimony, Sam Bankman-Fried was asked three straightforward control questions about Alameda Research and FTX customer money, and answered no, no, and no: whether he had directed his employees at Alameda not to spend FTX customer deposits, whether he had put in any policies to prevent Alameda employees from spending FTX customer money, and whether he had put in place any measures at Alameda to protect the FTX customer money. The Verge reporter Liz Goodwin noted the contrast: "Oh, but he was testifying to Congress about keeping customer funds safe." The examination was conducted by prosecutor Danielle Sassoon in the FTX fraud trial, dated 2023-10-31.


---


# Ellison testified FTX Ventures' $2 billion came from money allocated to Alameda

During week two of Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX fraud trial, Caroline Ellison, former CEO of the trading firm Alameda Research, testified in detail that FTX Ventures — the $2 billion venture fund — was funded with money that had previously been allocated to Alameda by third-party lenders. TechCrunch reported Ellison's account of the fund's funding source in trial coverage dated 2023-10-06.


---


# Market Maker: The Defence's Definition of Alameda's Role on FTX

A market maker is a financial entity that acts as a trading partner for customers looking to buy and sell cryptocurrencies. Defense lawyer Mark Cohen used that definition during his opening statement on 2023-10-04 in Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, reported by Fortune, arguing Alameda Research acted legally as an FTX customer, payment processor, and market maker — ordinary function, not self-dealing.
