# Index: The Verge's "Epic v. Google, explained" (Sean Hollister, 2023-11-05)

Navigation for "Epic v. Google, explained," Sean Hollister's reader-facing explainer at The Verge, published 2023-11-05 ahead of the trial that opened November 6th — "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued"; Hollister appended a December 15th, 2023 update marking it superseded. Notes grouped by the question each answers:

- **Background — the August 13th, 2020 trigger**: Epic's hotfix letting Fortnite V-Bucks be bought at a discount outside app store fees, Apple and Google pulling Fortnite, Epic's two lawsuits and the "Llamacorn" attack ad.
- **Competing legal claims**: Epic's monopoly and Play-payments-tying allegations versus Google's sideloaded-app-safety and free-app-store defenses.
- **Market definition**: "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing" versus phones and app stores generally.
- **Apple-case precedent**: the September 2021 ruling mostly in Apple's favor, with the Supreme Court possibly weighing in.


---


# Epic's August 13, 2020 Fortnite hotfix triggered app-store removals and two antitrust suits

On August 13th, 2020, Epic Games, the studio behind Fortnite — a free-to-play game that sells in-game items with its virtual currency V-Bucks — publicly announced it was bypassing Apple and Google's app store fees. It deployed a hotfix update to Fortnite without either company's knowledge, letting players purchase V-Bucks directly through Epic's own payment processing option at a discount. Until that date, such purchases on Android or iOS devices installed through an official app store triggered an in-app payment fee to Google or Apple. Apple and Google almost immediately reacted by kicking Fortnite off their app stores for breaking the rules. Then Epic, per The Verge's November 5th, 2023 account, sprung a pre-planned response: two lawsuits and an attack ad depicting a Fortnite hero throwing a unicorn-llama hammer into a giant screen reminiscent of Apple's famous "1984" Macintosh ad.


---


# Epic Told OnePlus and Carriers Could Not Bundle Fortnite Due to Secret Google Deals

In a 2023-12-12 interview with The Verge after the federal jury verdict in Epic's antitrust case against Google, Epic CEO Tim Sweeney recounted a concrete corroboration of his long-held suspicions: when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with other smartphone manufacturers such as OnePlus and with "carriers of all sorts," those partners told Epic they could not do a deal because Google had already done a secret deal with them. Sweeney cited this alongside his claim that Google was paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores, and paying other developers not to launch their own stores.


---


# "Walled garden" in The Verge's Epic v. Google coverage: a closed platform controlling distribution and payment

In its December 12, 2023 account of Epic's jury verdict against Google, The Verge sets "walled garden" in quotation marks as a descriptor for Apple — Epic's "rival," which the piece notes "almost entirely won a similar case two years ago." In that usage, the term denotes a closed mobile platform whose owner controls both app distribution and in-app payment: the same two powers the nine-person federal jury found Google held an illegal monopoly over, in "Android app distribution and in-app payment systems," and had illegally tied together through "its Google Play billing system to its app store." Apple's verdict, by contrast, went Epic's way only in part.


---


# The "Llamacorn" Gambit: Epic's Provoked-Takedown Lawsuit Strategy

The "llamacorn" gambit names Epic Games' deliberately provocative legal strategy, executed on August 13th, 2020. Epic secretly deployed a hotfix to Fortnite — its free-to-play hit, monetised through the virtual currency V-Bucks — letting players buy V-Bucks directly through Epic's own payment processing at a discount, bypassing the in-app payment fee (critics' "Google tax" or "Apple tax") charged to players on Android and iOS devices who installed Fortnite through an official app store. That breach of the developer agreements got Fortnite removed from both stores, as Epic anticipated: it filed suit against Apple and Google the same day and released an attack ad showing a Fortnite hero swinging a unicorn-llama hammer at a giant screen echoing Apple's "1984" Macintosh commercial. The removals and the ad were the publicity engine, not setbacks. The label comes from The Verge's explainer of Epic v. Google, published 2023-11-05.


---


# The Verge live blog: SBF's first day of direct testimony, FTX trial, 2023-10-28

The Verge's FTX trial live-blog post covering Sam Bankman-Fried's first day of direct testimony on 2023-10-28. It runs from Judge Lewis Kaplan's instruction to answer counsel Mark Cohen's questions and three sustained "Objection, narrative!" calls, through the morning vocabulary detour ("Amazon Web Services," "database," "market manipulation"), to Alameda Research's 2017 founding, its Alameda County naming and internal label "Wireless Mouse," the hires of Gary Wang, Nishad Singh and Caroline Ellison, and Bankman-Fried's claim he did not supervise Wang. It also looks ahead to prosecutor Danielle Sassoon's cross-examination, and cuts off mid-figure on the arbitrage result he described — 50 percent to 100 percent annualized returns — before the FTX founding and his 20 percent chance-of-success estimate.


---


# The Epic v. Google hypothesis: paid exclusion, not consumer preference, kept rival app stores off Android

Testable proposition from the Epic v. Google trial record, stated by Epic CEO Tim Sweeney in his interview with The Verge published 2023-12-12: rival Android app stores failed to reach devices because Google paid for that outcome — paying "other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores" and "paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores." Sweeney says he suspected these practices since 2018, early enough that critics called him a conspiracy theorist, and says the testimony confirmed them; when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with manufacturers like OnePlus and carriers of all sorts, they told him Google had already done a secret deal with them. Falsified if carriers, OEMs or developers declined competition for reasons documented independently of Google payments.


---


# Week in Review (WiR): TechCrunch's Weekly Tech News Digest

Week in Review, abbreviated WiR, is TechCrunch's weekly email digest of the past week in tech news. TechCrunch describes it as its column that highlights the major stories over the past few days, and pitches it as "a darn useful resource for folks on the go." The newsletter arrives in subscribers' inboxes every Saturday, and readers not yet subscribed are invited to sign up through a link in the email. The edition dated 2023-10-07, for example, gathered Sam Altman backing the teen founders' AI startup Induced AI, Google's hardware event and the Pixel 8, and TikTok's $4.99 ad-free tier test.

# TechCrunch Week in Review, 7 October 2023 — Story Index

TechCrunch's Week in Review (WiR) edition of 2023-10-07, titled "Sam Altman backs teens' startup, Google unveils the Pixel 8 and TikTok tests an ad-free tier," indexes its stories in a fixed order. # Black-and-White Moderation Policy

A black-and-white moderation policy is a rule set that classifies content in binary terms — permitted or forbidden — with no graded middle category. Because of this binary design, such policies cannot effectively moderate nuanced speech, as illustrated by Meta Platforms, whose content rules are described in a TechCrunch article published 2023-10-19: "The company's black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it." Content that describes violence without endorsing it fits neither the "allowed" nor the "banned" category cleanly, so it tends to be mis-flagged or removed. Meta was additionally criticized in the article for struggling with Arabic's cultural and linguistic nuances, a language with over 25 dialects.


---


# Simplicity vs. complexity as the deciding factor in Epic v. Google

In an article published by The Verge on 2023-11-07, the reporter covering the Epic v. Google opening statements argues the trial "may come down to simple v. complicated": the jury may reward whichever side it understands most easily. Her own shift grounds that argument. Walking into the courtroom on Monday morning, she thought it "impossible" Google could lose, reasoning that if Epic couldn't prove Apple's walled iOS garden was a monopoly, the comparatively open Android was harder still to convict. After both sides addressed the jury, she was "not quite as sure," because the presentations were asymmetric. Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein painted "a black-and-white picture of good and evil with itself as the clear underdog," calling Google a bully and a cheat that "bribes" or "blocks" rivals. Google lead attorney Glenn Pomerantz spent his 45 minutes explaining that Android's dominance is merely the natural outcome of competing with the iPhone. The reporter judges Epic's narrative "compelling" and concludes she isn't sure Google's opening countered it.


---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Google Summit Notebooks Printed a Racially Insensitive "Cotton" Phrase, August 2023

Attendees of Google's K&I Black Summit, held in August 2023, were handed third-party notebooks whose inside pages were printed with the phrase "I was just cotton the moment, but I came back to take your notes," a play on "cotton" reported by TechCrunch's Dominic-Madori. TechCrunch described the wording as "highly insensitive" and the summit audience as mostly Black, so the merchandise was not well received. Afterward, Google pledged to "avoid similar situations as [it engages] with [merchandise] vendors going forward," according to TechCrunch's Week in Review of 2023-12-09.


---


# Deriving Qualification Permutations Before a Final Matchday

A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

Sporting News applied this on 2023-12-12, reviewing the UEFA Champions League group stage ahead of its final match night and examining what teams from each group needed to qualify for the Round of 16, of which 16 places were at stake.

Group A shows the method at its simplest. Bayern Munich had already qualified, but Copenhagen, Galatasaray and Manchester United all entered the final matchweek with a chance of joining them. Galatasaray knew that if they beat Copenhagen at Parken they would go through. Copenhagen won 1-0 through Lukas Lerager's only goal, which took Copenhagen into the knockout rounds and left Galatasaray on 5 points from 6 games. Manchester United were eliminated after a 1-0 defeat to Bayern at Old Trafford, Kingsley Coman scoring, leaving them bottom of the group on 4 points.


---


# Group-stage dominance predicts a deep 2023/24 Champions League knockout run

Sporting News on 12 December 2023 wrote that Bayern Munich, Real Madrid and Barcelona "will surely be in the mix towards the sharp end" of the 2023/24 UEFA Champions League. Generalised, that editorial claim is a hypothesis: a dominant group stage predicts a deep knockout run.

The observed grounds. Real Madrid, the 14-time European champions, won all six Group C games for 18 points and +9 goal difference. Bayern Munich topped Group A on 16 points from five wins, +6 goal difference.

The test is each club's exit round this season. If any of the three falls in the Round of 16 or the quarter-finals, group-stage form carried no signal about knockout form and the hypothesis is falsified.


---


# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.


---


# Swift Lyric Titles Invading NFL Commentary, September 2023: Football Fans and Swifties Collide

On September 17, 2023, Travis Kelce scored a touchdown against the Jaguars and CBS announcer Ian Eagle called it "Kelce finds a blank space for the score," borrowing Swift's 2014 hit *Blank Space* to poke fun at Kelce's newfound Swiftie status. NFL Network's Rich Eisen added a slew of lyric references to a preshow — "shake it off," "anti-hero" and "all too well" — and Kelce answered the Instagram montage with "Well played Rich … Well played." Suddenly, football fans and Swifties were living through a surprising collision: Swift's lyrics were infiltrating NFL game commentary while her fans were furiously becoming football experts. All that needed to happen was for Swift herself to infiltrate a game, settling the rumours once and for all.


---


# Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." That denial of motive does not reach the documented record: a lengthy history of incidents reflecting inherent bias in Meta's processes, from both inside and outside the company, plus a third-party report Meta commissioned after the 2021 Hamas-Israel violence finding an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Calling removals a "bug" localizes harm to a single defect, while the bias here is distributed across language coverage, policy architecture, and escalation channels.


---


# Kelce's Sept 21, 2023 On-Air Response to Swift Rumors: Telephone Analogy and Arrowhead Challenge

On the Pat McAfee show on Sept 21, 2023, Travis Kelce addressed romance speculation with Taylor Swift: "It is hilarious how much traction this has actually got," comparing it to "that old game in school called telephone where everybody is just whispering in each others ear." He then disclosed he had invited Swift to a game: "I threw the ball in her court," telling her he had seen her "rock the stage in Arrowhead" and she "might have to come see me rock the stage in Arrowhead and see which one is a little more lit" (CBSSports.com, 2023-10-12).

# Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.

# Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Because Android permits sideloading, Epic cannot claim, as it did against Apple, that there is no other way to load apps. So Epic hypothesizes that Google makes sideloading and alternative app stores cumbersome enough that their formal availability is not effective competition — a claim Epic will support with the figure that 90% of apps are still downloaded through Google Play.

The hypothesis is falsified if consumers install alternative stores such as Samsung's Galaxy Store or Amazon's Appstore at scale absent Google's agreements with device makers and developers, including the Anti-Fragmentation Agreements (AFAs) that bar OEMs from enabling frictionless downloading outside Google Play.

In the months following its launch, ChatGPT gained paid tiers with additional features, including a plan geared toward enterprise customers. Epic Games' claim against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, rests on one argument: Google's agreements with Android device manufacturers and app developers are anticompetitive restraints under Sections 1 and 2 of the Sherman Act and under California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law, regardless of whether Android permits sideloading.

That sideloading point matters because it distinguishes this case from Epic's suit against Apple, where Epic alleged there was no other way to load apps. Here Android does allow sideloading, so Epic contends those agreements — not the absence of alternatives — are what restrain competition in two markets: distribution of apps to Android users, and payment processing solutions for content inside Android apps. Epic cites Anti-Fragmentation Agreements blocking OEMs from modifying Android for frictionless downloading outside Google Play, through which 90% of apps are still downloaded.

As of the Epic Games v. Google trial that began on November 6, 2023, Google required apps selling digital content on Google Play to use its own first-party billing system, Google Play Billing. Sizing down, or staking money the bettor did not deposit, caps the loss on a low-probability outcome while leaving the payout upside intact: if the longshot goes on to win, the bettor collects the full odds on the original price rather than a shorter one obtained by waiting, since with five weeks left in the 2023 regular season a longshot can still become a contender, and the payout falls the longer the bet is deferred.

In opening statements in Epic Games' antitrust suit over the Google Play Store, covered by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Google displayed Epic's own internal messages to the jury, including "How do we not look like the bad guys?" and "everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" The Sherman Act is the U.S. antitrust statute Epic Games planned to invoke against Google at the trial that began November 6, 2023, taking Section 1 and Section 2 claims alongside California's Cartwright Act and Unfair Competition Law. # Champions League Group Stage Advancement Model: Top Two Advance, Third Goes to Europa League

The UEFA Champions League group stage for the 2023/24 season ran on a fixed four-club, six-matchday format, and Sporting News's permutations coverage of Dec. 12, 2023 shows the reward structure at each tier. A Champions League group permutation is worked out by taking a club's position in the table before a matchday is played and enumerating the results — in that club's own fixture and in the other fixture of the same matchday — that would leave it inside the qualifying places. The output is a checkable list, not a prediction: each combination can be compared against the actual scores once the matches finish.

Sporting News applied this on 2023-12-12, reviewing the UEFA Champions League group stage ahead of its final match night and examining what teams from each group needed to qualify for the Round of 16, of which 16 places were at stake.

Group A shows the method at its simplest. Bayern Munich had already qualified, but Copenhagen, Galatasaray and Manchester United all entered the final matchweek with a chance of joining them. Galatasaray knew that if they beat Copenhagen at Parken they would go through. Copenhagen won 1-0 through Lukas Lerager's only goal, which took Copenhagen into the knockout rounds and left Galatasaray on 5 points from 6 games. # How Android's OEM licensing — Play bundling plus Anti-Fragmentation Agreements — constrains rival app stores

At the start of Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google on November 6, 2023, Epic's case against Google's Android app store rested on the terms Google imposes on handset makers rather than on any ban on sideloading, which Android does allow. Two contract layers do the work. First, Google bundles the Play Store with other Google apps, and Android OEMs (original equipment manufacturers) have to agree to that bundling in order to use Android. Second, the "Anti-Fragmentation Agreements" (AFAs) Google signs with those OEMs prevent them from modifying Android to allow for frictionless downloading of apps outside of Google Play. Together, Epic argued, these agreements make it hard for alternative app stores to succeed and reach consumers, and 90% of apps are still downloaded through Google Play. The concept describes expectations, not announced policy. An interest-rate-sensitive sector is an equity grouping whose share prices move more than the market when the policy rate changes, because its cash flows are long-dated or its customers depend on credit. ---

In a search-engine comparison published in The Age on 2023-10-22, the author writes that the test "did remind me how much data Google collects — not just my searches but anything I say to a smart speaker, any search result or ad that I click." The central argument of The Verge's 2023-10-26 profile of the New York restaurant Thai Food Near Me is that the name is "a small but powerful symbol of Google's far-reaching impact on businesses over the past two decades and the lengths their owners will go to try to optimize their operations for the company's platforms." The restaurant is named after a literal Google search query and is optimized for the digital platforms diners use to find places nearby, not for the person walking past on the street or getting a recommendation from a friend.

The reasoning is circular by design, and that is its force: the name is "both notable and obvious," because anyone who has spent time searching online understands the reference immediately. The singularity is a trope of science fiction describing the moment at which intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity. In 2010, the tech investor Peter Thiel had developed a fascination with it, according to an article in The Age published on 2023-12-09, and that fascination oriented his involvement in artificial intelligence: he was courting founders building "artificial general intelligence," or AGI, a machine that could do anything the brain could do. The 2023 article *How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence* (The Age, 2023-12-09) describes Eliezer Yudkowsky as an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher rather than a credentialed computer scientist, and as a leader of a community who called themselves Rationalists and, in later years, effective altruists. # Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.

Earlier in October 2023, in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make similar deals with Apple. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. Reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, citing The Information.

A testable proposition emerging from testimony in the U.S. government's Google antitrust trial (TechCrunch, 2023-10-31): a search engine of comparable product quality given equal access to paid default placement would reach competitive scale in online search. The evidence base is rival executives' own accounts. Earlier in October 2023, the CEOs of Microsoft and DuckDuckGo testified that their search engines would have been far more successful, even competitive with Google, had they been able to make deals with Apple like Google's — a deal in place since 2003. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said he was willing to spend $15 billion per year to get Bing into Apple's default search. The proposition is falsified if a rival granted default placement of that kind failed to grow share, and it is the direct negation of Google's defense that it is default because it is the best.

qid: Does 'The Verge' article suggest that Google's deals with companies like Apple are unnecessary due to a plethora of alternatives, while 'The Age' and 'TechCrunch' articles imply Google's actions are primarily driven by profit maximization and anticompetitive behavior, respectively?
context:
# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Cue's rebuttal to the DOJ: Apple does not measure the Google ISA as a share of its profits

On September 26, 2023, in the US v. Google antitrust trial before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed Apple's senior vice president of Internet Services, Eddy Cue, on the Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the default-search deal with Google, in place since 2002, that pays Apple billions of dollars a year and which Cue renegotiated with CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Against her point that the ISA accounts for a significant portion of Apple's profits, Cue replied that Apple does not look at the money that way: the profits figure omits the work Apple did to make its platform attractive enough for the deal to perform. He had already argued the deal was about more than economics, and that "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time."


---


# Cue's 2023-09-26 "No Valid Alternative" Argument for Apple's Google Default

Testifying on 2023-09-26 in US v. Google, Apple's Eddy Cue argued that Apple never seriously considered switching to another search provider or building its own search product, because "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time." He said there still isn't one.

The claim's scope is the 2016 renegotiation period, when Cue negotiated the current iteration of the Information Services Agreement (ISA) with Google CEO Sundar Pichai — the deal, in place since 2002, that makes Google the default search engine on Apple devices and pays Apple billions of dollars a year.

Cue's warrant was that the choice was product-driven rather than purely economic: the ISA is Apple's own evaluation, and he said "We make Google be the default search engine because we've always thought it was the best. We pick the best one and let users easily change it." Supporting that, he told DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw he'd never really considered walking away from the deal.


---


# Index: Eddy Cue testifies for Apple in US v. Google (The Verge, 2023-09-26)

Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:

- **The ISA**: the Information Services Agreement making Google default search on all Apple devices, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016.
- **The 2016 revenue-share renegotiation**: Apple sought a larger share of Google's search revenue from Apple-directed users; specific numbers were reserved for closed court sessions.
- **The no-alternative defence**: "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — Cue never considered switching providers or building Apple's own search.
- **Setup-choice arguments**: DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's iPhone setup screenshots (Appearance, location tracking, App Tracking Transparency) against Cue's "Setup is just critical stuff," plus the disputed ease of changing defaults.
- **Privacy versus payments**: Apple's privacy claims set against emails in which Cue railed at Google's privacy policies.


---


# Pichai: Google asked Cook in 2018 to preinstall Google on every iOS device

Testifying in the U.S. antitrust trial against Google on Monday 30 October 2023, Google CEO Sundar Pichai admitted that in 2018 Google asked Apple CEO Tim Cook to preinstall Google on every iOS device, according to TechCrunch's report of 31 October 2023. Pichai pitched the move as tying Google and Apple's services so closely together that they would become inseparable, and as mutually profitable: Google would gain more searches and the associated data, while Apple would collect more revenue under the two companies' existing search agreement. Cook declined. Apple does not preload third-party software onto its devices and was not going to make an exception for Google.


---


# Remedies floated against Google if Judge Mehta finds liability

In TechCrunch's November 13, 2023 roundup of the US v. Google antitrust trial, the remedies sketched for Google all hinge on one condition: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google. The article names three. First, Google may have to change its behavior and share its APIs with third-party developers. Second, it may be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and with wireless carriers. Third, Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines, so those rivals can improve their products and attract more users. The DOJ has said that Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday, and the government's case is that Google uses its platforms and partner deals to block competition in search and advertising, cutting rivals off from the data they would need to improve their products.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# The Article's Argument: The Burden of Proof Makes the Google Case an Uphill Battle

In "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", published by The Age on 22 October 2023, the author argues that the US antitrust suit against Google "could be an uphill battle" because the government "has to prove that Google somehow broke the law to achieve the status quo" — that is, show that Google's dominance as the default search provider was unlawfully won rather than earned by being, as Google contends, simply the best product. The same paragraph grants the case a countervailing value: for everyone outside the courtroom it "offers a rare opportunity for some insight into what the tech giant does with its enormous market share," specifically whether Google is still focused on being the best, or uses its ubiquity to squeeze users for money even at the expense of product quality, and how "organic" its results are.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.

Sporting News, writing on 2023-11-06 in its guide to line shopping, reports that the lines and odds at BetMGM Sportsbook are consistently competitive. # DraftKings and FanDuel: DFS origins shape their sportsbooks

Sporting News on 2023-10-04 listed DraftKings Sportsbook and FanDuel Sportsbook among the best sportsbooks for NBA Rookie of the Year futures, tracing both to daily fantasy sports (DFS) operation before they became legal online sportsbooks. # DraftKings Runs More Open Betting Markets Than Most Online Sportsbooks

In its guide to line shopping, Sporting News (2023-11-06) reports that DraftKings Sportsbook "has more open betting markets than most online sportsbooks, and the lines and odds are always competitive." The observation appears among four brands Sporting News names as the biggest US online sportsbooks, alongside Caesars, BetMGM, and FanDuel, each described as offering competitive lines in dozens of states.

# Live Odds Feeds Are the Easiest Line-Shopping Method

Sporting News (2023-11-06) names a live odds feed as the easiest way to shop lines in US sports betting. Such a feed displays the differences in lines and odds for the same bet across many of the top sportsbooks in the country in one place — a "one-stop shop" where comparing prices takes just seconds rather than manually hopping between apps. The feed works for moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets. The trade-off: manual shopping across multiple downloaded sportsbook apps takes longer but can reach more books, or the few that consistently offer the best lines and odds.

# Line Shopping Extends to Every Priced Market, and How to Execute It

Line shopping — checking the posted lines and odds for the same prospective bet at multiple sportsbooks — is not confined to one market. Sporting News' line-shopping guide (2023-11-06) states that you can shop around for moneylines, point spreads, totals bets, prop bets, and more, adding that finding the best line or better odds on any bet "is like finding money." The workflow it prescribes: pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs — on a live odds feed or on several sportsbook apps installed on your phone — to reveal that bet's odds and lines across books, and bet when one shows better odds or an improved line than the competition.

# Stake Sizing for NFL Award Longshot Bets: Keep It Small or Use a Bonus Bet

Sporting News' December 5, 2023 guidance on NFL award longshots (MVP, OPOY, DPOY, Coach of the Year, Comeback Player of the Year) is to keep the stake small, or to use a promotional bonus bet if one is available at the sportsbook. The reasoning is that a player or several players have relatively short odds because they have been the best at their position all season, and there is just as good a reason why longshots carry odds as long as the ones they do. So the longshot's price reflects a genuine, not merely overlooked, case against it.

Sizing down, or staking money the bettor did not deposit, caps the loss on a low-probability outcome while leaving the payout upside intact: if the longshot goes on to win, the bettor collects the full odds on the original price rather than a shorter one obtained by waiting, since with five weeks left in the 2023 regular season a longshot can still become a contender, and the payout falls the longer the bet is deferred.


---


# Manual Line Shopping: Install Multiple Sportsbook Apps and Tap Between Them

Sporting News (2023-11-06) describes the manual route to line shopping as installing several sportsbook apps on one phone and comparing odds by hand. The procedure: download and install more than one sports betting app on your phone, then tap around among the sportsbooks to compare lines and odds for the bets you plan. In each app, pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs to find the odds and line for that bet; moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets can all be shopped this way. Bet when you see an opportunity at better odds or an improved line compared to the competition. The trade-off: the manual task takes longer than an aggregated live odds feed, but you can check more sportsbooks, or the chosen few you feel consistently offer the best lines and odds.

(Note delivered above. My attempt to log completion to the team mission log was rejected because this session is non-interactive — no action needed unless you want that logged.)


---


# Some Sports Betting Apps Copy Lines Rather Than Set Their Own

As of Sporting News' line-shopping guide dated 2023-11-06, sportsbook pricing is not uniform across the market. The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services, which use computer models and algorithms weighing analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps, by contrast, simply copy those lines rather than produce prices of their own.


---


# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.

# FanDuel's competitive odds and heavy promo volume favor line shoppers (Sporting News, 2023-11-06)

In its guide to line shopping, Sporting News (2023-11-06) reports that FanDuel is committed to posting competitive odds and runs so many generous promos and odds boosts that it is always worth a look. The observation appears among FanDuel Sportsbook, alongside Caesars, BetMGM, and DraftKings.

# Why Line Shopping Pays for the Time It Costs

The argument for line shopping is a mismatch between what it gains and what it costs. Sporting News's guide "Line Shopping in Sports Betting – How to Find the Best Odds" (2023-11-06) puts the cost at "just seconds" when a bettor uses a live odds feed showing differences between sportsbooks, or longer when working manually by installing more than one sports betting app on a phone and tapping among them to compare.

The gain is larger. Betting volume is rarely the same at every sportsbook, so one may be forced to move a line or change odds while another is not; prices may also differ from the opening. Caesars Sportsbook's point spreads can be "a half-point to two points better than the competition's," and its moneyline odds may be more favorable. A half-point at that size changes which side of a posted number a spread wager settles on. As the guide puts it, shopping around lets a bettor "lay less, win more, and improve your chances."

# Google antitrust actions surrounding the Helena World Chronicle publisher suit, December 2023

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and covered by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, arrived while several other Google proceedings were live. This note indexes that surrounding docket.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (digital ad technology): the DOJ's monopoly suit over Google's ad-tech stack, pending alongside the publisher case in late 2023.
- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.
- Canada settlement (November 2023): Google agreed to pay Canadian media $73.5 million (100 million Canadian dollars) a year, distributed by newsroom headcount. Meta's negotiations remained unresolved; Meta had begun blocking news in Canada in August.


---


# Epic's Antitrust Argument Against Apple Mostly Failed at Trial

Epic's antitrust argument against Apple did not succeed as its "Apple tax" campaign implied. In The Verge's explainer of Epic v. Google, published November 5th, 2023, the Apple suit is described as having gone to court in 2021, with a ruling that September "mostly decided in Apple's favor" — Epic failed to #FreeFortnite with its Llamacorn legal gambit, the August 13th, 2020 hotfix that let players buy V-Bucks directly through Epic's own payment processing and got Fortnite pulled from Apple's and Google's app stores for breaking the rules. The judge also picked a market definition "different entirely" from the one Epic pressed, and both parties ended up waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in.


---


# Publisher's Google antitrust suit alleges spoliation of chat messages, echoing Epic Games case

The class action antitrust suit that Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023 alleges evidence of improper spoliation by Google — specifically the destruction of chat messages. The complaint ties that allegation to a known precedent: the same issue of destroyed chat messages was raised in Epic Games' recent lawsuit against Google over app-store antitrust conduct, a case Epic won. The spoliation claim sits alongside the suit's other concerns, including allegedly changed AdSense rates, and appears among the counts supporting its requests for damages and injunctive relief against Google.


---


# US v Google's ripple effect on parallel Big Tech antitrust cases

A ruling in US v Google may have a ripple effect on other Big Tech cases, since enforcers need one landmark judgment to demonstrate antitrust law remains relevant. The parallel matters named in a TechCrunch roundup dated 2023-11-13: the FTC sued Amazon in September for using anticompetitive and unfair strategies to illegally maintain its monopoly power; the DOJ has been investigating Apple for years over the company's policy for third-party apps on its devices and whether it unfairly favors its own products; and there's an ongoing case between the FTC and Facebook, wherein the agency calls on Facebook to sell Instagram and WhatsApp. The proposition is falsified if those cases proceed and settle unaffected by the Google judgment. Judge Amit Mehta hears the Google case.


---


# Hausfeld frames the Google publishers suit as a fight for AI-era press competition

Housefeeds counsel Hausfeld, in the website announcement accompanying the class action filed the week of 2023-12-15 in the U.S. District Court in D.C., cast the case against Google and parent Alphabet as necessary to restore competition in the digital news and reference publishing markets and to establish guardrails for the free marketplace of ideas in the AI era. The suit, brought on behalf of Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle and a class of news publishers, invokes both the Sherman Act and the Clayton Act. Hausfeld's framing positions the relief sought — class-wide damages plus an injunction governing how Google uses publisher content in AI products — as a structural remedy for press sustainability, not merely a compensation claim.


---


# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.

TechCrunch's Week in Review roundup of that event listed announced updates covering the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro, the Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2, plus "other goodies." TechCrunch's report of the announcements was published on 2023-10-07.

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. # Verge's "Epic v. Google, explained" Is Flagged Outdated and Left Unfinished

The Verge's explainer "Epic v. Google, explained," published 2023-11-05 ahead of the trial that began November 6th, 2023, was revised on December 15th, 2023 with the banner: "It's basically over now. What happened? Read this, this, and this to get the whole picture." That banner replaces outcome reporting with three unlabeled links. # Epic's Twin Antitrust Suits Diverged: Apple Settled in 2021, Google Waited to 2023

Epic Games sued Apple and Google on the same day, August 13th, 2020, both over in-app payment fees critics call the "Apple tax" and "Google tax," but the two cases then moved at wildly different speeds. The Apple lawsuit went to court in 2021, and a ruling came down that September mostly in Apple's favor, with both parties still waiting for the Supreme Court to potentially weigh in. The Google suit never got its day in court during those years, delayed again and again, so that Epic v. Google trial beginning November 6th, 2023 arrived "a mere 1,180 days" after Epic filed, per The Verge's article dated 2023-11-05.

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." # Index: CBSSports.com Swift–Kelce timeline (Oct 12, 2023) — structure and coverage

This page maps the internal structure of the CBSSports.com article "Taylor Swift-Travis Kelce timeline: Everything to know about rumored romance between pop star, Chiefs TE," published 2023-10-12. It has three parts: undated lede paragraphs (reporting Swift's attendance at five Chiefs games so far this season, including a Sunday game against the Chargers, with her last-week visit for Week 6 vs. the Denver Broncos on "Thursday Night Football"), dated timeline entries, and the break where the text ends.

Dated entries run chronologically: June 29, July 26, Aug. 5, Sept. 14, Sept. 17, Sept. 21, Sept. 22, and Sept. 24. Two entries share the date Sept. 24, and the second is truncated mid-word ("Swift min"), so its content is unavailable. Several entries pair a timeline fact with a quoted Swift lyric; others carry quotations from Kelce's "New Heights" podcast or the Pat McAfee show.


---


# The Kelce–Swift Timeline Argues by Accumulation, Not by Any Single Act

The CBSSports.com timeline dated 2023-10-12 supports its claim of a "rumored romance" between Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce by accumulation rather than by proof. Individually, each entry is ambiguous: Kelce's July 26 friendship bracelet with "my number on it" could be a jersey number, his September 21 invitation on the Pat McAfee show was spoken as a joke, and Jason Kelce's September 14 response "did not confirm them, but he also did not deny them." What makes the case, in the article's framing, is that the entries chain: Kelce's June 29 and September 22 Swift-bracelet gestures, Swift's attendance at five Chiefs games this season including the September 24 Week 3 game against the Bears and the article's present-day Sunday game against the Chargers, her cheering a three-yard touchdown in a 41-10 win, and being seen chatting with his mother, Donna Kelce. The inference holds only while the acts are read as coordinated.


---


# Offshore Sportsbooks Are Illegal and Fraud-Exposed, So They Cannot Enter the ROTY Odds Comparison

Comparing NBA Rookie of the Year odds across every "online sportsbook" reachable on the open internet is unsound. Sporting News' NBA ROTY guide of 2023-10-04 concedes that offshore sportsbooks "advertise widely on the internet, but they are illegal and offer no protection against fraud and other criminal activities." The obligation it states is to use "only legal online sportsbooks for any type of betting," so the permissible set for ROTY futures is the licensed, regulated books — for that piece, DraftKings and FanDuel — not the cheapest quoted price wherever it appears.


---


# The Availability Objection to Demar Hamlin as Comeback Player of the Year Favorite

A Sporting News article on NFL award longshots, published December 5, 2023, names Demar Hamlin the current favorite for Comeback Player of the Year while stating the objection to that position. Returning from a life-threatening injury like a cardiac arrest makes Hamlin "a great candidate," the piece grants, but it then concedes voters could look elsewhere, since Hamlin has seldom been active on game day and has rarely seen the field. The objection is that his on-field contribution is minimal beside an award meant to recognize a playing comeback. The article leaves the outcome resting on how vital voters deem playing to be.


---


# Russell Wilson as the Comeback Player of the Year longshot (Sporting News, Dec. 5, 2023)

A Sporting News awards-odds piece dated December 5, 2023 names Demar Hamlin the favorite for NFL Comeback Player of the Year and Russell Wilson the longshot. That framing makes Wilson the stronger candidate on the award's own terms. Hamlin's case rests on surviving a cardiac arrest, but the article concedes he "has seldom been active on game day and rarely seen the field," which Wilson's plainly is not: he returned to play well enough in 2023 that the article credits Broncos coach Sean Payton with having "resurrected Russell Wilson's career," after 2022 in Denver was a disaster. The article also states the award "will depend on how vital voters deem playing to be." If production matters, Wilson deserves the consideration.


---


# Swift's five Chiefs games after Kelce's invite suggest mutual interest, not publicity

Hypothesis: Taylor Swift's attendance at five Chiefs games this 2023 season — reported in CBSSports.com's Oct 12, 2023 timeline, spanning from the Week 3 Chicago Bears game on Sept 24 through the Sunday Los Angeles Chargers game at Arrowhead Stadium — reflects reciprocal interest following Kelce's public Sept 21, 2023 invitation on the Pat McAfee Show, rather than a one-sided publicity cycle. It is falsified if the appearances were arranged through the club or her entourage, or if she attended games Kelce was not playing in.


---


# Five Chiefs Games as the Swift-Kelce Speculation Marker

In a Taylor Swift–Travis Kelce timeline published by CBSSports.com on 2023-10-12, the article attributed intensified dating speculation to Swift attending five Kansas City Chiefs games so far in the 2023 regular season, including the Sunday game against the Los Angeles Chargers. The article also placed her first attendance at a Chiefs game in the month before its publication.


---


# The Kelce–Swift loop: each unconfirmed act fed the rumors that amplified the next

In CBSSports.com's timeline (published 2023-10-12), speculation and public signal reinforce one another rather than resolve into fact. Kelce's dated gestures generate coverage, and the coverage raises the stakes of the next gesture: June 29, a friendship bracelet for fellow tight ends, "taking a page out of Taylor Swift's book"; July 26, a bracelet with his number for Swift after her concert ("12-time Grammy winner," "44 songs"); Aug. 5, a named celebrity crush; Sept. 14, Jason Kelce neither confirming nor denying; Sept. 17, Ian Eagle calling a touchdown "Kelce finds a blank space for the score"; Sept. 21, an on-air invite on the Pat McAfee show ("I threw the ball in her court"); Sept. 22, a "Vigilante Sh--" bracelet; Sept. 24, Swift at Arrowhead for the Week 3 Bears game, Kelce's three-yard catch making it 41-0 in a 41-10 win. The loop holds only while nothing is confirmed, so its output is escalating attention — five Chiefs games attended — not established fact.


---


# Futures Odds Diverge Across Sportsbooks Because of Liability, So Timing Matters

In a guide to line shopping published by Sporting News on 2023-11-06, a model of sportsbook pricing explains why futures are the exception to the usual uniformity of odds. Most game lines are similar at different sportsbooks, but the odds in futures markets can vary significantly. The mechanism is liability: sportsbooks sometimes have higher liabilities for specific teams and offer better odds on others to lay that off. Timing is everything. Getting it right lets a bettor take advantage of changes in different futures markets due to liability, and the only way to find these opportunities is shopping lines.


---


# Jason Kelce Neither Confirmed Nor Denied Swift-Kelce Rumors, Sept 14, 2023

In CBSSports.com's Taylor Swift–Travis Kelce timeline (published 2023-10-12), the Sept. 14, 2023 entry is titled "Rumors aren't denied." Jason Kelce, the Philadelphia Eagles center who is Travis Kelce's brother and podcast partner on "New Heights" and whom the article describes as very close with his brother, was asked whether rumors of the two hanging out were true. He did not confirm them, and he did not deny them. The entry's stated substance is that non-denial — the source records no statement from Swift or from Travis Kelce at that date.


---


# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.

# OpenAI never published a research paper on ChatGPT itself

Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, observes pointedly that OpenAI — despite having released dozens of research papers on its models — never published one on ChatGPT. She made that remark in a TechCrunch article dated November 30, 2023, marking ChatGPT's first anniversary, while stopping short of calling ChatGPT an AI breakthrough per se.


---


# The Information Services Agreement (ISA): Google's default-search contract with Apple

The Information Services Agreement (ISA) is the contract that makes Google's search engine the default on Apple's products, in exchange for payments from Google to Apple of billions of dollars a year. The ISA has been in place since 2002; its current iteration was negotiated in 2016 by Apple executive Eddy Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai, over what share of the revenue Google earns from Apple users directed to its search engine Apple would receive. The agreement does not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during device setup. The ISA is central to the US Department of Justice's antitrust case, US v. Google, according to The Verge's courtroom reporting of 2023-09-26.


---


# Steam Deck OLED's die-shrunk AMD APU buys battery and cooling, not speed

The Steam Deck OLED, reviewed by Engadget on 2023-11-09, uses a die-shrunk version of the custom AMD APU in the original Steam Deck — the CPU and GPU are the same, just more efficient. Engadget compares the approach to the process Sony uses for the PS4 Slim and PS5 Slim. Instead of collapsing the chassis around the smaller silicon, Valve spent the savings on a bigger battery and a larger fan in the existing body. So there is no extra performance: developers keep the same performance targets and need no games built specifically for the new hardware. The device ends up about 30 grams lighter than the original, the equivalent of five quarters.


---


# Jacobsen's three drags on US consumer spending, October 2023

Brian Jacobsen, chief economist at Annex Wealth Management, identified three factors that in combination depressed the growth of US consumer spending in late 2023: higher energy prices, student loan debt repayments, and "real disposable incomes that have been on a declining trajectory since June". His verdict on the trio was blunt — it "doesn't bode well". He described the slowdown of US consumer spending growth as having "come to a boil during a hot summer, and the temperature is really starting to come down". The written opinion was reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 1 October 2023. Supporting the first factor, US crude settled at $US90.79 a barrel on the Friday before, down 92¢ that day but far above the $US70 of June, at the highest level in more than a year. The article dated this assessment to the 29 September 2023 close, when August data showed US consumer spending growth cooler than expected alongside slightly cooler inflation — a reading positive for inflation but a risk to the spending that had kept the US economy out of recession, since resumed US student-loan repayments diverted dollars away from purchases.


---


# Biderman's "User Experience Breakthrough" vs. an AI Breakthrough

In an interview published by TechCrunch on 2023-11-30, Stella Biderman, an AI researcher at Booz Allen Hamilton and the open research group EleutherAI, separated an "AI breakthrough" from what she called a bonafide "user experience breakthrough." The second is a change in how already-existing capability is reached and consumed by ordinary people, not a leap in the capability itself. ChatGPT, released a year earlier as a "low-key research preview," was that: a free, web-based, chat-focused interface on top of OpenAI's existing model GPT-3.5, taking generative AI mainstream. Previously, she said, "you needed to have some skill, albeit not be an expert, to consistently get usable stuff out of [text-generating models]." OpenAI has released dozens of research papers on its models but never one on ChatGPT.


---


# Axel Springer licenses its news content to OpenAI, week of 15 December 2023

In the week of 15 December 2023, German publisher Axel Springer signed a deal with OpenAI to license its news for AI model training, a TechCrunch article on that date reported. The agreement was cited as one example of publishers "trying to get ahead of" the threat that AI-powered search poses to their traffic. Overall, publishers expected to lose 20-40% of website traffic once Google's AI products fully rolled out, per The WSJ, and Google then drove nearly 40% of publisher traffic (Similarweb).


---


# The Steam Deck OLED's 62 percent Hades battery gain rests on a worn baseline

The headline 62 percent battery improvement Engadget reports for the Steam Deck OLED overstates the new machine's gain, because the comparison unit is not a neutral baseline. The reviewer tested against her own original LCD Steam Deck — the model she first reviewed at launch and calls her most-played device, the one whose thumbsticks turned gray and whose short battery life she listed as a downside. On *Hades* at 800p with a 60 fps cap and similar brightness, the OLED lasted four hours and 23 minutes against the original's two hours and 42 minutes. Engadget concedes the caveat directly: batteries degrade with use. The resulting figure also exceeds Valve's own claim of 30 to 50 percent, so some of that margin belongs to the aged cell rather than to the OLED.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Shang: ChatGPT's target shifted from domain-specific chatbots to general-purpose systems via prompting

Ruoxi Shang, a third-year PhD student at the University of Washington studying human-AI interaction, attributes part of ChatGPT's enduring popularity in a TechCrunch article published 2023-11-30 to a change in what such systems were built to be. Chatbots had existed for decades, but the models behind ChatGPT were far more sophisticated than what users were accustomed to. Training on vast data moved the design target away from specialized, domain-specific chatbots toward general-purpose systems that people drive through instruction prompting, on the condition that users need learn no new interaction language. Shang notes that "AI models have enabled conversational agents to conduct conversations nearly indistinguishable from human dialogues."


---


# Hades battery test: Steam Deck OLED vs LCD (Engadget, 2023)

In Engadget's November 9, 2023 review of the Steam Deck OLED, the reviewer used Hades, her most-played title on the original Steam Deck, to test Valve's battery life claims, running both machines at the same settings: 800p with a 60 fps cap and similar brightness. The Steam Deck OLED lasted four hours and 23 minutes before dying; the original LCD model died after two hours and 42 minutes. That is a 62 percent improvement, surpassing Valve's own estimate of 30 to 50 percent longer battery life. She notes her LCD battery has had time to degrade.


---


# Google Bard trained on news publisher content, Helena World Chronicle complaint alleges

In the class action antitrust complaint Helena World Chronicle filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in December 2023, the Arkansas publisher alleges that Google's Bard AI chatbot was trained on a dataset that included "news, magazine and digital publications." In support, the complaint cites a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article on AI training data. That Post reporting, done with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data, according to a TechCrunch account published 2023-12-15.

Wall Street ended September 2023 — its worst month and quarter of the year — with further losses on Friday 29 September 2023. ---


# Cue's rebuttal to the DOJ: Apple does not measure the Google ISA as a share of its profits

On September 26, 2023, in the US v. Google antitrust trial before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed Apple's senior vice president of Internet Services, Eddy Cue, on the Information Services Agreement (ISA) — the default-search deal with Google, in place since 2002, that pays Apple billions of dollars a year and which Cue renegotiated with CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016. Against her point that the ISA accounts for a significant portion of Apple's profits, Cue replied that Apple does not look at the money that way: the profits figure omits the work Apple did to make its platform attractive enough for the deal to perform. He had already argued the deal was about more than economics, and that "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time."


---


# Epic's day-one chart put Google's Play margins at 70 percent on $12 billion

During Epic's opening argument on day one of the Epic v. Google trial, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein showed jurors charts of Google's app profit margins: 70 percent on $12 billion in revenue a year, per Epic's figure. Bornstein used those charts to frame Google's alleged payments to competitors as protection of that margin.

# Default homepage placement causally raises search volume — Google's 2007 internal finding

Google documented internally, in 2007, that preselected placement on a user's browser homepage causally increases a search engine's query volume. Data from a 2007 Google product strategy meeting, presented at trial on October 28, 2023 by U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw to Google CEO Sundar Pichai, showed that when people changed their browser homepage to Google they performed 15% more Google searches, and when they switched away their Google searches dropped 27%. The meeting summary sent to Pichai and other Google leaders recorded that "Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share." The relation holds user inertia and switching effort constant: default placement itself supplies the volume. Reported by TechCrunch on October 31, 2023.

# S&P 500 energy stocks stayed the market's best performers since summer 2023 despite a 2 per cent drop on 29 September 2023

Energy stocks in the S&P 500 fell 2 per cent as a group on Friday 29 September 2023, more than double the loss of any of the other 10 sectors in the index, after a barrel of US crude sank 92¢ to settle at $US90.79; ExxonMobil lost 1.6 per cent and Schlumberger 4.3 per cent. The Sydney Morning Herald reported on 1 October 2023 that the sector nevertheless remained the market's standout performers since the summer of 2023, with crude still up sharply from $US70 in June.
