# Trial Index — United States v. Sam Bankman-Fried, Day 2 (2023-10-04)

This index covers day two of the United States v. Sam Bankman-Fried trial on 2023-10-04, reported by Fortune. It orders the day's four movements: jury selection that Wednesday morning; the government's opening by prosecutor Thane Rehn, portraying Bankman-Fried as a lying "man" who stole billions; the defense opening by Mark Cohen countering with a good-faith "boy" startup founder; and the prosecution's first two witnesses, beginning with FTX customer Marc-Antoine Julliard, a London-based cocoa trader who said he never recovered almost $100,000. The article closes before the day's adjournment.


---


# The Prosecution's "Man," Not "Boy," Framing of Sam Bankman-Fried

In his opening statement on 2023-10-04, FTX trial prosecutor Thane Rehn rejected the media's "boy" genius label for crypto founders. He called Sam Bankman-Fried a "man" who "stole billions of dollars from thousands of victims," per Fortune — refusing the sympathetic startup archetype and asserting an adult actor's culpability.


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried: FTX founder and criminal fraud defendant

Sam Bankman-Fried is defined here as the founder of the failed cryptocurrency exchange FTX and the defendant in a criminal fraud trial, as reported by The Verge on 2023-10-10. He was on trial on seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The Securities and Exchange Commission alleges that FTX was a fraud "from the start," with a "multi-billion-dollar deficiency caused by his own misappropriation of customer funds." Those characterizations come from the government's allegations, not from findings the article reports as settled.


---


# Cohen's Startup Analogy as Warrant for Bankman-Fried's Practices

In his opening statement at Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial (Fortune, 2023-10-04), defence lawyer Mark Cohen repeatedly argued that “working at a startup is like building a plane as you’re flying it” and that businesses sometimes fail. He extended the analogy: as that plane approached the “eye of the storm,” Bankman-Fried did not act like someone who was guilty. The warrant Cohen offers for the business practices between FTX and Alameda Research is startup risk-taking, not fraudulent intent.


---


# SBF Criminal Trial Began 2023-10-03 on Seven Counts of Fraud and Conspiracy

The highly anticipated criminal trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO of the bankrupt crypto exchange FTX, began on Tuesday, 2023-10-03, according to a TechCrunch article dated 2023-10-01. The trial was to determine whether he is guilty of seven counts of fraud and conspiracy. A former federal prosecutor quoted in the article said: "The odds seem to be stacked against him at this point."


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's appearance and demeanor in court, 2023-10-04

Fortune's account of day two of Sam Bankman-Fried's trial in New York on 2023-10-04 records what it observed in the courtroom: his cheekbones were more prominent after spending about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison, and he spent most of his day there staring into a laptop while seated between his two attorneys.


---


# August 14, 2023 Superseding Indictment Calls SBF's Conflict-of-Interest Statements Lies

In a superseding indictment filed August 14, 2023, federal prosecutors alleged that Sam Bankman-Fried lied about consumer protection at the collapsed cryptocurrency exchange FTX. Specifically, the indictment states that Bankman-Fried's public claims that FTX was "avoiding or managing conflicts of interest" and that "as a general principle FTX segregates customer assets from its own assets across our platforms" were lies. The filing was made in the Southern District of New York case ahead of his fraud trial, as reported by The Verge on September 28, 2023.


---


# Cohen's Closing Argument: Bankman-Fried Gave Up Wealth Rather Than Steal, Fortune Says

Mark Cohen, defending Sam Bankman-Fried at FTX's criminal trial in New York, argued in his opening statement on 2023-10-04 that when the walls came closing in and his "plane approached the 'eye of the storm'," Bankman-Fried behaved as an innocent would, being willing to give up his personal wealth to make customers whole. Cohen concluded that the founder of two billion-dollar businesses "didn't steal any money."

Source: Fortune, 2023-10-04.


---


# Rehn's Core Allegation: SBF's Success "Was Built on Lies"

In his roughly 30-minute government opening statement on Oct. 4, 2023, in Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn's central claim was that Bankman-Fried's apparent success — "all of that, all of it, was built on lies" — because "behind the curtains, he was not what he appeared to be." The warrant is the divergence between Bankman-Fried repeatedly telling FTX customers their money was "safe and secure" and his alleged "secret access" to that customer money via Alameda Research.


---


# Rehn's Opening Portrait of Bankman-Fried as "On the Top of the World"

In his opening statement at Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, government prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury: "One year ago, it looked like the defendant was on the top of the world." Bankman-Fried ran a supposedly thriving crypto exchange, jetted between international locales, hobnobbed with celebrities like Tom Brady and Larry David, and repeatedly emphasized to customers that their money was safe and secure. Fortune reported this on 2023-10-04, day two of the trial.


---


# FTX: The Crypto Exchange at the Center of the Bankman-Fried Trial

FTX is the cryptocurrency exchange whose former chief executive, Sam Bankman-Fried, stood trial in October 2023 on allegations that he stole customer funds. In opening statements on the second day of the trial, prosecutor Thane Rehn told the jury that Bankman-Fried had repeatedly emphasized to FTX customers that "their money was safe and secure" but that "all of it, was built on lies". Defense lawyer Mark Cohen countered that "FTX was no Ponzi scheme" but a "very innovative, successful company", and that Bankman-Fried "didn't steal any money".


---


# High-Profile Spectators in Court on Day Two of the Bankman-Fried Trial

Day two of Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial, reported by Fortune on 2023-10-04, drew an audience "replete with big names": Bankman-Fried's professorial parents and Damian Williams, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York. The article cites that line-up as evidence of the case's prominence.


---


# Why the FTX trial is bigger than Sam Bankman-Fried

The criminal trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, which began in late September 2023 as reported by The Verge on 2023-09-28, is likely to matter beyond whether the founder of FTX and Alameda Research is convicted, because the evidence entered in open court could be rough on the entire crypto industry. Bankman-Fried faces seven criminal counts: two counts of wire fraud and five counts of conspiracy charges. The reputational stakes, the article argues, lie in unpredictability rather than outcome — the industry must absorb whatever the government introduces. Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University, framed it directly: "How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point?" Her answer: "This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out."


---


# Sam Bankman-Fried's FTX trial began with jury selection on 3 October 2023

TechCrunch reported on 2023-10-06 that the trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, former CEO and co-founder of the collapsed crypto exchange FTX, kicked off with jury selection on October 3. The case against him involves seven counts tied to fraud and money laundering at FTX and sister company Alameda. Courtroom access is limited, with no devices allowed.

# LinkedIn Announced a Suite of AI Features Across Job Hunting, Marketing and Sales Products, Week of 7 October 2023

In the week of 7 October 2023, LinkedIn unveiled a string of new AI features spanning its job hunting, marketing and sales products, according to Ingrid's reporting in TechCrunch's Week in Review digest published 2023-10-07. The announcements comprised three named additions: a big update to LinkedIn's Recruiter talent sourcing platform, with AI assistance built into it throughout; an AI-powered LinkedIn Learning coach; and a new AI-powered tool for marketing campaigns. The item was one of several in that week's roundup, which also covered Google's hardware event and a TikTok ad-free tier test.


---

# Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.

# Procedure: Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures (Sporting News, 2023-10-04)

---


# The Sportsbook Business Model: Balanced Action Wins Either Way

Per Sporting News (2023-11-06), a sportsbook's objective on each market is balanced action, not picking winners. "Every sportsbook's goal is to even out the betting on both sides of every bet," which lets it earn the profit already built into the odds and lines — the margin commonly called the vig — without worrying about which side wins. Lines move when the public bets heavily on one side; the originals come from oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms fed by analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data.


---


# Sportsbook Opening Lines Come From Computer Models Run by Oddsmakers

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), the best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and dedicated oddsmaking services to produce their lines and odds. Those oddsmakers and oddsmaking services run computer models and algorithms that weigh analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, among other inputs, to develop the lines and odds before betting opens. Not every operator does this work itself: other sports betting apps simply copy the lines that the oddsmakers and oddsmaking services set. The models' inputs are therefore the origin point for the prices that later move on public betting.


---


# Offshore Sportsbooks Are Illegal and Fraud-Exposed, So They Cannot Enter the ROTY Odds Comparison

Comparing NBA Rookie of the Year odds across every "online sportsbook" reachable on the open internet is unsound. The argument's scope is any available promotion at an online sportsbook, not merely the ROTY market. The reasoning: sportsbook bonuses arrive attached to conditions, so a welcome bonus or promo code claim accepted without reading those terms can turn out to be one you cannot actually cash out — the odds page's own instruction to qualify for a bonus by following its link is exactly the step where restrictions bite.


---


# Some Sports Betting Apps Copy Lines Rather Than Set Their Own

As of Sporting News' line-shopping guide dated 2023-11-06, sportsbook pricing is not uniform across the market. The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services, which use computer models and algorithms weighing analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps, by contrast, simply copy those lines rather than produce prices of their own.

Sporting News' page "NBA Rookie of the Year Odds – Wembanyama the early favorite," dated 2023-10-04, indexes the pre-season 2023-24 NBA Rookie of the Year futures market in four sections: "Current NBA ROTY odds" (odds by player), "Who are the NBA RoY odds favorites?" (the case for Victor Wembanyama, Scoot Henderson and Chet Holmgren), "How to bet on NBA Rookie of the Year" (sportsbook mechanics), and "Best sportsbooks for NBA Rookie of the Year odds" (DraftKings, FanDuel).

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.


---


# Steps to Open a Funded US Sportsbook Account Before Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures

Precondition (per Sporting News, 2023-10-04): you are in a US jurisdiction where online sportsbooks are legal. The source warns that offshore sportsbooks advertise widely but are illegal and offer no protection against fraud.

1. Visit the online sportsbook, click its "sign up" or "register" button, and fill in the details form.
2. Accept the sportsbook's terms and conditions.
3. Claim the welcome bonus by following the referring site's link to the sportsbook; if a code is needed, it appears on that site. Read the promotion's requirements first, since restrictions may apply.

Sporting News' December 5, 2023 guidance on NFL award longshots (MVP, OPOY, DPOY, Coach of the Year, Comeback Player of the Year) is to keep the stake small, or to use a promotional bonus bet if one is available at the sportsbook. The reasoning is that a player or several players have relatively short odds because they have been the best at their position all season, and there is just as good a reason why longshots carry odds as long as the ones they do. So the longshot's price reflects a genuine, not merely overlooked, case against it.

Sizing down, or staking money the bettor did not deposit, caps the loss on a low-probability outcome while leaving the payout upside intact: if the longshot goes on to win, the bettor collects the full odds on the original price rather than a shorter one obtained by waiting, since with five weeks left in the 2023 regular season a longshot can still become a contender, and the payout falls the longer the bet is deferred.

Sporting News (2023-11-06) names a live odds feed as the easiest way to shop lines in US sports betting. The trade-off: manual shopping across multiple downloaded sportsbook apps takes longer but can reach more books, or the few that consistently offer the best lines and odds.

qid: Which company is portrayed as an antagonist in a trial covered by The Verge, is associated with notions of foul play according to The Age, and is accused of harming news publishers' bottom lines through anticompetitive means as reported by TechCrunch?
context:
# Helena World Chronicle's D.C. class action alleges Google's anticompetitive siphoning of publisher content

The class action antitrust suit against Google and its parent Alphabet filed this week, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, was brought by Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher of two weekly newspapers, in the U.S. District Court in D.C. The complaint accuses Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior violating U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. Its core allegation is that Google "siphons off" news publishers' content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means — "starving the free press" and costing publishers "billions of dollars." The suit specifically cites new AI technologies such as Google's Search Generative Experience (SGE) and the Bard AI chatbot as worsening that harm.


---


# Complaint's core allegation: Google is "starving the free press" at a cost of billions

The central harm asserted in the class action antitrust complaint filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. is that Google is "starving the free press" by sharing publishers' content on Google, losing them "billions of dollars." The plaintiff, Helena World Chronicle, an Arkansas-based publisher that owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, brings the claim against Google and parent company Alphabet under the Sherman Act and other U.S. antitrust law, framing Google's redistribution of news content inside its own products as anticompetitive conduct that diverts publishers' content, readers and ad revenue.


---


# Google's changing AdSense rates cited as a further publisher harm in the Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. The Arkansas publisher — which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers — pleads that rate change alongside its better-documented claims about Google's AI search products as anticompetitive conduct under the Sherman Act, in the market its complaint calls the "digital news and publishing line of commerce." TechCrunch's account of the AdSense allegation is one clause: no rate figures, effective dates, or mechanism are given.


---


# Google Weaponized Epic's Internal Messages at Trial, November 2023

In opening statements in Epic Games' antitrust suit over the Google Play Store, covered by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Google displayed Epic's own internal messages to the jury, including "How do we not look like the bad guys?" and "everything we're attempting is technically a violation of Google's policy, right?" Shown without surrounding context, those lines served Google's effort to recast Epic — which had opened by painting itself as the underdog up against a bully and a cheat — as a company that knew it was breaking the rules while it was doing so.


---


# Google faced three search and app-store antitrust trials at once in mid-November 2023

As of mid-November 2023, Google was simultaneously litigating three antitrust matters touching search and app distribution, according to a TechCrunch report dated November 13, 2023. First, the Justice Department's landmark case against Google over search was roughly two months in, before Judge Amit Mehta. Second, Google had settled a separate antitrust lawsuit with dating site Match Group the previous week. Third, on November 6, 2023 Google went to trial against Fortnite maker Epic Games, which sought to prove Google engages in anticompetitive behavior regarding its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.


---


# DOJ's theory of harm in US v. Google: platform deals starve rivals of search data

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The DOJ has said Google gets 16 times more data than Bing does everyday. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# Epic's own mention of Project Liberty blunts Google's bad-faith angle

Google's attempt to cast Epic's Project Liberty as proof of bad faith runs into one complication: in the opening statements of Epic's 2020 monopoly suit against Google, reported by The Verge on 2023-11-07, Epic mentioned Project Liberty in its own opening. A fact the jury hears first from the side it is supposed to embarrass lands as disclosure, not exposure — so the same detail is a weaker sting when Google reaches for it later. Epic lead attorney Gary Bornstein spoke first, portraying Google as a bully that pays competitors not to compete.


---


# Complaint's SGE argument: Google's "walled garden" built on publishers' content

The Helena World Chronicle complaint, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. in the week of 2023-12-15 and reported by TechCrunch, contends that Google's Search Generative Experience keeps users inside Google's "walled garden" while reusing publishers' material. It argues that SGE, which it says "plagiarizes" their content, offers web searchers a conversational way to seek information but ultimately keeps them on Google rather than sending them onward. According to the complaint, Google's recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with "the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce." The complaint adds that publishers cannot block SGE, because it uses the same web crawler as Google's general search service, GoogleBot.


---


# Google calls Helena World Chronicle antitrust suit "meritless"

A Google spokesperson rejected the Helena World Chronicle class action filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. (TechCrunch, 2023-12-15) as "meritless," denying the complaint's central allegations — that Google breaks the Sherman Act by "siphoning off" publishers' content, readers and ad revenue, and that AI products including Search Generative Experience and Bard worsen the harm.


---


# Reach of the retracted Wired piece on Google query manipulation, October 2023

In October 2023, Wired published, then removed for not meeting its standards, an opinion article by lawyer and privacy advocate Megan Gray alleging that Google had revealed during the US antitrust trial that it manipulates search queries for ad revenue — for example replacing "children's clothing" with "NIKOLAI-brand kidswear". The Age reports that the extent of its sharing on social media and boosting in write-ups at other outlets shows how willing people are to accept foul play by Google, amid a standing suspicion of privacy invasion and inappropriate data handling.

SOURCE: The Age, "Is Google Search better than the rest? And is that fair?", 2023-10-22.

# Cooler US consumer spending cuts both ways: easing inflation, weakening growth

Economic data released Friday and reported on 1 October 2023 showed growth in spending by US consumers was cooler than expected in August, alongside inflation that was also a touch cooler than expected. That slowdown runs in two opposing directions. Fewer dollars pouring into purchases eases demand-pull pressure, giving companies less encouragement to try to raise prices further and supporting the Federal Reserve's attempt to push still-high inflation down to its target. But softer consumption may also dent what has been a big driver keeping the US economy out of a recession. Running through the discussion of Google's search dominance in *The Age* article of 2023-10-22 is the recurring claim that "Google Search was a lot better 10 years ago". The counter-argument: conceding that perception, the article calls it a stretch to attribute any decline to Google's monetisation practices — the suspicion that it uses its ubiquity to squeeze people for money even at the expense of product quality. In The Age's search-engine comparison (2023-10-22), the author draws one structural lesson from testing Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo: the Google Search bar functions as much as a way of returning to familiar sites as of looking up information. A rival provider that has not recorded those prior destinations therefore raises a switching cost that is behavioural rather than qualitative — moving away would be "temporarily annoying simply because it wouldn't remember all the places I've been".

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. # Fed's data-dependence at risk if US economic reports get postponed

Stated as a hypothesis: postponements of scheduled US economic reports could undermine the Federal Reserve's insistence that it will make its upcoming interest-rate decisions based on what incoming data say about the economy.

Second, it may be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and with wireless carriers. Third, Google might end up having to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines, so those rivals can improve their products and attract more users. # The Singularity as the Trope Orienting Peter Thiel's AI Giving

The singularity is a trope of science fiction describing the moment at which intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity. In 2010, the tech investor Peter Thiel had developed a fascination with it, according to an article in The Age published on 2023-12-09, and that fascination oriented his involvement in artificial intelligence: he was courting founders building "artificial general intelligence," or AGI, a machine that could do anything the brain could do. The same fear ran through the community of "Rationalists" — later called effective altruists — clustered around the internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky, who argued that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators.

Thiel made his fortune through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Elon Musk in the early days of PayPal.


---


# AI governance as a fight over who owns a trillion-dollar future

The public argument over whether artificial intelligence should be controlled or set free is also a contest for ownership. According to a December 9, 2023 report in The Age, the debate "has pitted some of the world's richest men against one another": Elon Musk, Larry Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, tech investor Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft, and Sam Altman of OpenAI. Each "have fought for a piece of the business – which one day could be worth trillions of dollars – and the power to shape it." The report names the paradox at the centre of that competition: the people who say they are most worried about AI are among the most determined to create it and enjoy its riches, justifying their ambition by claiming they alone can keep AI from endangering Earth.


---


# OpenAI as the pivot of AI's control-versus-freedom argument

In *The Age*'s report of 2023-12-09, "How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence," the argument over whether AI "should be controlled or set free" is shown to run through OpenAI rather than through the abstract idea of the technology. The reason is ChatGPT: thanks to that chatbot, OpenAI "has fundamentally changed the technology industry and has introduced the world to the risks and potential of artificial intelligence." A lab valued at more than $US80 billion ($A123 billion) thereby became the shared reference point for a debate conducted among Silicon Valley founders, chatbot users, academics, legislators and regulators, and one that pits Elon Musk, Larry Page, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Peter Thiel, Satya Nadella of Microsoft and Sam Altman of OpenAI against one another.

The claim is tested by what happened inside that same company months later, when rebel board members tried to force out Altman on the belief they could no longer trust him to build AI that would benefit humanity. Over five chaotic days, the control-versus-freedom argument stopped being a policy abstractions and turned into a single boardroom confrontation, one whose outcome giant investors and employees threatening to follow Altman out the door ultimately reversed when the board backed down. That episode "gave the world its first glimpse of the bitter feuds among those who will determine the future of AI" — and confirms the argument's logic: because OpenAI made both the promise and the hazard legible at once, every contest over AI's direction is now conducted by reference to it.


---


# Peter Thiel: Facebook and PayPal Wealth, Patron of Singularity-Focused AI Research

Peter Thiel is a Silicon Valley tech investor whose wealth came from an early investment in Facebook and from his work with Elon Musk in the early days of PayPal, according to a profile of AI's founders published by The Age on 9 December 2023. The article says Thiel had developed a fascination with the singularity, a trope of science fiction describing the moment when intelligent technology can no longer be controlled, and that he acted as a funder worth courting: in 2010 Demis Hassabis, then a 34-year-old neuroscientist seeking money to build artificial general intelligence, attended a cocktail party at Thiel's San Francisco town house, having prepared for a year because he knew Thiel loved chess.


---


# Eliezer Yudkowsky: internet philosopher behind the Rationalist AI-safety milieu

The 2023 article *How ego and fear fuelled the rise of artificial intelligence* (The Age, 2023-12-09) describes Eliezer Yudkowsky as an internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher rather than a credentialed computer scientist, and as a leader of a community who called themselves Rationalists and, in later years, effective altruists. They believed AI could cure cancer or solve climate change but worried bots might do things their creators had not intended, arguing that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators. Yudkowsky ran a Thiel-funded AI lab and an annual conference on the singularity, and Demis Hassabis's two British co-founders were among those connected to him.

Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# DOJ's Theory of Harm in the Google Antitrust Case: Defaults Cut Rivals Off From Data

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, as reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, the government's core allegation is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, and that this same lock-up hinders competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The theory therefore runs in two linked steps: owned distribution plus paid defaults deny rivals visibility, and denied visibility denies them the query data that would let their products reach a quality high enough to challenge Google. The claim over Google's dominance in the online search market was filed in 2020. It is separate from a claim filed in January by the Department of Justice along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, which aims to halt Google's anticompetitive scheme, unwind its monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising. Google's counter is that it is simply doing business, since partners want the best default engine.

- U.S. Department of Justice v. Google (2020): the earlier civil antitrust suit over search and search advertising.
- Epic Games v. Google: the app-store antitrust case, which Epic won; the Helena complaint borrows its finding of improper spoliation of evidence — Google's destruction of chat messages.

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# Google paid $26.3 billion for default search placement in 2021, court told

Testifying on 28 October 2023 in the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, Google's search head Prabhakar Raghavan stated that Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phone makers and platforms for making Google the default search engine. ---

Helena World Chronicle's class action against Google and parent company Alphabet, filed in the U.S. District Court in D.C. and reported by TechCrunch on 2023-12-15, alleges that Google's changing AdSense rates have economically harmed news publishers. ---

In the Justice Department's antitrust case against Google, roughly two months old as of 2023-11-13, the government's core theory of harm is that Google uses its platforms and its deals with partners to block out any competition in search or advertising, hindering competitors from accessing the data they would need to improve their products. The remedies on the table track that logic: if Judge Amit Mehta rules against Google, the company could be banned from making anticompetitive and exclusive deals with smartphone and computer manufacturers and wireless carriers, forced to share its APIs with third-party developers, or required to turn over all or most of the data it has collected to other search engines so they can improve their products and attract more users.


---


# Google Search Antitrust Trial: the 2020 Dominance Claim

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. That combination — a licensing deal that pays for a publisher's archive as training data while also giving that publisher's newest work privileged placement in a chatbot's responses — made the deal notable beyond the parties involved, and it was reported in TechCrunch's running ChatGPT timeline alongside other December 2023 OpenAI news, including the reopening of ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.


---


# Meta's moderation bias against Palestinian users: effect, not intent

Disparate moderation outcomes for Palestinian users on Meta's platforms are a function of the company's policy and tooling design, not of declared intent: absent intent to censor is fully compatible with systematically unequal effect. Meta told TechCrunch on 2023-10-19 that it never intends to "suppress a particular community or point of view," and its newsroom post, updated Oct. 18, stated "we apply these policies equally around the world and there is no truth to the suggestion that we are deliberately suppressing voice." That denial of motive does not reach the documented record: a lengthy history of incidents reflecting inherent bias in Meta's processes, from both inside and outside the company, plus a third-party report Meta commissioned after the 2021 Hamas-Israel violence finding an "adverse human rights impact" on Palestinian users' freedom of expression and political participation. The mechanism is design. Meta struggles with Arabic's more than 25 dialects and has been criticized for under-diversified language resources; its black-and-white policies preclude moderating nuanced content, such as material discussing violence without condoning it; and advocacy groups have raised concerns that partnerships with government agencies such as the Israeli Cyber Unit politically influence policy decisions. Calling removals a "bug" localizes harm to a single defect, while the bias here is distributed across language coverage, policy architecture, and escalation channels.


---


# US Economic Data Calendar After 1 October 2023: Jobs, Inflation, and the Fed Meeting

As reported by The Sydney Morning Herald on 1 October 2023, the latest monthly update on the US jobs market was due the following week, with a couple of important reports on inflation coming the week after that. The Federal Reserve's next meeting on interest rates ends on 1 November 2023. The Fed has insisted it will make upcoming rate decisions based on what incoming data say about the economy.

# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.


---


# Some Sports Betting Apps Copy Lines Rather Than Set Their Own

As of Sporting News' line-shopping guide dated 2023-11-06, sportsbook pricing is not uniform across the market. The best sportsbooks employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services, which use computer models and algorithms weighing analytics, statistics, injury and roster news, performance, and matchup data, to set their lines and odds. Other sports betting apps, by contrast, simply copy those lines rather than produce prices of their own.


---


# Sporting News' Line Shopping Guide — Section Map and Cross-Links (2023-11-06)

Sporting News' "Line Shopping in Sports Betting - How to Find the Best Odds" (2023-11-06) is ordered as: how sportsbooks set odds and lines; shopping for the best lines at online sportsbooks, covering the best way to shop lines and the recommended sportsbooks Caesars Sportsbook, BetMGM Sportsbook, DraftKings Sportsbook and FanDuel Sportsbook; how to find the best lines and odds for any bet; line shopping for futures; whether you can get a better line or odds after you've already bet; and value.

Two "See more" cross-links branch outward: "How to bet on sports in the US" follows the odds-setting section, and "NFL futures bets" closes the futures section.

# Manual Line Shopping: Install Multiple Sportsbook Apps and Tap Between Them

Sporting News (2023-11-06) describes the manual route to line shopping as installing several sportsbook apps on one phone and comparing odds by hand. The procedure: download and install more than one sports betting app on your phone, then tap around among the sportsbooks to compare lines and odds for the bets you plan. In each app, pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs to find the odds and line for that bet; moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets can all be shopped this way. Bet when you see an opportunity at better odds or an improved line compared to the competition. The trade-off: the manual task takes longer than an aggregated live odds feed, but you can check more sportsbooks, or the chosen few you feel consistently offer the best lines and odds.

(Note delivered above. My attempt to log completion to the team mission log was rejected because this session is non-interactive — no action needed unless you want that logged.)

# Steps to Open a Funded US Sportsbook Account Before Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures

Precondition (per Sporting News, 2023-10-04): you are in a US jurisdiction where online sportsbooks are legal. The source warns that offshore sportsbooks advertise widely but are illegal and offer no protection against fraud.

1. Visit the online sportsbook, click its "sign up" or "register" button, and fill in the details form.
2. Accept the sportsbook's terms and conditions.
3. Claim the welcome bonus by following the referring site's link to the sportsbook; if a code is needed, it appears on that site. Read the promotion's requirements first, since restrictions may apply.
4. Make an initial deposit through the site's deposit options.

Postcondition: a funded account able to reach the basketball → NBA → futures tab and place a Rookie of the Year wager.


---


# Live Odds Feeds Are the Easiest Line-Shopping Method

Sporting News (2023-11-06) names a live odds feed as the easiest way to shop lines in US sports betting. Such a feed displays the differences in lines and odds for the same bet across many of the top sportsbooks in the country in one place — a "one-stop shop" where comparing prices takes just seconds rather than manually hopping between apps. The feed works for moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets. The trade-off: manual shopping across multiple downloaded sportsbook apps takes longer but can reach more books, or the few that consistently offer the best lines and odds.


---


# DraftKings Runs More Open Betting Markets Than Most Online Sportsbooks

In its guide to line shopping, Sporting News (2023-11-06) reports that DraftKings Sportsbook "has more open betting markets than most online sportsbooks, and the lines and odds are always competitive." The observation appears among four brands Sporting News names as the biggest US online sportsbooks, alongside Caesars, BetMGM, and FanDuel, each described as offering competitive lines in dozens of states.


---


# Offshore Sportsbooks Are Illegal and Fraud-Exposed, So They Cannot Enter the ROTY Odds Comparison

Comparing NBA Rookie of the Year odds across every "online sportsbook" reachable on the open internet is unsound. Sporting News' NBA ROTY guide of 2023-10-04 concedes that offshore sportsbooks "advertise widely on the internet, but they are illegal and offer no protection against fraud and other criminal activities." The obligation it states is to use "only legal online sportsbooks for any type of betting," so the permissible set for ROTY futures is the licensed, regulated books — for that piece, DraftKings and FanDuel — not the cheapest quoted price wherever it appears.


---


# Why the Same Bet Is Priced Differently at Every Sportsbook

The Sporting News guide to line shopping (Nov 6, 2023) argues that price differences between sportsbooks are structural, not accidental, and that this is the reason line shopping "always makes sense."

Each sportsbook sets its own market: some employ oddsmakers and oddsmaking services using computer models and algorithms, while other betting apps simply copy those lines. Some books therefore open at different prices "right from the jump." Then each book responds to its own money. Since a sportsbook's goal is to even out betting on both sides so it can earn the profit built into the odds without worrying which side wins, it moves a line or changes odds when the public bets heavily on one side.

The decisive point is independence: one sportsbook may be forced to move a line because of betting, while another is not. That produces a divergence on the identical bet, and the divergence is the opportunity — a chance to lay less, win more, and improve your chances.


---


# Line Shopping Extends to Every Priced Market, and How to Execute It

Line shopping — checking the posted lines and odds for the same prospective bet at multiple sportsbooks — is not confined to one market. Sporting News' line-shopping guide (2023-11-06) states that you can shop around for moneylines, point spreads, totals bets, prop bets, and more, adding that finding the best line or better odds on any bet "is like finding money." The workflow it prescribes: pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs — on a live odds feed or on several sportsbook apps installed on your phone — to reveal that bet's odds and lines across books, and bet when one shows better odds or an improved line than the competition.


---


# Line Shopping: Checking Odds Across Multiple Sportsbooks

Line shopping is the practice of checking the lines and odds for a prospective bet at multiple online sports betting sites. Sporting News' guide to line shopping, published 6 Nov 2023, defines the process this way and describes its result as "quite often better odds and improved lines." The aim is to book a wager at improved odds or a more favourable line than a single sportsbook would offer, since betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook.


---


# Procedure: Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures (Sporting News, 2023-10-04)

Sporting News (2023-10-04) gives these steps for an NBA Rookie of the Year futures bet, once you hold a funded account at a legal online sportsbook:

1. Open the basketball section of the sportsbook website.
2. Select the NBA.
3. Enter the futures tab, where Rookie of the Year odds and NBA MVP odds are posted.
4. Choose your Rookie of the Year selection — Victor Wembanyama was the early favorite, with Scoot Henderson and Chet Holmgren also cited.
5. Enter the stake amount and finalize the bet slip.

Postcondition: a recorded futures ticket on that player, settling at season's end. Offshore sportsbooks are illegal and offer no fraud protection.

# The Age's Own Caveat: Arrowhead Sighting Does Not Confirm a Romance

The Age concedes, in its own words, that "none of this actually confirms Swift and Kelce are actually dating." # NAB's forecast of an RBA hike to 4.35 per cent in November 2023

In a report covered by The Sydney Morning Herald on 2023-10-01, the National Australia Bank forecasts the Reserve Bank of Australia will lift the cash rate again in November 2023, to 4.35 per cent. The forecast sits against the market expectation cited in the same article that the RBA will keep rates on hold at its October meeting, with interest-rate sensitive sectors such as healthcare and consumer companies among the weakest on that view.

The proposition is falsifiable by the RBA's November 2023 decision: either the cash rate moves to 4.35 per cent, or it does not.


---


# fiat@ftx: the FTX account tracking Alameda Research's debt

"fiat@ftx" was the internal FTX account that tracked how much money Alameda Research owed to FTX. Sam Bankman-Fried testified that he learned of the account in June 2022, while his senior staff were focused on fixing a software bug that had overstated Alameda's debt to FTX by about $8 billion, but said he did not discover what the account was for until October.


---


# Index: "Sam Bankman-Fried didn't ask where the $8 billion went" (The Verge, Oct 31, 2023)

Navigation index for The Verge's October 31, 2023 courtroom report on the June 2022 thread of Sam Bankman-Fried's self-testimony at his fraud trial — seven counts of wire fraud and conspiracy. The decomposition entries attach to these parts of the article: the software bug overestimating Alameda's debt to FTX by about $8 billion, found by Adam Yedidia; Bankman-Fried's discovery of the fiat@ftx account in June 2022 but not its purpose until October; staff telling him "they were busy and I should stop asking questions because it was distracting"; his "no, no, and no" on directions, policies and measures protecting FTX customer money; Yedidia's padel tennis court exchange in June or July, and Judge Lewis Kaplan's intervention; and the Alameda balance sheet of June 13, 2022 listing the borrowed money as "ftx borrows."

# Interest-rate-sensitive sectors: equities priced off the policy rate

An interest-rate-sensitive sector is an equity grouping whose share prices move more than the market when the policy rate changes, because its cash flows are long-dated or its customers depend on credit. Rates rising compress valuations in both cases, since higher yields on government debt make riskier assets less attractive at any price.

In The Sydney Morning Herald's reporting of 1 October 2023, healthcare and consumer companies were named among the weakest sectors on the ASX as markets expected the RBA to keep rates on hold, with National Australia Bank forecasting another hike to 4.35 per cent in November. The 10-year US Treasury yield sat at 4.58 per cent, near its highest since 2007.

Sam Bankman-Fried testified on October 31, 2023 at his fraud trial that correcting the FTX software bug — one that had overestimated the amount Alameda Research owed FTX by about $8 billion — did not remove the ledger gap: even after the fix, Alameda still owed FTX about $8 billion. Brian Jacobsen, chief economist at Annex Wealth Management, identified three factors that in combination depressed the growth of US consumer spending in late 2023: higher energy prices, student loan debt repayments, and "real disposable incomes that have been on a declining trajectory since June". His verdict on the trio was blunt — it "doesn't bode well". He described the slowdown of US consumer spending growth as having "come to a boil during a hot summer, and the temperature is really starting to come down". The article dated this assessment to the 29 September 2023 close, when August data showed US consumer spending growth cooler than expected alongside slightly cooler inflation — a reading positive for inflation but a risk to the spending that had kept the US economy out of recession, since resumed US student-loan repayments diverted dollars away from purchases.

# Wang's testimony places a transfer instruction on the 12 November 2022 drive to the Bahamas Securities Commission, but not inside the meeting

Gary Wang testified that on 12 November 2022, after FTX declared bankruptcy, Sam Bankman-Fried asked him to drive together to the Bahamas Securities Commission for a meeting. Defence lawyer Mark Cohen answered that Alameda was a successful hedge fund and pointed the finger at Ellison, who, he said, did not adequately protect her hedge fund from the inherent risk of the crypto markets. By then she was a former lieutenant turned government cooperator, which is why she was not among the prosecution's first two witnesses.


---


# Adam Yedidia Testified Under Immunity, Having Texted "I Love You Sam" Before Resigning

Adam Yedidia, college roommate of FTX founder Sam Bankman-Fried, testified at Bankman-Fried's fraud trial with immunity because Yedidia was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud. The Verge's report of 2023-10-26 lists Yedidia first among the people who "loved Bankman-Fried most in the world" and are now caught up in the case. Before the break, Yedidia texted Bankman-Fried: "I love you Sam," followed by "I'm not going anywhere." Those messages were sent before Yedidia realized FTX had stolen customer funds — at which point, Yedidia resigned.


---


# The government's model of the Bankman-Fried scheme: Alameda as the conduit

In his opening statement on 2023-10-04, Fortune reported, prosecutor Thane Rehn identified Alameda Research, "a crypto hedge fund he also owned," as "the key to his alleged scheme." Using Caroline Ellison, his on-again off-again girlfriend and Alameda's CEO, as a front, Bankman-Fried had "secret access" to customer money — both cash and crypto.

# Index: Eddy Cue testifies for Apple in US v. Google (The Verge, 2023-09-26)

Index to The Verge's 2023-09-26 report on Eddy Cue testifying in US v. Google, the DOJ antitrust trial over Google's search business, before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC. Sub-topics covered:

- **The ISA**: the Information Services Agreement making Google default search on all Apple devices, in place since 2002 and renegotiated by Cue with Google CEO Sundar Pichai in 2016.
- **The 2016 revenue-share renegotiation**: Apple sought a larger share of Google's search revenue from Apple-directed users; specific numbers were reserved for closed court sessions.
- **The no-alternative defence**: "Certainly there wasn't a valid alternative to Google at the time" — Cue never considered switching providers or building Apple's own search.
- **Setup-choice arguments**: DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw's iPhone setup screenshots (Appearance, location tracking, App Tracking Transparency) against Cue's "Setup is just critical stuff," plus the disputed ease of changing defaults.
- **Privacy versus payments**: Apple's privacy claims set against emails in which Cue railed at Google's privacy policies.


---


# Default search engine: the placement a device maker sells, not a choice a user makes

A default search engine is the query service preselected by a browser or device maker, so a user searches through it without setting anything up. That passivity is the whole commercial point: the preselection, not the ranking, is the scarce asset distributors sell. Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to hold that slot; about $18 billion went to Apple, a partner since 2003. The yield was measurable early. A 2007 Google email showed users who moved their browser homepage to Google did 15% more Google searches, and those who switched away dropped 27%.


---


# DOJ's theory in *US v. Google*: default deals capture search entry points

In *US v. Google*, the antitrust trial over Google's search business heard before Judge Amit Mehta in Washington, DC, the US Department of Justice's case turns on the agreements Google signs to be the default search engine. Reporting on Apple executive Eddy Cue's testimony on 2023-09-26, The Verge states that the Justice Department is focused on the deals Google makes — with Apple but also with Samsung and Mozilla and many others — to ensure it is the default search engine on practically every platform. The Apple contract, the Information Services Agreement (ISA), has been in place since 2002 and pays Apple billions of dollars a year. DOJ lawyer Meagan Bellshaw pressed that Apple offers its users a choice about lots of things, big and small, while the ISA did not allow Apple to offer users a choice of search engines during setup.


---


# Kent Walker's defence of Google's search default status, 2023

Responding to the US trial on Google's blog, in a report published by The Age on 2023-10-22, Kent Walker, Google's president of global affairs, defended the company's position as the default search engine on three grounds. Users, browsers and device makers favoured Google's search product, he said, simply because it was the best in the business. Default status was not determinative, he argued: changing from Google Search to any other search provider was easy, and the company competes with many others on phones and PCs. "People don't use Google because they have to, they use it because they want to," he said. "This lawsuit simply ignores how intensely competitive and dynamic the technology industry is today."


---


# Google's Antitrust Defense: Paying $26.3 Billion for Defaults Is "Just Doing Business"

In the U.S. government's antitrust trial over search, reported by TechCrunch on 2023-10-31, Google's defense rests on a single claim: it is merely doing business. Partners choose Google as the default search engine because it is the best engine, consumers benefit from that quality, and therefore paying for placement does not make its actions illegal. That position has to carry the figure Google search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified to in court on October 28, 2023: Google paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, to be the default. About $18 billion of that went to Apple, whose default deal with Google dates to 2003. CEO Sundar Pichai, who testified at the same trial, said the spending was decided with the consumer in mind, so Google could take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies' devices.


---


# Google Search Antitrust Trial: the 2020 Dominance Claim

The U.S. antitrust trial being heard in October 2023 is the 2020 claim over Google's dominance in the online search market, in which Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified on the Monday covered by TechCrunch's Oct. 31, 2023 report, defending the deals that make Google the default search engine. It is distinct from the separate claim filed in January 2023 by the Department of Justice with eight states, including New York, California and Colorado, which seeks to break Google's monopoly in digital advertising, not search.


---


# Hypothesis: OpenAI's GPT store becomes the default "app store for AI" in 2024

In a TechCrunch piece dated 2023-12-19, the prediction is that OpenAI will push its GPT store hard through 2024 as the default "app store for AI" — the platform people get their AI tools from — following Apple's store model "all the way to the bank," and at the expense of Hugging Face and open-source models. Originally planned for a December launch, the store was delayed by the November C-suite upheaval that left Sam Altman more fully in charge, accelerating OpenAI's shift toward a "ship it" mindset.

Falsification: the store fails to ship, or becomes only a minor distribution channel for AI tools.


---


# OpenAI's December 2023 Axel Springer Deal Covered Both Model Training and Live ChatGPT Answers

In December 2023, OpenAI announced a content agreement with Axel Springer, the Berlin-based news publisher that owns Business Insider and Politico, which OpenAI framed as helping "provide people with new ways to access quality, real-time news content through our AI tools." The agreement had two distinct limbs. First, OpenAI would train its generative AI models on Axel Springer's journalism. Second, it would add recent Axel Springer-published articles to ChatGPT, so the reporting surfaces inside answers rather than only shaping the underlying model. That combination — a licensing deal that pays for a publisher's archive as training data while also giving that publisher's newest work privileged placement in a chatbot's responses — made the deal notable beyond the parties involved, and it was reported in TechCrunch's running ChatGPT timeline alongside other December 2023 OpenAI news, including the reopening of ChatGPT Plus subscriptions on December 13, 2023.


---


# The Singularity as the Trope Orienting Peter Thiel's AI Giving

The singularity is a trope of science fiction describing the moment at which intelligent technology can no longer be controlled by humanity. In 2010, the tech investor Peter Thiel had developed a fascination with it, according to an article in The Age published on 2023-12-09, and that fascination oriented his involvement in artificial intelligence: he was courting founders building "artificial general intelligence," or AGI, a machine that could do anything the brain could do. The same fear ran through the community of "Rationalists" — later called effective altruists — clustered around the internet philosopher and self-taught AI researcher Eliezer Yudkowsky, who argued that machines more intelligent than humans could turn on their creators.

Thiel made his fortune through an early investment in Facebook and his work with Elon Musk in the early days of PayPal.


---


# Gemini: Google's flagship generative AI model family

Gemini is Google's flagship generative AI model, unveiled during the week of 2023-12-07 and meant to power a range of Google products and services. One of those services is Bard, Google's ChatGPT competitor, which began receiving a "lite" version of Gemini called Gemini Pro on 2023-12-06. In blog posts and press materials published alongside that announcement, Google touted Gemini's superior architecture and capabilities, claiming that the model meets or exceeds the performance of other leading generative AI models such as OpenAI's GPT-4.

# Sports Betting Lines Move With Public Action and New Information

According to Sporting News (2023-11-06), betting lines and odds are not static once posted by sportsbooks. They are subject to change based on the betting public's reaction and any additional information that comes to light ahead of the game — sportsbooks will move the line or change the odds if the public bets heavily on one side. Because the betting is rarely the same at every sportsbook, one may be forced to move a line while another is not.


---


# Procedure: Betting NBA Rookie of the Year Futures (Sporting News, 2023-10-04)

Sporting News (2023-10-04) gives these steps for an NBA Rookie of the Year futures bet, once you hold a funded account at a legal online sportsbook:

1. Open the basketball section of the sportsbook website.
2. Select the NBA.
3. Enter the futures tab, where Rookie of the Year odds and NBA MVP odds are posted.
4. Choose your Rookie of the Year selection — Victor Wembanyama was the early favorite, with Scoot Henderson and Chet Holmgren also cited.
5. Enter the stake amount and finalize the bet slip.

Postcondition: a recorded futures ticket on that player, settling at season's end. Offshore sportsbooks are illegal and offer no fraud protection.


---


# Live Odds Feeds Are the Easiest Line-Shopping Method

Sporting News (2023-11-06) names a live odds feed as the easiest way to shop lines in US sports betting. Such a feed displays the differences in lines and odds for the same bet across many of the top sportsbooks in the country in one place — a "one-stop shop" where comparing prices takes just seconds rather than manually hopping between apps. The feed works for moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets. The trade-off: manual shopping across multiple downloaded sportsbook apps takes longer but can reach more books, or the few that consistently offer the best lines and odds.


---


# A Placed Bet Locks In the Odds or Line Posted at Wagering

Sporting News (2023-11-06), in its guide to line shopping, states the rule in one sentence: "When you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted." A ticket is priced at the moment it is accepted. Subsequent moves — a spread shifting because the public bet heavily on one side, or odds changing on fresh injury and roster news — apply to bets still to come, not to the wager already placed, whether those later changes would have helped or hurt.


---


# Line Shopping Extends to Every Priced Market, and How to Execute It

Line shopping — checking the posted lines and odds for the same prospective bet at multiple sportsbooks — is not confined to one market. Sporting News' line-shopping guide (2023-11-06) states that you can shop around for moneylines, point spreads, totals bets, prop bets, and more, adding that finding the best line or better odds on any bet "is like finding money." The workflow it prescribes: pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs — on a live odds feed or on several sportsbook apps installed on your phone — to reveal that bet's odds and lines across books, and bet when one shows better odds or an improved line than the competition.


---


# Once a Bet Is Locked, a Moving Line Can Only Be Answered With New Action

Sporting News (November 6, 2023) states that when you bet, you lock in the odds or line as currently posted. A wager already placed cannot be repriced if the market later moves in your favour, so the available procedure is to respond with fresh action rather than to revisit the original ticket. Because lines shift when the public bets heavily on one side, and because each sportsbook's book differs, a subsequent move usually appears as improved odds or a more favorable line somewhere else. The step is to place additional action there, at that new price.


---


# Stake Sizing for NFL Award Longshot Bets: Keep It Small or Use a Bonus Bet

Sporting News' December 5, 2023 guidance on NFL award longshots (MVP, OPOY, DPOY, Coach of the Year, Comeback Player of the Year) is to keep the stake small, or to use a promotional bonus bet if one is available at the sportsbook. The reasoning is that a player or several players have relatively short odds because they have been the best at their position all season, and there is just as good a reason why longshots carry odds as long as the ones they do. So the longshot's price reflects a genuine, not merely overlooked, case against it.

Sizing down, or staking money the bettor did not deposit, caps the loss on a low-probability outcome while leaving the payout upside intact: if the longshot goes on to win, the bettor collects the full odds on the original price rather than a shorter one obtained by waiting, since with five weeks left in the 2023 regular season a longshot can still become a contender, and the payout falls the longer the bet is deferred.


---


# Sporting News' Line Shopping Guide — Section Map and Cross-Links (2023-11-06)

Sporting News' "Line Shopping in Sports Betting - How to Find the Best Odds" (2023-11-06) is ordered as: how sportsbooks set odds and lines; shopping for the best lines at online sportsbooks, covering the best way to shop lines and the recommended sportsbooks Caesars Sportsbook, BetMGM Sportsbook, DraftKings Sportsbook and FanDuel Sportsbook; how to find the best lines and odds for any bet; line shopping for futures; whether you can get a better line or odds after you've already bet; and value.

Two "See more" cross-links branch outward: "How to bet on sports in the US" follows the odds-setting section, and "NFL futures bets" closes the futures section.


---


# DraftKings and FanDuel: DFS origins shape their sportsbooks

Sporting News on 2023-10-04 listed DraftKings Sportsbook and FanDuel Sportsbook among the best sportsbooks for NBA Rookie of the Year futures, tracing both to daily fantasy sports (DFS) operation before they became legal online sportsbooks. That lineage shows in DraftKings' variety of futures bets, intuitive app and competitive welcome bonus, and in FanDuel's one of the largest followings in the country, one of the best sports betting apps, and quality welcome bonus plus promotions for existing customers.


---


# NBA Futures Markets Span the Whole Season, Including Rookie of the Year

NBA Rookie of the Year is one of the NBA futures markets, so wagering opens before the start of the NBA regular season and continues throughout the year, as with other NBA futures odds. Sporting News described (4 October 2023) these markets as settled on season-long outcomes, with odds posted at online sportsbooks and grouped under the NBA futures tab.


---


# Manual Line Shopping: Install Multiple Sportsbook Apps and Tap Between Them

Sporting News (2023-11-06) describes the manual route to line shopping as installing several sportsbook apps on one phone and comparing odds by hand. The procedure: download and install more than one sports betting app on your phone, then tap around among the sportsbooks to compare lines and odds for the bets you plan. In each app, pick a side, then use the drop-down menus and tabs to find the odds and line for that bet; moneylines, point spreads, totals and prop bets can all be shopped this way. Bet when you see an opportunity at better odds or an improved line compared to the competition. The trade-off: the manual task takes longer than an aggregated live odds feed, but you can check more sportsbooks, or the chosen few you feel consistently offer the best lines and odds.

(Note delivered above. My attempt to log completion to the team mission log was rejected because this session is non-interactive — no action needed unless you want that logged.)

# BetMGM Offers Consistently Competitive Lines Plus Frequent Promos and Odds Boosts

Sporting News, writing on 2023-11-06 in its guide to line shopping, reports that the lines and odds at BetMGM Sportsbook are consistently competitive. The publication adds that sports betting promos and odds boosts abound at BetMGM, so a bettor will find a better price on many bets there. Sporting News names BetMGM among the top online sportsbooks for line shopping.

# The Epic v. Google hypothesis: paid exclusion, not consumer preference, kept rival app stores off Android

Testable proposition from the Epic v. Google trial record, stated by Epic CEO Tim Sweeney in his interview with The Verge published 2023-12-12: rival Android app stores failed to reach devices because Google paid for that outcome — paying "other developers off to convince them not to launch their own stores" and "paying carriers and OEMs secretly not to carry competing stores." Sweeney says he suspected these practices since 2018, early enough that critics called him a conspiracy theorist, and says the testimony confirmed them; when Epic tried to bundle Fortnite with manufacturers like OnePlus and carriers of all sorts, they told him Google had already done a secret deal with them. Falsified if carriers, OEMs or developers declined competition for reasons documented independently of Google payments.


---


# Index: The Verge's "Epic v. Google, explained" (Sean Hollister, 2023-11-05)

Navigation for "Epic v. Google, explained," Sean Hollister's reader-facing explainer at The Verge, published 2023-11-05 ahead of the trial that opened November 6th — "a mere 1,180 days after Epic originally sued"; Hollister appended a December 15th, 2023 update marking it superseded. Notes grouped by the question each answers:

- **Background — the August 13th, 2020 trigger**: Epic's hotfix letting Fortnite V-Bucks be bought at a discount outside app store fees, Apple and Google pulling Fortnite, Epic's two lawsuits and the "Llamacorn" attack ad.
- **Competing legal claims**: Epic's monopoly and Play-payments-tying allegations versus Google's sideloaded-app-safety and free-app-store defenses.
- **Market definition**: "Android app distribution" and "Android in-app payment processing" versus phones and app stores generally.
- **Apple-case precedent**: the September 2021 ruling mostly in Apple's favor, with the Supreme Court possibly weighing in.


---


# Google's rebuttal to Epic: open Android and you hurt its users and its competitiveness

Opposing the remedy Epic Games sought at the trial that began November 6th, 2023 — breaking up Google's control of Android app distribution and in-app payment processing so developers stop paying the "Google tax" — Google argued, as reported by The Verge on November 5, 2023, that a win for Epic would rebound against Android itself. In Google's telling, it could make Android phones less safe by dismantling basic protections against sideloaded apps. It would also damage Android's ability to compete with the iPhone, because it (arguably) can't run a competitive app store by giving it away for free. The safety and competitiveness predictions are Google's own claims about a hypothetical outcome, not established findings, and The Verge flags them as such with "according to Google, anyhow."


---


# TechCrunch's Guide to Following Its SBF Trial Coverage

TechCrunch's running hub for the Sam Bankman-Fried trial, dated 2023-10-06, gathers the outlet's coverage in one place. Jacquelyn Melinek, TechCrunch's crypto expert, has reported on the ground since the trial began with jury selection on October 3 — access being limited because no devices are allowed and reports are physically put together inside the courtroom or sent to overflow rooms. The hub links Melinek's breakdown of how FTX went from the third-largest crypto exchange, valued at a peak of $32 billion, to bankruptcy. It also points to TechCrunch+ analysis of what to expect from both the prosecution's and the defense's arguments and the takeaways from the opening arguments, the Chain Reaction newsletter (Thursdays at 12 p.m. PT), and the Chain Reaction podcast, which hits listeners' feeds every Thursday.


---


# AI Tool Customer Withdrawal Predicted for 2024 as Marketing Claims Face Review

In an article published 2023-12-19 on TechCrunch, the hypothesis is advanced that a considerable customer withdrawal from AI tools will occur during 2024. The reasoning is that marketing claims made for machine learning systems—often adopted by companies merely to avoid falling behind—will face their quarterly and yearly reviews, and will very likely be found wanting. The measurable benefits will fail to justify the costs and risks involved. On the far end of this spectrum, lawsuits and regulatory action against AI service providers that cannot back up their claims are anticipated as a consequence of the same dynamic.


---


# Google's User Choice Billing Counter to Epic's Payment-Processing Market Claim

Facing Epic Games' antitrust trial against Google that began November 6, 2023, Google answers Epic's claim of a foreclosed market for payment-processing solutions inside Android apps by pointing to its own alternative-billing program, User Choice Billing — and to Epic's refusal to use it. Introduced in November 2022 and still in pilot testing at trial time, User Choice Billing is open to all developers selling apps in the 35 markets where it is available, including the U.S., and cuts the standard commission — otherwise 15% to 30% under Google Play's first-party billing requirement — by 4% for companies that use their own payment processing. Spotify and Bumble were the initial testers, and Match, having settled with Google the week before the trial started, will also take advantage of the option. In Google's framing, developers who want to process payments themselves are invited to do so at a lower rate; Epic simply declined the offer.


---


# Week in Review (WiR): TechCrunch's Weekly Tech News Digest

Week in Review, abbreviated WiR, is TechCrunch's weekly email digest of the past week in tech news. TechCrunch describes it as its column that highlights the major stories over the past few days, and pitches it as "a darn useful resource for folks on the go." The newsletter arrives in subscribers' inboxes every Saturday, and readers not yet subscribed are invited to sign up through a link in the email. The edition dated 2023-10-07, for example, gathered Sam Altman backing the teen founders' AI startup Induced AI, Google's hardware event and the Pixel 8, and TikTok's $4.99 ad-free tier test.


---


# Epic's OEM evidence: the cancelled OnePlus deal and the Google–Samsung agreement

Epic Games' antitrust case against Google, tried from November 6, 2023, leads with an agreement theory, because Android allows sideloading and Epic cannot claim, as it did against Apple, that no other way exists to load apps. Two episodes carry that theory. Epic had an agreement with the device maker OnePlus to make Epic games available on OnePlus devices through the Epic Games app, and OnePlus cancelled the deal over concerns that the arrangement would have it bypassing the Google Play Store. The trial will also examine a deal between Google and Samsung that Epic says was designed to prevent the Galaxy Store from becoming a competitive threat and to require Google Play Billing on apps distributed by Samsung. Epic places both inside the "Anti-Fragmentation Agreements" (AFAs) it cites, which prevent Android OEMs from modifying Android to allow frictionless downloading of apps outside Google Play.


---


# 2024 ROI Reviews Will Find Hyped Machine-Learning Purchases Wanting

Hypothesis from TechCrunch's "8 predictions for AI in 2024" (published 2023-12-19): the hype built up in 2023 will be very hard for companies to follow through on. Machine-learning systems that enterprises adopted specifically in order to not fall behind carry vendor marketing claims, and those claims will face their quarterly and yearly reviews during 2024 — where, the authors expect, they will very likely be found wanting. The mechanism is reassessment, not a sudden drop in capability.

Falsified if enterprise reassessments broadly validate the vendors' 2023 claims and the purchased ML features pass their quarterly and yearly ROI reviews.


---


# OpenAI's product-company turn: Altman's post-November 2023 authority displaces board caution with appetite for markets

TechCrunch's 2023-12-19 predictions essay argues that OpenAI will run as a product company in 2024 because the leadership shake-up in November 2023 left Sam Altman more fully in charge, displacing the previous board. The consequence trickles down at every level of the company as a "ship it" mindset, exemplified by the GPT store — the "app store for AI" originally planned for launch in December but delayed due to the C-suite fracas — which OpenAI will push hard as the place to get AI toys and tools, never mind Hugging Face or any open source models. The mechanism is a swap of governing temperament: the caution and academic reserve that the previous board exerted gives way, in TechCrunch's phrasing, to an unseemly lust for markets and customers.

# Manchester United and Newcastle United Out of Europe After Finishing Bottom of Their 2023/24 Champions League Groups

Manchester United and Newcastle United will play no further part in European competition in 2023/24, having been eliminated by finishing bottom of their UEFA Champions League groups, Sporting News reported on 12 December 2023. # Bayern's 1-0 at Old Trafford on 12 December 2023 ended Manchester United's European season

Manchester United 0-1 Bayern Munich at Old Trafford on 12 December 2023, the final matchweek of the 2023/24 UEFA Champions League Group A: Kingsley Coman scored the only goal for Thomas Tuchel's side, in what the Sporting News described as "a limp display" from the hosts. # Navigating Sporting News' Champions League group-stage permutations review (12 December 2023)

Sporting News' 12 December 2023 article "Champions League permutations, scenarios: What teams need to qualify from groups for 2023/24 Round of 16 stage" is organised Group A through Group D onward, each section pairing a standings table (GP, W, D, L, GD, P, with qualifiers marked "(Q)") with prose on the decisive fixtures and what each club needed in the final matchweek of the 2023/24 UEFA Champions League group stage.
